The little brown hen was there clucking; " Cut, cut," she said, quick as a wink ; %hen "Cut, cut," again, only slower, And then she would atop short and think. And then she would say it all over, She did look se Mad and so vek'd, For, mama, do you know, she'd forgotten The word that she ought to clack next. . So I slid," Ca-claw-cut, ca-claw-cut," ; As loud and as strong as I could, And she look'd round at me very thankful, . I tell you it made her feel good. Then she fiapped and said," Cut-cut-ca-davr-cut," She ceweinbered just how it went then, ' t r i But it's well I ran into the garden, She might never have cluck'd right:again. ,

THE SONG OF THE CAMP. ca• • "Give us a song!" the soldiers cried, The outer trenches guarding, sa • When the heated guns of the camps allied • . Grew weary of bombarding. The dark Redan, in silent scoff, Lay grim and threatening under, And the tawny mound of Malakoff; No longer belched its thunder. There was a pause. The Guardsman said, • "We storm the forts to-morrow; ▪ Sing while we may; another day Will bring enough of sorrow:' They lay alons; the battery's side, Below the wnoking cannon— Brave hearts from Severn, and from Clyde, And froni the banks of Shannon. They sang of love, and not of fame; Forgot was Britain's glory ; Each heart recalled a different name, But all sang "Annie Laurie." Voice after voice caught up the song, , Until its tender. passion Rose like an anth-m, rich and strong— Their battle-eve confession. Dear girl, her name he dared not speak; Yet, as the song grew louder, Something upon the soldier's shack Washed off the stains of powder. Beyond the darkening ocean burned 7.. The bloody sunset's embers, While the Crimean valleys learned flow English love remembers. An& once again a fire of hell Rained on the Russian quarters, With scream of shot, and burst a shell, And bellowing of the mortars. Sweet Irish Norah's eyes are dim For a singer dumb and gory, And English Mary mourns for him Who sang of "Annie Laurie." Oh, soldiers! to your honoured rest Your truth and valour bearing— " The bravest are the tenderest, The loving are the daring !" BAYARD TAYLOR.

Towards the end of the performance a peasant walked up to the lion tamer and said—" Sir, I have come to earn the £1.00." General horror. The lion tamer replied with a derisive sneer, "So, you want ttgo into the lion's cage?" "Aye, sure," said the peasant. "Come on, then! There, I will open the trap-door for you, and you can step in." "Well, yes," answered the honest countryman, turning to the audience with a broad grin on his face, "I - am going in, but the beast will have to come out first. You know the paper only says—anyone going into the cage shall have £lOO. A Western settler who supposed that he had musical tastes went to the nearest township and purchased a music stag, taking it home with him in his trap. In the course el few days, however, he brought it back and depended restitution of the money paid, as the stool was no gdod—no good at all. The seller examined it, and said that it was in perfect order, and the screw all right, and therefore that it should not be thrown back on his hands. "Well," said the settler, " I took it home careful, as you could see for your- self ; and I gave it a turn, and the missns she gave it a turn, and every one of the children gave it a turn, and never a lane could one and all of us screw out of it. It's no more a music stool than the four-legged washing stool the missus seta her tub on!" Mosnerasso IN CLAY.—Modelling in clay is decidedly al profitable branch of women's work; and as so few excel in 'modelling, compared with the large number of those who paint on china, crystoleum, &a., it is a field in which there is at present no excessive competition. The work can easily be done at home, provided there is a room which can be used as a studio; and the outlay is very small, the tools be- ing so few in number. A three-legged stool for modelling figures, or an easel for flowers and fruit, is necessary. In the former case the artist stands, in the latter a high stool can be used. The clay is not expensive but it should be bought properly prepared, and must be kept damp, in a cool place, and in a box free from air.—Cassell's Family Maga- zine. AFTER Ovwmas.—During the late war in the States t, Captain in a certain regiment stationed near Alexandriatj Virginia, despatched a private soldier to the town one day, for some fresh oysters, with the parting injunction, Don't' come back witliont them!" Off went the man, and no more was seen of him for several days. The indignant and disappointed Captain reported him a deserter, and gave him up as a "lost child." Bat lo! after a lapse of nine days, the Captain beheld his reported deserter, Bally, coming into camp, leading in a train of four-horse waggons loaded with oysters. Approaching and respectfully saluting the amazed and speechless officer, Baily laconically "reported : " "Here are your oysters, Captain Baker; couldn't find a• in Alexandria. so I chartered a schooner and made a voyage to Pc Mess Monroe and Norfolk for them. There's about two hundred bushels—where do you want 'em, sir?" Baily, it seems, did really make the trip, hired his men, and Bold ' oysters enough in Georgetown, before "reporting," to pay all expenses and leave him a profit of BM. The two hun- dred bushels were divided among the regiment, and Bally returned to his duty as if nothing unusual had transpired.— Harper's Monthly. A Imeruann's DILEMMA.—The Rev. George Trask, of Massachusetts, was noted throughout the State as an able unil eloquent lecturer against tobacco and all intoxicating drinks. At one time he had addressed a large and attentive audience, and, among other things, said in his lecture that no man habitually using tobacco and, whiskey could expect to live more than five or six years after beginning to use them. And so earnest and positive was he in his address, and so attentive his audience, that at its close he confidently .Shalleaged any reply, and invited any questions on the sub- ref. After a moment's silence a man rose and said: "I like what you have said, Mr. Trask, but I would like to ask a question. One of my neighbours is an old man, some seventy-five years obl, and he has used both tobacco and whiskey—all he could get __ever since he was thirty years old, that is, for some forty-five years. How do you recon- cile that with what you said, that amen using both tobacco and whiskey couldn't live more than five or six years?" Mr. Trask was somewhat startled, and to gain thnefor col- lecting his thoughts, began wilting some questions. "How btu aa a-old did you say the man was?" "Seventy-five years:, And he has been using both tobacco and whiskey ever liTeThan since he was thirty?" "Yes, using them constantly and freely." "What kind of a man is he? Does he seem to ! take much interest in heinees, or in anything that's going on?" "No, I don't think he does." "Does he seem to love „atria asybody ?" "Well, no." "Does he seem to hate any- .l.lß raa, body ?" "No, I don't think he does; he seems rather in. different to everything." "Well," said Mr.. Track, who by ti! etee i this time had gathered up his wits, "your old nut has evi- dently been dead for some forty years. mad the only mistake you've made is that you did not burY ,him."—Harper's ea a-au, 21°ThiAlli•

SCIENTIFIC NOTES. The appearance of a new weekly science , Yatura in Italy is announced. rt is under the, of Professor Paoloplantegazza, and includ+m the leading Italian men, of science. The first practical discoverer of the electric v gaph kas been found in the person of a medical gentle= , now resid- ing at Maltnesbury (Atistralia)—Dr. Davy by name. A 'lnib-counnittee has been appointed by the Victorian Royal Society to inquire into the matter. In the American Naturalist for the current month, Dr. S. V. Clavenger in an article entitled "The Disadvantages of the Upright 'Position," refers to the arrangement of the , valves of the circulatory system as affording proofs of the I evolution of man f coin the lower animals. I In the Revue Scientifique M. Gustave d'Eichthal pleads for the adoption of Greek as the universal language of science. He dwells upon the richness of the idiom, the flexibility of the language, and the readiness with, which it lends itself to the formation of new terms. It has been resolved by the committee of the Central Meteorological Society of Switzerland, to establish a num- ber of observatories throughout the country for the better study of atmospheric disturbances. Special attention will be devoted to hailstorms, an unduly neglected branch of I observation hitherto. Hail is a very frequent phenomenon in Switzerland—much more so than in England—and we may confidently hope that a better knowledge of this little understood rneteer will result. The form of electric lamp known as the Lampe-Soleil his given so much satisfaction at the South Kensington Museum (where it has been on trial for the past six months) that a two year's contract has been entered into, the light being supplied at the same cost as gas. The proprietors of the Egyptian Hall are also going to adopt the system. This lamp has been before the public for several years, but has neVefattracted much attention. Arte e Storia describes the recently-diacovered Roman I mosaic at Nimes as the beat yet found after those of the , Villa Borghese and the Vatican. It is in good preservation, and represents a Roman emperor on his throne and the half I nude figure of a woman stooping to receive the presents of some soldiers, while some hunters lead a lion and a wild boar. The corners and border of the mosaic are very fine, representing objects of the chase, partridges, snakes, horses, wild cats, leopards, deer, &a. The Municipal Council has voted £l2O for the work of transporting the mosaic to the Museum, and entrusted the work to M. Mora. The list of the English Committee of the Amsterdam In- ternational Agricultural Exhibition has been published. The exhibition is to open on the 25th August, and will close on the 6th of the following month. On the committee are the Duke of Bedford, Lord Moreton, Lord Walsingham, Mr. Jenkins, Dr. Voelcker, and Walter Gilbey, ,who represent the Royal Agricultural Society; also Sir Brandreth Gibbs and Professors Sheldon, Wrightson, and Carroll. Amongst members of Parliament are Messrs. Howard, Pell, and Bar- clay. Messrs. Barham, Roumieu, Tisdell, and Moreton re- present the Dairy Farmers' Association, and the press finds its representatives in Messrs. James Macdonald, J. C. More- ton, John Coleman, W. E. E. Bear, and James Long. Mr. Menzies will represent the Highland Society. WESTMORLAND SlLEEP.—Westmorland . mountain sheep have in them part Scotch, Herdwick, and Rough, not all Herdwick. I should say there are one-third Rough sheep, or, as they are called in Westmorland, Blaekfaced sheep, the rest part-bred Scotch and Herdwick. They are shaped as other sheep Possessing horns, both ewes and rams. Good bred Herdwicks do not possess horns, excepting the rams, I although I have seen and bought wethers with horns, but I can at any time see more without home than with. In speaking of price, 5z0.,..k, may safely say that very few Herdwicks—the other breeds are worth more-were bought I in the back for 'feeding Off under 30s. and up to 405., so 1 " R.'s" butcher price is a littlE out of it. I may here say that a number of sheep will be, and have been, sold for less 1 money to the butcher than they actually cost in the back I end. I never heard of Herdwicks weighing 251bs. per qr., I although I have feed Rough sheep up to 301b5. per quarter. I With regard to the origin of the Westmorland Blackfaced 1 mountain sheep, I once heard a great breeder say that they were bred from Scotch ewes put to a goat, to give them bone and hardiness, then followed again with Scotch rams. How far this statement is true I will leave the readers to judge.' I certainly have seen sheep that resemble a goat very much in features, shape, and colour of wool.—" Amicas" in Agri.- cultural Gazette. The modest discoverer thus speaks of himself: "Ye talk about your • Herschel' or your • Livingstone' in style In finding out • Uranus' or the sources of the Nile; 'Twee with the eye or telescope their laurels they have won. With mental view I found the earth went nevtrzmnd the sun." An astronomer who can afford to despise Herschel because he only made his discoveries by means of the telescope, in- ' stead of evolving them from his inner consciousness, is alto- gether above criticism. Rums IN MEXIC`O.—Some ancient rains of a very inter- esting character have lately been found at Sonora, in Mexico. There is a pyramid of vast size with a winding roadway to the top. The height of this pyramid is given as 750 feet, which must surely be a mistake, as the famous one of Cheops, in Egypt, is only 448 feet in height. A short distance from the pyramid is a small mountain, in the rocky sides of which are hewn hundreds upon hundreds of rooms, some measuring 5 feet by 10 feet, and others 16 to 18 feet square. The rooms are 8 feet high, have no win- dows, being cat out of solid rock, and are all entered from the top. The walls are covered with hieroglyphics, and stone implements of every sort are scattered about. The discovery has given rise to much speculation. In southern ISonora, at the present time, there is a race of Indians called the Mayos, who are highly intelligent, and it is supposed by some that the ancestors of this race may at a remote period have occupied the rock-hewn city. The Mayos are described as a people with fair skin, light hair, and blue eyes. They are moral, industrious, and frugal, have a written language, and (it is said) know something of ma- thematics.—Seience Monthly. PUMPING BY "Sucriorr." A correspondent recently writing to the American Machinist says :—" In all theory, and in all my practice, I have been led to believe that it was impossible to raise water by suction over 28ft. or 30ft., and that it was not good practice to pump it over 25ft. But my attention was called to the fact, that at a certain establish- ment in this city they were pumping water by suction 27ft., having considerable curiosity„ I called to investigate. The engineer stated as a fact that they. were pumping water by suction 37ft., that ii, from the Buda& of the water to the suction valve of the pump, 37ft., with but slight varia- tions. About 2511. from the bottom end of the suction pipe is a tee with nipple and elbow. From this elbow, a stand pipe of the same diameter as the suction pipe extends to the same height and is`covered with a cap. There is a check valve at the bottom end of the suction pipe. The ex- planation is :—Fill both pipes with water, then screw the cap airtight on the top of what I should call the stand pipe, and the action of the pump will suck the water out of the tend pipe and form a vacuum in it that will sustain the water in the suction pipe, so that the pump will lift the water the 37ft without any trouble." BOILER EXPLOSlONS.—Notwithstanding the Vigilant in- quiry which is now always made into the cans* of boiler explosions, in many cases the occasion Af such citastrophes is still wrapped in mystery. M. Vignei has recently called attention to a very old experiment, made by Problponny, of Ghent, in 1846, which may throw some Belt On the matter. In this experiment, ordinary water is placed in a clean glass tube, open at one end, and boiled long enough to drive away not only the air above the surface of the water, but all the air dissolved in the water. Then when the upper part of the tube is full of pure steam, the mouth is hermetically sealed and the tube is left to cool. When cool,- it is about half full of water, above which is vapour of water at a very low pressure. The tube being thus prepared, its lower end is plunged into a bath of glycerine or oil, which is gradually heated. No ebulition is visible in the tube when the tem- perature reaches 234 deg. F. At 240 deg. F., however, the colunA of water bursts, as it were, in two, with a sudden explosion, and part of it is flung against the sealed end with such force as often to break it open. Now in industrial works, it happens that a boiler, having been filled with water, works for three or four hours without receiving a furthur supply. It may then be cooled down, and the next time it is wanted it may very probably be fired up again without starting the feed pump, the water level being judged suffi- ciently high; but the water in such a boiler will be in the same condition as that in the test tubs; that is, it will be deprived of all air, and consist of water below and vapour above, the latter, however, being probably at a much higher pressure than that of the water in the tube. The water has no free surface in its interior due to the presence of bubbles of air, from which evaporation can take place. Conse- quently, as in the, test tube, there will be delay in vaporising —at least, until the expansion becomes great enough to overcome the pressure of the saperincumbent vapour, and a sudden flashing into steam, which will be of the nature of an explosion, and may easily overcome the resistance of the - 'boiler.—Science Monthly. stool I

Of course all such figures depend upon the food the animal re- ceives. It must not be forgotten that the urine of animals, I excepting perhaps swine, is extremely rich in nitrogen, and contains much more than is found in a similar quantity of the solid droppings of the beast. In addition to this , quality, however, the nitrogen is worth as much as that I found In the ammonia salts, and is far more valuable than that found in solid matter. It is of great value to the soil, and is not immediately taken up and exhausted. A writer in the Rural New Yorker says that the nitrogen found in Bpoolbs. of cow urine, if purchased in an available condi- tion, would cost 375. As one of the above-named professors 1 states, the urine of the cow is valued by the Belgian farmers at 405., and, indeed, they are actually willing to pay this NM for It. The farmer is careful to save every atom of ordinary dung, and yet if science is to be believed the urine is worth four times as much—first, because it contains twice as much nitrogen; and, secondly, because it is available at i once. It s true that many of our farmers whose education has been more advanced are looking at this matter and taking a step in the right direction; but it is not alto- gether the fact that mandke tanks are the best receptacles for the liquid. A NATURALIST'S PETS.—There was perhaps not a house- hold in the kingdom like that of the late Mr. Frank Buck- land, the celebrated naturalist. Of course there is Mr. Cross's, in Oldhall-street, Liverpool, who deals in wild and tame beasts of all kinds, but that is somewhat like a me- nagerie, whereas Mr. Buckland lived and studied among his pets, which included a collection of monkeys, rats, hares, and we know not what. It was his delight to observe the habits and tricks of these animals, and in his "Notes and Jottings from Animal Life" he evidently has had infinite pleasure in doing this. Ile had four monkeys—Little Jerk, Tiny, Oarroty Jane, and Jenny. His studio, it appears, was called the monkey room by the servants, and there lived ba- it also Judy the marmoset, Joe the tame hare, Jemmy the anricat, the laughing jackass, and the old gray parrot. Little Jack was the life of the miscellaneous party, for he was always in mischief. "Like all little people," we are told, "he has a good idea of his own consequence, and he thinks that I, his master, am terribly afraid of him, for he makes the most hideous faces at me, and chatters in such a manner, that one would think he was at least a big gorilla; perhaps he is, in his own estimation. He can't bear being laughed at, and if I laugh at him he gets perfectly savage." Jenny was a monkey bought to keep Tiny company when another monkey, called the Old Hag, died. Her mind, it seems, was entirely given to eating, drinking, and grumbling. Carrotty Jane went upon three legs, and though thin as a skeleton was always eating. " When I was working at the Scotch herring report I used to receive sprats," wrote Mr. Buckland, "and young herrings nearly every morning. These I used to broil for luncheon, and the monkeys used to steal them off the gridiron. The monkeys, all but Little Jack, would also drink beer; when Tiny wanted beer she crossed her hands in a devotional attitude, and looked in a supplicating manner first at the glass and then at me." Must monkeys have cheek pouches, and in feeding they cram these with food which they eat at leisure.

of Liberalism, he could look upone a retrospect of the past with a gratification that few of those present could realise. From the programme that was before 'him he observed that they were to coneider the question of "Itedistrilmtion of Seats." If he . might be permitted to say so, there was another question coming before the redistribution of seats which would occupy a great deal of attention, and he would refer to it a moment or two, viz., the great franchise question. (Applause.) The franchise he understood to be one of those questions, or that great clues- , non which :should equalise the representation in the eounties andhorogghs and place them on the same level. , Lie hoped that that would be done in its entirety, and that there would be no exceptions. That bill, which they hoped' . to have before tatsena within .4 few days, would indicate the with on the part of the Government that no man should be greater or lest than another, and that no man Should be ' before or after another, but that so tar as the electoral fran- ,ohise was concerned each should 'tend on the same footing. (Applause.) However, he had great respect for a venerable friend of theirs on the franchise question, and that was the 40s. freeholder. s Lsughter.) He . had great respect for him, teem:in the 40s. freeholder had done a good deal for the people of this country, bat, he thought his occupation had gone. (Hear, bear, and laughter.) He believed him- self that the franchise of this country should be very simple indeed—an occupation franchise applyaig ao the peer Its well as the peasant, placing the poorest mottled, the saute equality as the rich man, giving no man but one vote, no Matter how: much property he: possessed. (Hear, hear.) He had a very vivid recollection of the Reform Bill of 1832, and what took, place. after that.. There wail .such an upheaving in the country that they had little idea of, none but a Liberal candidate had the slightest possible chance of election. Immediately following a that Reform. Bill within a year oa, the . new House Of Parliainent he saw th'e grandest thing tnatethe world had ever seen—the bill for the emancipation of the slave trade throughout the British dominion. (Ap- plause.) Then came in rapid succession the great and grand measure of a new Municipal Act, which gave govern- ing powers to towns like Manchester, Leeds, Glasgow, Birininghana, Warrington, and other towns which had no government of its own before. Previously, everybody con- stituted themselves self-governors. They scarcely realised how much they owed to the Municipal Reform Bill. (Ap- plause.) The next was a rectification of the poor law system, previous to which the condition of poverty of the poor had been something beyond description Since then, the poor had been well cared for and housed, and Einem:o4 treated ; and that because the law compelled the Guardiapaa to do it, or if teey did not they would be removed from. their office very soon. A great many other measures came into operation within a few years of that, and the climax of that grand period appeared to him to be the repeal of the corn laws. (Applause.) If they had not had that Reform Bill of 1832, with the redistribution Of seats, he, would tell them that they would have had none of this. The repeal' of the paper tax, the navigation laws, and ' other matters were the outcome of that Reform Bill. About the year 1842 he witnessed the introduction of Mr. Fergus O'Connor's grand charter, and despised as it was that day it was worthy of the consideration of the greatest statesman at the present moment. The charter consisted of five points, the first being universal suffrage, the second annual Parliaments, the third voting by ballot, the fourth no property qualification, and the fifth paid members of Parliament. Those were the five points comprised in the petition to the House of Commons, and signed by two or three millions of people who were only a little in advanoe of their time, but who were looked upon as wild enthusiasts not to be considered for a moment. But he had seen since that time the greatest Conservative minister of the present day, the father of the present Lord Derby proposing that one of the five points of that charter should become the law of the land, and he carried it. That was to do away with the property qualification for Members of Parliament. He had seen another Conservative minister, the successor to tha Early of Derby, who caina as near to Mr. Fergus O'Connor that they might have shake* hands and said they were exceedingly glad to see each other, but he did not go quite to the extent of household ,auffrage, although he enacted that famous measure of 1860 which gave household qualification to boroughs, and which they were just now legoing to add to the ,counties. (Applause.) Those(' two points of the charter ' were enacted by Conservative ministers, and then again another more important an: equally important point of the coarter was enacted by the Government waich followed that of the late Lord Beaconsfield—Mr. Gladstone's Govern- ment—(applause)—for they 'enacted that votes should be taken by ballot, and that they had to-day. (Applause.) So they observed that three lout of the five points had become the law of the land with Very trifling exception. Then, too, he witnessed Lord Palmeratties Reforqa Bill, but he never intended to carry it although he brought it in. Lord Pal- merston had a good deal to do with "shams "—(laughter) —and that Reform Bill was one of the greatest "shams" that he ever brought under the notice of the people of this country. Lord Russell's Bill appeared to his (the chair- man's) mind to be a satisfactory one, and would have proved such but their friends the Tories, the enemies of all pro- gress, could not admit that Bill in 1866, and through the instrumentality of a cave the Bill of Lord Russell's was de- feated. What, he asked, was the result of that? The Ministry went out of office, but the question of reform had laid such a hold on the minds of the people that no matter what Ministry came into office they were ,determined to carry the measure, and so it was on the question which would occupy ,Parliament ins few, days,. even if the Go- vernment were defeated the voice of the people would de- mand having that measure carried. (Applause. Having spoirlen ,of the Bill of 1867, he said they were coming now to anbther Franchise Bill, and he had not the least doubt that in the hands of the present Govern- ment it would be of such a character as they had a perfect right to expect from men who thought honestly of the sub- ject at the present time. (Applause.) Coming to the matter before them, that of the redistribution of seats there, he confessed he was very much at fault as to his acquaint- i ance with the terms of it. The question appeared to him beset with enormous difficulties, and how those difficulties were going to be settled he could not quite tell but he felt assured that in the hands of the Ministry now in power, it did not matter what the difficulties might be, their inten- tion being honest and straightforward, that no man should gain at the expense of another man, they would make such a re-arrangement of seats as should be to the general benefit of the whole community. (Applause.) How it would be brought about he could not tell, and it could only be left to the very wisest people to say what the right thing should be. They were determined that England should be governed by Englishmen for Englishmen and nothing else. (Applause.) The Lacaunen commenced his address by observing that his subject, "The redistribution of seats," formed part of the great question of Parliamentary reform. The matter of the franchise, of course, took precedence. The contention of the Conservatives that the two parts should be joined and brought into one Bill was not an honest and sincere de- sire to advance the question of reform, but a desire to harass and hamper the Government. He thought they could not help considering that they could have had an extension of the household suffrage, and left out the county. It seemed monstrous that residents in the county or outside the borough should be deprived of the right of voting in the election of members of Parliament. The anomaly was seen in the fact that the same class of men were not allowed equal rights. For instance, in Wigan they had a large number of miners who were privileged to go to the voting booth, whilst at Tyldesley, a few miles off, the same class of men were not allowed the right to vote. There was no argumeat, he contended, which could favour such an anomaly as this, and the wonder was that the present state of affairs should have been continued so long. The great value of the extension of the suffrage to the counties was that it would bring in a class of men who, with rare excep- tions, had not held a vote before, and that was the agricul- tural labourers. (Hear, hear.) They might pride them- , selvee on their manufactures, but there was no doubt that agriculture was the largest and most important industry they had, and it seemed strange and unjust that the men who were the main support of that industry should be deprived as a body of any right to 'elect members of Parliament. (Applause.) They could do without the landlords of the country if they came to a push—(langleter)—and without their grooms, gamekeepers, rat catchers, and suadry other officials, and they could even do without the farmers them- selves ; but without the agricultural labourers that great industry would cease and the land would become nheultiva- -1 ted. They had a right to vote, and it was a great injusticel that they should have been deprived of it so long. (Ap- plause.) Although the franchise question took precedence of that of redistribution of seats, it was by no means the most important part of that question. The redistribution of seats was far away more important than the other. In consider- log the matter it was well to bear in mind what the last reform bill did, and giving the Conservatives all the credit they laid claim to with respect to that, he would say it was not a , good bita bec,aurse it did oot deal honestly and thoroughly with the question Of redistribution. If they com- pared it with the bill of 1832 they would find that the first measure was far greater aad much more honest. What did the Reform Bill of 1832 do? It laid its hands on no less than 67 rotten boroughs, and totally Swept them away. Each of these boroughs had returned two members to Parliament though everyone had a less population than 2,000. Besides this, it partially disfran- chised 30 boroughs having each less than 4,000 of a popu- lation. By this means 144 seats were gained, which were distributed amongst the counties, 'And the larger constitnences. Sixty-five mem- bers were given to the Engl ieh and Welsh counties, and 44 new borou hs.,, itweree 6C,lrveeclate,dto, hlraevlianngdaaltnode ?ill b ion of seats effected by 0,, t 11 te r,,6,6seinzanb der!. The 'ue i v1:14, eign ~.. , • •

tb- Reform Act 1867 was much less satiefactory than the eceding one. It totally disfranchised only boroughs and -se were for bribery—viz: Lancaster Totnes, and Great rmouth, each of which had two seats, and Reigate, which had ,one seat, making seven alto- Ober. Not a single constituency was totally disfranchised on account of the smallness of. its population, although there were a large number of towns of less than 10.000. inhabitants. Instead of-this 38 boroughs of less than 10,000 inhabitants were deprived of one member. This gave 45 rats to be disposed of elsewhere, 13 of which gere given to the counties, 14 to 12 new constituencies, and the remainder went to increase the representation of the large.towns.. Four of these—Manchester, Leeds, Birming- ham, And Liverpool.had the number of their members in- caeased to three, 'though the benefit they derived from this Was lessened by their being put under the minority, clause. The effect- of this arrangement to-day Was that while they wouldilf the same rule which applies to other towns were applied fo them, return 9 Liberals and 3 Conservatives; they now return 7 Liberals and 5 Conservatives. Mr. Bright, a few yeard before that Bill was passed, drew, up a scheme for reform Which, how- ever, was not carried. In this scheme every borough of less than 8,000 inhabitants was ,to be disfranchised, and where' the population was less than 16,000 to have one member taken away where previously there were two ,repreisenta- tives. If such a Bill had been carried it would have been a reflection in the political light of this country, and give a better representative system than at present existed. Redistribution was, to use Mr. Bright'S words, "the soul of reform." Regarding electoral districts', there seemed to be an objection to such a system, but he did' Inot know why it should be so, as they were the order of the a ' oar all over the world where there was a Constitutional I Government. England claimed to be the mother of Prerlia- ments. In fact, she was so, because she created the, very idea of parliamentary government. When Simon de Mont- fort called the burgesses together to assist the king in governing the country, he did one of the most original and wisest things that had ever been done in the world. Never- theless they were much behind other countries in the matter of representative government. Whilst in most countries, they had universal suffrage and payment of members, and he believed in every country in the world where there Was a Parliament they had electoral districts, sci that " bbgey"• held before the eyes of the people te alarm them was not such a dreadful thing after all. Their present Parliament- ary system was practically no system at all. Aragegarded the metropolis, the whole' area of which formed _one-sixth of the total population of Great Britain, and _where they had the intelligence" culture, and industry of the country concentrated, yet the metropolis was worse represented ac- cording to its size 'than any other part of the country.' London was represented by 22 members; less than a third of what it ought to have if it had a fair and equitable sys- tem of representation. They had the borough of Maryle- bone with 498,311, Finsbury 524,480, Lambeth 498,967, Tower Hamlets 438,910, which would be looked upon as g-eat cities in any other part of the world, these only re- turned two members each to Parliament, whilst on the other hand they had little boreughs of 16,000 or 17,000 inhabi- tants represented by two members in Parliament. Thea as regarded county representation, they had Rutland, with a population of 21,434, sending two members to Parliament, compared with south-East Lancashire, with a population of 534,963, which only sent two members. The strange thing aixiut it was that whereas the highest population of the county constituencies having three members was 14,5,000, yet there were 28 constituencies with a greater .population thaa that returning oaly two members. In Ire- land the same inequality existed. It had been declared by the ministers that they meant to extend the suffrage in Ireland as well as in England. (Hear, hear.) There were fire constituencies in Ireland under 6,000 inhabitants, 12 under 7,000, and 16 under 10,000 Then the number of electors in proportion to the population was much less than in England. Thus in Portarlington there were only 142 electors, in Kinsale 190, in Ennis 254, in New Ross 261, and in Dungannon 279. As a contrast they had Belfast with a population of 207,000 and 21,000 electors, and Dublin with a population of 273,000 and 12,000 electors, returning only two members each to Parliamerl. They also had eight counties each with a population of more than 140,000 returning only two members each. The whole of the small boroughs of Ireland under 20,000 inhabitants, which sent 26 members to Parliament, had a less popu- lation than Dublin, which sent only two. (Whew!) Taking Lancashire, again, they had Warrington, Bury, Rochdale, and Burnley sent only one member to Parliament,i but they were good men and true, the total population of , those towns being 227,370, or nearly a quarter of a million. There were five placed he would mention as a comparison. There was Eye with a population of 6,293 represented by that gifted orator and peculiar charm of the House of Com- mons, Mr. Ashmead Bartlett—(laughter);—Knaresborongh, with a population of 5,000, represented by Toni Collins; Woodstock, with a population of 7,027, represented by that 1 philosopher and accomplished statesman Lord Randolphl Churchill—(reneWed laughter);—Bridport, with a popula- tion of 6,790, represented by Mr. Warton ; and Hertford, with a population of 8,556, represented by Mr. Po.lfour. When those members were in Parliament the four Lancashire gentlemen representing nearly a quarter of a million of electors would be out-voted by men who only represented 33,000, which he characterised as unjust and shameful. (Hear, hear.) As to the modes of re-distribution he wrote a pamphlet a little while ago on that question in which he suggested that they should proceed on the old lines and that they should totally disfranchise all towns of less than 10,000, and partially disfranchise towns of less than 20,000. Leading statesmen, however, were in favour of something more radical than that Mr. Forster had declared for some- thing as near electoral districts as they could possibly get, whilst 'Mr. Chamberlsin—(applause)—was in favour of electoral districts, and his word would carry great weight, but he did not think they would get such a system as the Opposition in the House of Commons would be quite too strong for anything of the kind. However from the ex- pressions used by leading Liberal statesmen and by leading politicianl3 generally he believed there would be a very com- prehensive scheme of redistribution put into force. He thought the large towns would get a much larger share of representation than they had at present, and they would- make a clean sweep of some of the small boroughs of the country. They did not aim so much at being theoretically perfect if they could only get something in the main which would be just and equitable they would be satisfied, only he hoped they would not leave the Bill to the tender mercy of a Conservative Government. With respect to the House of Lords, that, House thought the Bill should be sub- ject to amendments. As a comparison, if a number of brigands were to eeiae an unfortunate traveller, rifled his pockets and ill-treated- his person, and then send him away and say that they had made amendments of him, it would be pretty much the same as the House of Lords amending bills. (Laughter.) They would strike out everything valuable and introduce everything mischievous, and then send back the Bill amended. But the people of England would say what they did in reference to the Bill of 1832, that they would have the Bill, the whole Bill, and nothing but the Bill. If the House of Lords refused to deal with the question in the way they wished it would come, the question was how should they deal with the House of Lords. (Applause.) In reference to the question of minority or proportionate representation, he noticed that a number of people were in favour of this, but he was glad to see that the leading statesmen of this country had de- clared against it. particularly Mr. Bright. Proportionate representation was a fallacy. It was said that supposing at an election in Manchester 30,000 men voted for the Liberals, and 25,000 for the Conservatives, it was not fair that the 25,000 should be unrepresented. That was not a true prin- ciple. When a minister appealed to a constituency he laid down a policy, and said "I want you to say yes or no to this policy," and the majority decided it. That was the old English plan, and he hoped there would be no departure from it. (Applause.) Ia his concluding remarks the lec- turer said he must impress upon his hearers the importance of dealing with these questions to the utmost of their ability, as its results had a great deal to do with the constitution of the House of Commons itself. At the passing of the last Reform Bill it was said that one of the results of the exten- sion of the democratic suffrage of this country would be the degredation of the House of Commons. True the House of Commons had become degraded, but it was not through the democracy that it had become degraded. (Applause.) If they wanted to find out those who bad dragged the House of Commons in the mire, frittered away the time of the House and made the House a laughing stock, they must go to the small constituencies—to Woodstock— (laughter)—whose gifted representative bad wasted the time of the House by the rare distinction of infusing vul- garity into political discussions. (Hear, hear.) It was such men who had degraded the House of Commons and hampered its proceedings, and one of the inevitable results of the red:stribution of Seats would be to raise the character of the House, restore it to its old prestine vigour, because the one reason why the time of the House had been frittered away was owing to those representing small constituencies having scarcely any responsibilities. The people of Eng- land had done great things in the past, and there were great things to be done in the future, not the least being the reform of Parliament itself. (Applause.) The usual votes of thanks were paved to the lecturer and chairman at the close. A gentleman was giving a boy some peanuts the other day. The mother said, "Now, what are you going to say- to the gentleman ?" The little fellow looked up and replied "More !" A man picked up a purse in the street, and advertised the fact. In ten days he was visited by 61 men' women, boys, and girls, all claiming to have lost money. The sum was but 11 dollars, but of each visitor who called the finder asked, "So you lost 50 dollars, did you ?" Nine•tenths of the applicants promptly replied,." Yes, sir." "Au," said he, "yours was another purse." A ll'utErzo.—The name of friendship •is sacred: What you demand in that name I have not the power to deny you.—Longfellow.—Friends, without which the world is but a wilderness.—Bacon.—A friend loveth at all times. . . . A man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.— Solomon.—A friend in prosperity is a pleasure; in adversity, a solace; in grief, a comfort; in joy, a cheerful companion; and at all times a second self.—Anon. NISI PIOUS COURT. ACTION AGAINST THE LANCASHIRE AND YORK' SHIRE R4ILWAY COMPANY. PARKER V. THR LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE EAU, WAY COMPANY.—This was an action to recover damages for personal injuries sustained by the plaintiff, John Edward Parker, residing at Roby, member of the Huyton-with-Roby Local Board, in an accident on the defendant 00132Pan7:8 railway. Mr. Aspinall, Q.C., and Mr. French were.fer the plaintiff, and Mr. Russell, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Pickford for the company. The defendants did not dispute their lie" bility, and the oply question fer the jury was as to the amount of compensation. The plaintiff had been for 20 years and more in the employment of Messrs. Evans and Sons, wholesale druggists, of Liverpool, and his total income amounted to nearly £BOO a year. On the 12th July last he was travelling on the defendant company's line between Bacup and Ramsbottom, when-the accident occurred. It appeared that there was something wrong with the line. The engine and someof the carriages left the line, and ultimately the engine was upset, add the carriage in which the plaintiff - WAS was very violentlY 'shaken. The plaintiff was flung violently about the Car- riage, and his nervous system had received such a shock that he had been unable to follow his occupation since the occurrence. The plaintiff still suffered great pain, and had lost the power of walking any reasonable distance. The actual loss theplaintiff had incurred from the time of the accident amounted to £4BB. The case concluded on ,Aed. nesday, and the jury awarded the plaintiff £750. 1 LOCAL PRISONS ATI,LIVERP • ASSIZES: , •

A Calvinistic Methodist Chapel, near Cdedpoeth, ham, was burned down on Sunday morning. MEN. FOR MISS FORTESCITE.—It is announced that Lord Garmoyle left London on Wednesday night for the East. The death is announced of Mr. William Forster, J.P., of Hornby Castle, ancashire, and Bradford, the head of one of the largest manufacturing firms in Bradford. • The strike of 3,000 men in the Belfast shipbuilding trade IS virtually over, the men having offered to accept two- thirds of the proposed reduction, and the employers have agreed to these terms. Mr. Thomas Cheney, M.A., for several years editor of the Times, died on Monday morning at his Chambers, Ser- jeants'-inn, aged 58. He had been for some time suffering from an abscess, the result of low fever. A bust of the late Earl of Beaconsfield was unveiled at the St. Stephen's Club, Westminster, on Wednesday, by the Marquis of Salisbury, who was the chief speaker at a banquet subsequently held in connection with the cere- Mony. "Miss Fortescuerthe plaintiff in the action against Lord Garmovle, claims £50,000 compensation for "broken vows?' The lady retired from the stage in anticipation of the wed- ding, and the sum she claims is regarded as a fitting coin- Pensation for " the loss of position to which she would have been entitled as the wife of a peer." It is feared that the City of Cork Steampacket Company's steamer Upapa, which left London last Thursday and Ply- Mouth en Saturday morning, was lost in the gale on Satur- daY night. She had a crew of 24 men, and the captain's Wife and daughter were on board; audit is thought probable that she had taken in some passengers. On Saturday morning, while Charles Evans, a barber, W& s cutting the hair of Joseph Baker, a publican, at a house in Lancaster-street, Birmingham, an explosion of gas oc- curred, and both men mere injured, the latter so seriously that he had to be removed to the hospital. The doors and Windows were blown out, and the building was otherwise

damaged. SPORTSMEN IN e PLIOUT.—A somewhat serious accident befel a train containing sporting men and others which left Birmingham about 12-15 on Tuesday for Sutton Coldfield. On arrriving at Sutton Coldfield it dashed through the sta- tion and ran into the bank, upsetting the engine. 'Several Passengers were severely shaken, while the guard in the foremost break was seriously injured. THE MILES PLATTING Drumme—The supeeintendents and all the teachers and officers of the schools connected with St. John's, Miles Platting, have " resigned " the work in which they have been engaged. In addition to the schools, the missions, guilds," and "societies "in connection with the church are to be dissolved, and "it is also probable" that the work of visiting the sick will be suspended. CHARGE OF Muunme.--At Monmouth assizes, on Tues- daY, Patrick Gallaghan was indicted for the murder of Wm. Jones, at Rhyinney, on the night of the 27th January. The prisoner and deceased were seen together, the latter being drunk. Next day Jones was found lying dead in a deep gutter with his head fearfully battered and his Pickets rifled. The defence was that the injuries were in- flioted by a series of falls, and the .jury returned a verdict of not guilty. Ma. Greer:semen's New Ann.—Simeon Shorter, the Bir- mingham workman who presented Mr. Gladstone with an axe, has received the following letter:—" Mr. Gladstone desires me to express to you his best thanks for the detailed account of the making of the axe which you kindly pre- !tented to him. Although Mr. Gladstone is loth to deface ite • Polish in any degree, he feels bound to contemplate makiog a trial with it in order to see the effect of an axe made Wholly of steel." Hwy Ellen FOR MILE ADULTERATION,—A milk dealer named Dearbley Was on Monday, at Huddersfield, fined £2O for selling adulterated milk. The evidence showed that a *ample of theefluid wleich Dearnley was hawking in the streets as milk contained the extraordinary proportion of 91 Per cent. of water. On four previous occasions the defen- dant had been-heavily lined for similar offences. btatisti7 Clans tell us that the people of England pay about a million a year for water which is sold as milk. PROPOSED REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS. On Monday night, at a crowded Liberal meeting in Birming- ham, Sir John Bennett, after lecturing on the House of Lords, moved :—" That in the opinion of this meeting the time has come for dispensing with the Bishops in the House of Lords,'and the privilege of a seat by the accident of birth should be abolished in order to bring into more hat- Monious action the hereditary and irresponsible with the Chosen representatives of the people." The resolution was enthusiastically carried. GREAT FIRE AT Dumenn.—A sad accident, resnitieg in the deaths of four firemen, occurred on Monday morning at Dundee. Fire broke out in a large jute-waste works in Arklay-street,belonging to Mr. J. Bradford, and the brigade worked for several hours without much success. Whilst a number of firemen were standing on ladders directing the hose-pipes, a great mass of the building fell upon them Without the slightest warning. Four members of the bri- gade were buried beneath the ruin, and others had marvel- bus escapee. The damage to property is estimated at 430,000. Ma. MICHAEL' DAVITT HOOTED AT NEWCASTLE.—Mr. Michael Devitt was announced to speak in Newcastle Town Hall on Tuesday night, on "The Irish problem and its solution." On rising he was greeted with persistent howl- nag and hissing. A rush was subsequently made for the platform, but was prevented by the police, a large staff of whom were present. Mr. Devitt drew a revolver, which he held in his hand for a few minutes. The disturbance lasted fully an hour and aqn irter ; but the disturbers were even- tually ejected after several free fights, in which some of the Combatants were severely wounded. Swocxisia MURDER AT LIVERPOOL.—The rising gene- ration of Liverpool roughs will, it may be hoped, take Warning from a case tried at the assizes in that city on Mon- ;day. On Christmas Eve an unoffending lad of thirteen was atteseked in one of the main thoroughfares of Liverpool by four yeouths ranging in age from fifteen to eighteen years, Who maLreated him with all the ferociousness which dis- tinguishes ate barbarous freaks of corner-men "of more Mature age, ant; the poor child died in a fe w hours from the Violence he sufferted• The offendees were, happily, seeured, and on Monday they ie-ere convicted. Three of them were sentenced to ten years, auj the ringleader to twelve years' Penal servitude. •• ALLEGED LIBEL ON A Dunr.—Tlaa Queen's tench Divi- Zion refused on Saturday to make the rule absolute for a Criminal information against Mr. Labouchere, M.P.' the Proprietor of Truth, for a libel on the Duke of Yellambrosa. The defence- was a purely technical one, and the Court decided that there were no grounds for making the rule absolute. IRELAND. AGRARIAN OUTRAGE. A farmer named Curtis was brutally murdered near. New Boss on Monday night, being found on the highway with his throat cut and several st .bs in the body. The murder is stated to be an agrariau one. THE BARBAVILLA MURDER.—The trial of the four men Lestrange, Magrath, Swords, and Elliott, who were indicted for conspiring to murder Mr. Thomas Smythe, of Barba- villa, Westmeath, concluded in Dublin on Wednesday, after occupying the Court since Monday. Chief Justice Morris summed up the evidence, but the jury, after two and a half hour's consideration, were discharged without agreeing to a verdict. An application for bail was refused, the Judge re- ferring counsel to the Queen's Bench. MR. LAVITT ON THE FRANCHISE BILL.—Mr. Devitt, speaking in Glasgow, said he was strongly of opinion that even if Ireland was to be deprived of eight or ten seats it would be better that that should happen than that the coun- try should lose the benefit of the household suffrage measure. • Mr. Parnell would be justified in making a deter- mined stand against any reduction of seats; but he hoped that the opposition would not be carried so far as to imperil the extension of the Franchise Bill to Ireland. SETTING FIRE TO A LAND LEAGUE HUT.—At the Dublin Commission Court, on Thursday, the three Orange- men, Mr. Matthews, proprietor of the iyrone Courier, and two men, named Richardson and Gibsoo, were found guilty of maliciously setting fire to a Land League hut near Pomeroy, county Tyrone. The jury recommended them to mercy on the ground of the high political feeling existing in the North of Ireland at the time of the occurrence. Mat- thews was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment, and the other two to six months each. A PEER HIS OWN ADVOCATE.—The extraordinary spec- tacle t3resented last week, in the Dublin Landed Estates Cotirt, of a peer of the realm appearing as his own advo- cate, is explained by the Earl of Leitrim hi a letter to the Dublin papers. His lordship denies that he mistrusted his own legal advisers, and states that he was professionally advised to appear himself. He accuses the Board of Trinity College with acting dishonestly and dishonourably towards him as their tenant, in torturing the law to their own advan- tages. He challenges them to bring action for libel against him, and then he will meet their counsel with counsel. He denies that he Was excited in court. ASSAULTING "SKIN THE GOAT'S 7' DAUGHTER.—At Dublin, on Monday, Emily Thomson was sentenced to six months' imprisonment and bound over for a similar period, for assaulting the daughter of Fitzbarris, otherwise "Skin the Goat," the man who drove the Phomix Park murderers in a cab from the park, and who was one of the "Invinci- ble " convicts removed from Dublin to England last week to serve his life sentence of penal servitude. Prisoner struck Miss Fitzharris, a respectable-looking girl, and called her the daughter of a murderer, stating that she and her people were living on blood money. She had repeatedly threatened the prosecutrix, who went in fear and dread of her. On being sentenced, the prisoner threatened to make another attack on her on coming out of jail.

POLITICAL. Mr. T. B. Potter, M.P., delivered his nineteenth annual address to his constituents in the Town Hall, Rochdale, on Wednesday night. A resolution assuring him of cordial ap- preciation of his services in Parliament and pledging him continued support was passed. In the division in the House of Lords on Tuesday night eleven peers who are usually classed as Liberals voted against the Government. Earl Fitzwilliam was one of the seceders. Four Bishops voted—Hereford and St. Albans 'or the vote of censure, and Exeter and St. Asaph for the,

_ Government. .LORD HAIITINGTON AND DISESTABLISIMENT IN SCOT- LAND.—At a recent Conservative banquet at Buckingham one of the speakers asserted that Lord Hartington had told, the citizens of Glasgow that, if he thought it would in any way add to his political popularity, he would even vote for the disestzblishment of their church. Major George Ven- ney, the Liberal candidate for the borough, having written his lordship on the subject, has received the folloWing reply, dated Devonshire House, February 10 :—I have to say that there is no foundation whatever for the statement alleged to have been made by the speaker. When I was at Edinburgh•some years ago I stated my opinion on the Es- tablished Church of Scotland in a speech which I made; but I certainly never used any expression in the least degree resembling those which are quoted in your letter. Ido not think that in the speeches I made at Glasgow a day or two afterwards I made any reference to the subject."

THE WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF COMMERCE AND RAILWAY RATES. At a meeting of the Couucil of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce; held at the rooms, Bewsey-street, on Monday last, there being present Messrs. Charles BrOadbent (presi- dent), H. Bleckly, John Fairclough, and Joseph Davies (secretary), a circalar was read from the Bristol Chamber of Commerce containing a communication from the President of the Board of Trade (Mr. Chamberlain) on the subject of his proposed Bill to _extend the powers of the Railway Commissioners. -In it he stated it was evident there would be much opposition, and unless he was cordially ' supported by the trade of the country he could not hope to carry his proposals. The Bristol Chamber had adopted a memorial to the .Board of Trade, and they asked the War- rington Chamber to co-operate with them so as to strengthen Mr. Chamberlain's hands. Mr. BLECBLY thought their own Chamber should adopt a different and separate memorial, because that of the Bris- tol Chamber involved a good many matters which did not apply to themselves. He had drawn out a short document just before coming to that meeting, and which stated in a general way what their grievances were. It was as follows: "The memorial of the Warrington Chamber of Colmnerca showeth that the attention of your memorialists has been frequently called to the unequal rates charged by railway companies on the carriage of goods, to the unsatis- factory classification of goods, to the indefinite nature of terminal charges, to the great expense and diffi- culty which traders have to encounter in any attempt made to redress in cases of overcharge or of doubtful charges, and your memorialists desire earnestly to impress upon your honottrable body the absolute necessity which exists for a removal of these grievances by the earliest possible legisla- tion, and they are of opinion that the recommendations of the Select Committee of the House of Commons appointed in 1881, giving permanent increased power to the Railway Commission, and securing by this means to the trading com- munity an inexpensive tribunal which should be easy of ac- cess for the adjustment of disputes with railway companies, would remove in great measure the hardship and injustice which at the present time exist."—Mr. Burettes, continuing, said he was anxious that the legislation on the subject should take such a form that the trading community would have an opportunity of seeking redress for any wrong without being put to any great expense, and at the same time that the railway company should feel that they were asking to force something from them which they were not bound to give. He daresay they had read the speech of Sir Edward Watkin, and it seemed that theeereat outcry of the railway companies was that traders claimed too much. and that they wanted to rob the railway company and put their hands into their pockets, so to speak. He did not wish that Chamber to raise such an impression. (Hear, hear.) They required what was fair according to law, and if the law did not give them what was right they should seek to alter that law. He did not wish to make any allegation in the terms of the memorial that they could not stand by. (Hear, hear.) The President and Mr. Fairclough having expressed them- selves in favour of the memorial as drawn up by Mr. Bleckly, it was accordingly adopted and directed to be pre- pared and presented to the Board of Trade. The CHAIRMAN then referred to a resolution passed by the Warrington Working Men's Committee, to the effect that a deputation be appointed to wait upon the President of the Chamber of Commerce, suggesting to him the desir- ability of the Chamber taking the initiative as early as possible in calling a public meeting to consider the injury at present caused to the trade of the district by the exces- sive rates charged in many instances by the various railway companies for the transit of manufactured and other goods to and from Warrington. The President said that the deputetion came to his house OR Friday evening, being in- treduced by Mr. Thomas Morris, and they talked over the matter in its various aspects in a sensible way. Some statistics were given in support of their views. One case, and such a. one he could tell himself, where a ton of wire could be brought from Westphalia to London for 5s less than a ton of wire could be sent from War- rington to London. The main point for that Council to de- cide was as to whether they should agree to the request of the deputation to call a public meeting in Warrington. After some discussion the Council came to the following decision :-"Having seriously considered the matter, and fully recognising the importance of the subject, it was deemed not desirable for this Chamber to promote such a public meeting, but rather rely en the memorial sent by the Chamber to the Board of Trade, and it was resolved that a copy of the memorial be sent to Mr. Henry Roberts." aux SHIP CANA.L. • A conversation arose on the receipt of a letter from Mr. Adamson asking the Chamber to memoralise in respect of ' the proposed Ship Canal. THE EGYPTIAN CRISIS. FALL OF SINKAT. Th.- distressing announcement of the fall of Sinkat has produced great excitement. The intelligence reached Lon- don on Tuesday afternoon, and was confirmed by statements in both Houses. Some days ago a rumour to this effect ob- tained currency, but in the absence of confirmatory tele- grams it was hoped that it was without foundation. Now, however, there is no longer room for doubt. After a defence of nearly six months, Tewfik Bey and his gallant six hun- dred, having blown up the town's fortifications and spiked the guns, sallied out to make one last desperate effort to cut their way through the enemy and reach the coast. The beleaguring Arabs then fell upon them, and the slaughter was complete. Sad to say, a later telegram states that the victorious barbarians afterwards took possession of the town and put all the inhabitants, who were chiefly women and children, to the sword. Ample reinforcements have been ordered to Suakim from Cairo and elsewhere, and a con- siderable portion are already on their way to Port Said. A number of superior officers, who were on Tuesday Placed under orders for the seat of war, left London for Dover on a few hours' notice. A meeting of the Cabinet was held on Tuesday morning, at which the policy to be pursued at Suakim and on the Red Sea littoral was under consideration. The Channel Squadron was directed at once to proceed to Egyptian waters, and preparations were made to forward infantry,cavalry,guns, and camels from Suez to Suakim with the object of relieving the garrison at Toka. Another battalion of marines has been sent out CO Egypt. Indeed, the military situation generally demonstrates that the Government contemplate vigorous ; measures on a large scale. The Standard' 8 correspondent at Suakim telegraphs the following:—The news of the fall of Sinkat was brought in by a letter from Mahmoud Ali Bey, a friendly chief, who said that the garrison sallied out, and for a long time repulsed the attacks of the rebels. At length all were destroyed except a small party of prisoners. Fur- ther reports have been brought in by natives, and it is said that only four men, 30 women, and the Cadi of Sinkat have been spared. Tewfik is reported to have pointed out to his men that by fighting they might save themselves, by remaining all must in a few days die of hunger, while fight- ing was impossible. Having animated his men with his own spirit, be burned all the stores, spiked the guns, and blew up the magazine. Then, each man having filled his pouches with as much ammunition as he could carry, the SOO issued out. Osman's hordes at once rushed down to the attack. Tewfik and his men fought nobly, and for a long time repulsed every effort to break their ranks, but at last numbers prevailed. With a tremendous rush the Arabs burst into one of the sides of the square, and a general mas- sacre then took place, not a single man escaping. It is sup- posed that the four men spared were left behind sick and unable to march. EXPECTED SUCCESS OF GORDON'S MISSION. A telegram from the British Vice Consul at Suakim announces that the news of the intended despatch of the British expedition has spread rapidly, and that the rebels are dispersing. The following telegram was repeived on Thursday after- noon at the Foreign Office from Sir E. Baring; it bears date 4th February, 4-45 :—Gordon reports telegraph between Khartoum and Shendy repaired. Says—" lam leaving for ' Khartoum. Believe you need give yourselves no farther anxiety about this part of the Soudan. People, great and small, are heartily glad to be free from union, which only caused them sorrow."

ROUSE .OF LORDS, MONDAY. Lord Woleeley's recent statistical error in regard to the physique of recruits for the army, and the reinforcement of 'our Arms in Egypt, were referred to.—On the motion of the Earl of 4ONGFORD a ' return was ordered, showing the charges that the several companies supplyreg water within the metropolitan districts are authorised by law to levy.

Colonel Clarke has left England to assume his position as British Commissioner in Basutoland. A Vienna telegram states that documentary proof has been found by the police that the Socialists in Austria were conspiring against the life of the Emperor. It is announced from Constantinople that two hundred Albanian political prisoners, who have been imprisoned here for the last three years, have been released by order of the Sultan. STOPPAGE OF Corroia MILLS IN Amitnice.—Thirteen mills at Fall River have been closed by the proprietors. Seven thousand workmen, including a number of weavers, are thrown out of employment. A Lisbon journal states that there is a probability of the appointment of an Anglo-Portugese commission to settle the question of the Congo navigation and the delimitation of Portugese territory in that region. SAD ACCIDENT TO • WEDDING PARTY.—AR accident of a peculiarly melancholy nature occurred in Austria on Mon- day. A wedding party were crossing the Theiss when the ice gave way and 35 persons Were drowned. GREAT FIRE IN Russia.—A fire •which broke out on Monday in the MOSCOW Bazaar was mastered at midnight, after 10 warehouses had been burned down and four others more or less damaged. The loss is estimated at upwards of 1,000,000 roubles. DISASTROUS FLOODS IN ORlO.—Very serious reports have been cabled respecting the floods in the United States. Portsmouth(Ohio) has been submerged, the waters reach- ing the highest point ever known. It was estimated that 20,000 people would have to be provided with food and clothing between Wellsburg and Moundsville. At Cincin- nati the floods were higher than during the memorable floods of 1882. MASSACRE OF CHRISTIANS IN CHINA—The Paris Clerical journal Le Monde states that an attack has been made on the Catholic missions in Tonquin, and a considerable num- ber' of converts massacred, together with a priest and a num- ber of catechists. The Monde seems to have been favoured with the exclusive possession of this news, and no confirma- tion has reached Europe from any quarter. Should it un- fortunately prove to be true, we may expect an outburst of indignation against the heathen Tonquinese. ANOTHER MYSTERIOUS DISAPPEARANCE IN BRUSSELS.— Much concern has been felt in Brussels for the safety of M IMascart, a young official attached to the Ministry of Public Instruction, who unexpectedly disappeared eight days ago, and has not since been heard of. As he had in his posses- sion between seven and eight thousand francs, it is feared he has been murdered. The excitement caused by this mys- terious disappearance is increased by the tact that, in spite of the minute researches of the police, no clue has been dis- covered as to the whereabouts of M. Deschamps, a wealthy business man, who disappeared three months ago. It is generally feared that the example of the Brothers Peltzer, who managed to murder M. Bernays without his body being discovered for many weeks, is being followed by some gang of audacious criminals. THE WEST COAST OF AFRICA,—The search after a scien- tific frontier is, apparently, about to get us into trouble on the West Coast of Africa. King Amatifoo, of Kinjobe, objec a very strongly to the presence of the Anglo-French Delimi- tation Commission near his territories, and refuses in the most decided manner to have a " line " drawn within his boundaries. At the last acccounts Amatifoo had called out 3,000 or 4,000 warriors, to oppose whom our people at Cape Coast were sending forward 20 Houssas with rocket tubes. In reference to the work of this Commission it is in- teresting to note that a Committee of the French Chamber of Deputies advises that body to reject the Convention already agreed upon between our Government and that of France. The Committee find the Convention, of course, highly dis- advantageous to France. DEATH OF CETEWAYo.—Cetewayo'B death is again re- ported. After his recent defeat at 'Ulundi, it e as repeatedly stated that he had been killed, and when this report was contradicted it was alleged that he had died, but neither report was accurate. There does not appear to be any reason. however, to doubt the truth of the present an- nouncement. The King nes living in the British camp in the Reserve Territory, and the news of his death must, therefore, be assumed to have tome through official chan- nels. He is said to have died suddenly on Friday in last week from heart disease. Only a few days ago the Under Secretary for the Colonies, in the course of debate, stated that it was difficult to tell what to do with Cetewayo, who was a cause of disturbance in Zululand, who could not be removed into Natal, and who would be unwelcome at the Cape. His decease thus removes an embarrassment, and Will, it is to be hoped, tend to promote peace in the country of which he was formerly King. • THE TONQUIN DIFFICULTY.—The Times published on Wednesday a lengthy telegram from a correspondent at Haiphong, which was sent off on January 22. The French were making preparations to attack Bac nth, on Tuesday last. The place was to be assaulted by 8,000 men, moving in three columns, with the support of a flotilla of gunboats. He states that the Bogu forts are garrisoned by 4,000 men. At Theping and neighbouring places about 20.000 men are quartered, ready to concentrate at any point. Seven 25- ton guns and a large number of smooth-bore weapons are mounted at the Bogu forts. The islands have heavy bat- , teries, and so also has the south side of the river. The latter position is commanded by a hill, crowned with a fort, whinh is now occupied by 2,000 soldiers.. At Whampoa, close to the works for the proposed blocking of the river. stroi.g well planned earthworks have been constructed, with Krupp guns more formidable than those in the Bogu forts. With the existing defences and the precaution taken of blocking the river, leaving a narrow passage only, the con- clusion was that a successful attack on Canton would be extremely difficult to carrry out, especially if the defence be conducted by the Europeans mow in the Chinese service.

Buttawnso oF • FLYWRREL. The flywheel at the Phoenix Ironworks, Cradley, broke on Wednesday morning while making about 55 revolutiOns per minute. A roof about 70 feet long was totally destroyed by the falling iron, and the men rushed in all directions to save themselves. Some jumped into the Stour, and two of these were injured, but only one man was hurt by the direct effects of the acci- dent. There were several marvellous escapes. Besides the ' wreck in the works, much damage was done at Mr. Hugbes's flour mill near. A massive piece of the wheel struck the stack half way up, cutting out several yards of masonry and rendering abolition necessary. The boiler was in lured by the iron and brickwork falling on it. THB PRABDS BE LIVERPOOL CORN MERCHANTS.—The frauds committed on the North-Western Bank, Liverpool, by two corn merchants, named John Herd and William John Mullins, came before Mr. Justice Butt at the Liverpool Assizes on Wednesday. Mullins pleaded guilty at the out- set, and Herd did so after the case for the prosecution had teen gone into. It appeared that Mullins had until recently I been only the clerk of the other prisoner, and that though he had been nominally a Partner of late his position re- mained unchanged, and while holding him to some extent culpable, the Judge considered that he bad acted under coercion. Mullins was sentenced to threa and Herd to 18 months' imprisonment, with hard labour.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TuttEsnAT. THE IMPORTATION OF FOREIGN CATTLII.--LOrd CAM. LINGPORD introduced the Government Bill for conferring larger powers on the Privy Council with regard'to stopping the importation of cattle from countries where foot-and- utioath disease exist. He said the Council had endeavoured to Carry out faithfully the extended responsibilities of the Act of 1f2711, but many of the local authorities had shown great, want of carefulness and energy. Good effects had followed the system lately pursued, although it might have been harrassing and inconvenient. The Government as wall as the farmers were weary of the present state of things, and in the hope of assuring agriculturists of pro- tection against infection from abroad, they bad introduced this bill, although they did not think the country could be hermetically sealed against the intro- duction of disease. The bill, in certain circumstances, im- posed an obligation on the Privy,Council to exclude fireign cattle, but they were not prepared to abandon the alterna- tive system of slaughter at the ports, which was highly desirable in the case of certain countries —After some dis- cussion, the bill was read a first time, and their Lordships adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TRMISDAY. THE EGYPTIAN EXPEDITION.—A large number of ques- tions were asked respecting the Egyptian Expedition.— The CRANCIALLOn of the EXCHEQUER, answering Sir S. Northcote, said he had no doubt it would be necessary to ask for additional military and naval estimates to meet the charges of the expedition. No delay would' take place in submitting the estimates.—ln reply to Mr. Bourke, the , PREMIER said the Government had no permission from the Sultan of Turkey with reference to operations in the Sou- dan, and the. action of her Majesty's Government had in no way infringed the rights of the Sultan of the country. Tat VErrE OE GENSURE.—On the resumption of the de- bate on the proposed vote of censure on the Government Sir W. LAWSON moved as an amendment:—" That this House, whilst declining at present to express an opinion on the Egyptian policy which Her Majesty's Government have pursued during the last two years, with the support of the House, trusts that in future British forces may not be em- ployed for the purpose of interfering with the Egyptian people in the selection of their own Government." Sir Wilfrid said he wished to know why the Leader of the Opposition came forward with a vote of censure now. He ought to have done so a year ago. The right hon. gentle- man did not condemn the Government for, doing wrong, but for not having succeed in doing wrong. The vote of censure should be applied to those who got us into this trouble Sir S. Northcote and Lord Salisbury. They began it at Willis's rooms in 1832, when they made fire and thunder speeches under the presidency of the chit- man of the bondholders.—The amendment was seconded by Mr. LA.BOUCHERE.—Mr. GLADSTONE said the Government must vote against the amendment. After the challengdt they had received from the Opposition it would be impossaekfor them te ask the House to decline to express an opinion on their past policy in Egypt, and they also objectedAto that part of the amendment which proposed to lay down a rule as to the future.—Mr. FORSTER said the qasti on was not whether the Government had always done what was right in this matter, but whether tile course of action they were now engaged in was likely to be advantageous to this coun- try and to Egypt-Sir C. Drum also spoke, and ably de- fended the policyeat the Government.
