THE STRIKE AT RUNCORN. The strike has a considerable bearing upon Runcorn. Of the 500 men who have left work, over 200 live in that town, which is an important station in the Navigation Com- pany's organisation. They differ from the ordinary class of boatmen inasmuch as a large proportion of them are thrifty, honest fellows, and manage out of their hard earned wages to save a portion for a "rainy day," which bas unfortu- nately now arrived. It is stated that the action of the company has been taken in order to enable their concern to compete more successfully with the enterprise of the rail- ways, but the men complain that it is unfair to tax them when the shareholders are receiving a dividend of 91 per cent. The Runcorn flatmen ceased work on Monday morn- ingeand on the afternoon of that day they were paid off at the Navigation Co.'s Offices. It was rumoured that unless they returned to work on Wednesday, the reduction instead of being Is. per week would be farther reduced to 2s. per week, but this statement we have reason to believe is totally de- void of foundation. It is satisfactory to find that the flat- men are making no hostile demonstrations. They are, in fact, conducting themselves in an exemplary fashion, and the amount of drinking is not so great as might have been expected. On the other hand, a Cocoa Company wbose shareholders have never received any return upon their .venture is receiving a good share of the flitmen's patronage, and their clean and bright-looking rooms have been filled with the men on strike, who were to be seen quaffing cocoa and coffee instead of the insiduous beer and stout of the publican. On Wednesday morning the Runcern fletmen journeyed to Warrington on foot to attend a meeting there, and they returned in the evening in the same manner, marching through the town in soldierly array to Devon- shire-square. Although it was raining heavily at the time, they formed themselves into a group, and sang with reverent heartiness the doxology, and after giving three rounds of cheering, they quietly dispersed. ATTEMPT AT INTIMIDATION: At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. J Brundrit and Captain C. W. H izlehurst, a fletman named George Ireland was brought up in cnstody charged with being drunk and disorderly on the towing path of the Bridgewater Navigation Company on the previous day, and further for the purpose of compelling one Thomas Bonnet to abstain from working a canal boat belonging to the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Limited ; did then and there unlawfully and without legal authority use violence and threats to the said Thomas Bennett.—The prisoner pleaded guilty to being drunk, but said he had no recollec- tion whatever of the assault.—The facts of the case as given in the evidence of Thomas Bennett, the prosecutor, Stanley Leathwood, a fireman at Reynolds' tannery, Wm. John- son, horse driver, and P.S. Lowndes, were these. The pri- soner, who is a powerful-looking young fellow, was in the employ of Mr. Abbott, Runcorn, but identifying himself with the men on strike, he left his situation. On Wednes- day morning he was on his way to Warrington to attend the meeting there, but being under the influence of drink his motions were somewhat erratic, and he did not arrive at his destination. On the same morning Bennett was steering the flat Violet from Preston Brook to Runcorn, and when ap- proaching Astmoor Bridge, Halton, the prisoner, who was there, threw stones at him, and cursed him very much. He characterised him as a " knobstick," and said he had no business to be doing the work that another man ought to be doing. He then jumped aboard the barge, seized Bennett by the neckerchief, and threatened that unless he immedi- ately left the boat he would throw him into the canal. Ben- nett took the prisoner's alternative, and got upon the towing path, and was followed by the prisoner, who struck him twice on the breast, and a struggle on the ground ensued Afterwards the prisoner set the horses, which were attached to the boat, at liberty, and concluded by rolling a barrel of acid from Mr. Reynolds's tannery into the water. At a later period be was apprehended by P.S. Lowndes. The pri- soner, who had no explanation to make in extenuation of his cenduct, was fined 10s, and costs 7s SI, for being drunk.— Mr. Brundrit said the second charge was that of intimidat- ing a person from doing his work, and in the opinion of the Bench this was a very serious matter. With the merits of the strike the Bench had nothing whatever to do; and so far as they could see they did not know what the prisoner had to do with it. By his conduct he had made himself liable to a penalty of £2O, or three months' imprisonment, but on this occasion the Bench did not intend to use to the fell the powers conferred upon them. They wished the prisener and everyone else, however, to understand that this kind of thing would not be permitted. He was glad to know that the men on strike had behaved BO far in an exemplary' way, arid he hoped they would con- tinue to do so. Teere was no reason why the prisoner , should have interfered between the masters and the men. He would be fined 20s. and costs 13s. ad. for the assault ; in default a month's imprisonment with hard labour. There I was a large number of boatmen in the court, and they in- timated to the Superintendent of Police that the fines, which amounted to £2 us. 21 would be paid.

FRODSHAM zoo•YEARS AGO AND 50 YEARS HENCE. HISTORICAL LECTURE BY MR. THOMAS RIGBY, OF surroN. On Monday evening a lecture was given in the girls' school, Frodsham, by Mr. Thomas Rigby, of Sutton Weaver, in connection with the Frodsham Literary and Debating Society, the subject being " A walk round Frodsbam 200 years ago and 50 years hence." Dr. F. P. Weaver presided, and there was a large attendance, including most of the leading families in the neighbourhood. The CHAIRMAN in a brief introductory speech referred to the public services rendered by Mr. Rigby, and said he had no doubt they would have an interesting lecture. Mr. RIGBY, in the course of his lecture, said " A walk round Frodsham 200 years ago" may begin at Frodsham Bridge, where there was at that time an upper way to the Parish Church and a lower way to Frodsham town. The town, a fair continued street with handsome buildings, and at the west end of it a fair house, which having been a castle, continues still the name of Frodeharn Castle. The church is fair and pleasantly situated on the hill over the town, and extends the bounds of the parish to alarge pre- cinct. Those buildings about the church carry the name of Overton in relation to another village beneath called Netherton, together with the Woodhouses. a member of it, and over them all a high towering hill with a beacon upon it, and between all these and Mersey lies a fair and fruitful marsh of a large extent, and all this and much more make but that one lordship belonging to Sir Thomas Savage, and next unto it another almost of the Same nature and condi- tion, both high and low, called Helsby. So wrote Daniel King in the year 1655; and the lecturer then gave an extract from the works of the same historian of the Astons of Aston Hall and the Savages of Rocksavage. The town of Frodshana says Ormerod forms a broad street of a mile in length, another street diverges at right-angles in the centre of the town towards the church and the high grounds of Overton. This street was called Chirchstrete in the reign of Henry VI., the broad or main street was called le Highstrete, and there was then another Shipstrete. There was theh a market held on Saturdays, and two fairs on the 15th May and 21st August. In 1804 there were 109 houses 1,250 inhabitants in the town. On the church of Frodsham, situate at Overton, I need say but little to an audience in its national school. It has lately undergone a complete restora- tion. and is now among the handsomest buildings in the county ; strength and beauty, substahtial build, fair propor- tions and chaste effect being its chief characteristics. Over- ton Church is of great-antiquity, the registers commence in 1558. It was greatly ruined before 1599 and extensively re. paired in 1724, and again, as I have said, restored about two years ago. The free school of Frodsham was a neat fabric of stone, built about 1660 within the yard of the church, but taken down many years ago. and a new school-house erected on a plot of land lying between the church and the vicarage, says Ormerod, and he adds, "The present able master is Mr. Pollard. who has occupied the office for, many years," the exact number is a period which it is hoped ms be yet extended. The Castle of Frodsham must now have 4 brief notice. It stood at the west end of the town guarding a narrow pass on the Chester road between the steep precipices of Overton Hills and the river Mersey. It is said to be built of red stone, the arches semi-circular and of early Norman work, the walls being of enormous thick- ness. A print of the ruins of the Frodsham Castle, taken in 1727, is in Ormerod's History, produced, and there des- cribed as "only an eminent ruin of antiquity." In 1721 the ruined castle of Frodsham and adjoining estate was sold by Lord sarrymore's trustees, who had succeeded to it by inheritance from the Savages to John Daniel, Esq., of Daresburv. In 1750 the castle again changed hands, being purchased by FrAncis Ashley, Esq., who uprooted the Old Castle from its foundations and built upon its site the handsome mansion now the property of our much respected neighbour, E. A. Wright, Esq., dl'. In disturbing the foundations an ancient lamp, several coffins, a curious plate, And a cannon ball were found, and at a later period an ancient English coin, by the late Joseph Stubbs, Esq., the limn owner of the house. Beyond these records there is nothing to reveal the exact site of the old eastle or to give ail adequate idea of its size. The thick walls in tathe c of the present residence may be part of itsdions, and 1-thiare are slight indications in the groundsun of other walls which may be silently going to decay, but beyond these 1 there is no trace left of the building. With the cloud eons palaces of Shakespeare's capped towers and the gorg epitaph, It has dissolved, and Like the baseiens fabric of a dream. Left not a wre 1 behind, A historical sketch of the Astons, of Aston, followed, which would have afforded a lecture in itself, and the Lecturer then gave a graphic forecast of Frodsham as it May be in ' 50 years hence, in which electricity and the Manchester Ship Canal were prominently noticed. At the close of the lecture Mr. RIGBY courteously showed a number of antique articles to those interested, which had been contributed by the Lecturer, also be Mary Kirkham (of Helsby), Mr. William Handley (of Runcorn), Henry Llnaker, Esq. (of Frodsham), and the sketches and rubbings! of tablets by Mr. Joseph Higher, of Frodsham Bridge. A. cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the Lecturer on the motion of Mr. R. HOLLAND, seconded by:Mr. E. A. WRIGHT, J.P ~ and brought a most enjoyable Meeting VI to close.

i.. - FIRE --AT THE CO-OPERATIVE 1` -' ' STORES, WARRINGTON. , Shortly hefore four o'clock on Saturday morning, a fira broke out in the bakehouse connected with the Co-operative Stores, Sankey-street. and a considerable amount of damage was done. The bakehouse was a two-storey brick building, standing at the rear of, and in close proximity to, the main block of buildings. The room on the ground floor, which was used as the bakehouse proper, contained about 600 loaves ef bread, and the kneading troughs were filled with some six or eight bags of flour in "sponge." The upper room was used as a store-room, and was well stocked with flour and empty bags. As soon as the fire was discovered, and an alarm had been raised, the door of the warehouse, a two-storey building which abutte upon the bakehouse, was broken open, and several cart loads of bags of flour were carted to a safe distance from the burning building. The fire brigade, under Supt. Turner, arrived on the scene with the reel cart about 9 minutes after the ringing of the fire bell, but the flames had then got such a hold on the building that the men wisely directed their efforts towards keeping the fire within the limits of the bakehonse. Two jets were speedily got into play, the connections being obtained with the mains in Sanket -street, and as there was a plentiful supply of water the flames were subdued about five o'clock, not, however, before the roof had fallen in and the building had been made a mere wreck, the bare walls alone remain- ing intact. Had it not been for the strenuous exertions of the fire brigade, doubtless the fire would have reached the adjoining buildings, as a one time it threatened to do, and considerable devastation would have then boen very pro- bable. As it wa, damage estimated at about £.500 was done, but this is covered by insurance in the Hand•in-hard , 8 ,ciety and the Royal Insurance SOcietY.' ll'otthstandling--- the unseasonable hour, the fire Was witnessed by a large Crowd of people. We have received the following communication reaped-' lug the fire : Sir,—As our "Warrington Fire Brigade has been some- what unfavourably criticised of. late, I have great pleasure in bearing testimony to its very great efficiency on the occasion of the fire on Saturday morning last. Very shortly after the alarm was givm the-men- arida- -their-apparatus were on the spot and quickly at work under the superin- tendence of Mr. F. Turner, Whose coomess and energy proved his fitness for the position he occupies. Had it net been for the prompt action of the firemen, ably seconded bY the police and the kindly help of g, utlemen in the neighi bourhood, there is reason to believe that it would soon have become one of the most caliinitous fires that has been seen in Warrington for many years past.—l am, yours, etc., Taos. RUSK/NIANA.—I am convinced that it is by his personal conduct that any man of ordinary power will do the great- est amount of good that is in him to do. Whenever you see want or misery, or degradation in the world about.yon there, be sans, either industry has been wanting or industry has been in error. You keep the Sabbath, in imitation of God's rest. Do, by all manner of means, if you like; and keep also the rest of the week in imitation of God's work. It may be proved with much certainty that God intends no man to live in this world without working; but it seems to ' me no less evident that He intends every man to be happy in his work. The real science of political economy . . . is that which teaches nations to desire and labour for the I things that lead to life, and which teaches them to scorn. and destroy the things that lead to destrurtion.—The Raskin Birthday Book. A BLIND POETESS.—For the ?last eighteen years of her, life, Janet Hamilton was blind. Her assiduity in reading by the dim oil lamp, or even the flickering light of the cot- tage fire, had contributed to this result. In any case, the world of darkness behind the sightless orbs is a painful thing to think of. In the case of Janet Hamilton, the de- privation was especially severe, for she was shut out from that world of light, colour, and form, the glow of flower, the gleam of leaf, the sparkle of the stream, wnich she loved with a poet's love. One compensation she had, and that was the singular force of her power of picturing the past. So closely and lovingly had she observed, and so intensely had she felt the sights and scenes of the outward world, so readily and vividly could she represent them, that the imagery of the past was almost as powerful as the real world of the present could have been. Her contentment under the loss of vision was unbroken.—Geed Words. JANET HAMILTON AND SHAKSPRILE —lt was not until after her marriage that she became acquainted with Shakspere. I This was the opening of a new world to her. But she had , to read him stealthily. In her rank in Scotland at the I time, Shakspere was somewhat in the _index Expurgatorius of popular judgment. But "I was drawn to him," she tells us, "as if by special instinct." She read him by snatches as she held her child in her arms, or rocked it in the cradle, and when a neighbour chanced to look in on her, she quietly pat the "profane author" in a hole of the wall, conveniently near at hand. This "special instinct" of which she speaks is the key to the whole of what is called 1 self-education. There is a preparedness in a likeness of soul ! which enables a man or woman to profit, through assimila- tion, with the best authors. Without this, no profit of any true or quickening kind is ever got. Janet Hamilton thus drew from this "well of English undefiled "—drew both diction and grammatical form. The influence is seen in Qte parity of her style, the strength and simplicity of har Saxon words, which fitted so well with her ex- cellent vernacular Scottish sprung from a common source. It is seen further in the almost uniform absence not only in her verse, but in her prose, pf that stilted and pedantic verbalism, from which self-taught writers, even such as Barns and Hogg, are seldom tree.—Professor Veitch in Good Words. The dancers move through the quadrille with little jerking steps, without bending their knees. They must keep their eyes staring, heads thrown back, necks stiff, and hands with all their fingers spread. They bow with a jerk, dance together, or turn round with the palms of their hands fiat together and fingers spread; always and in every way they, try to imitate the movements of jointed wooden dolls. The stare it necessary—no turning to look at partners; and arms should be always angular or straight. .Before each figure the four or eight dat,,, re may stand dOck still, till they are wound up one by one (with a spoon 4r an iron bed-key), and begin to jerk hands and feet in time to the music. "Hunt the Sixpence" will be a new and prettier form of "Hunt the Slipper." All the hands are put under the edge of the table-cover, and a sixpence is passed round from hand to hand, while one player, walking round the table, trios to guess where it is, and catches through the table-cover any pair of hands, whether belong- ing to the same player or to two that sit next each other. The hands caught must at once be ars., out and shown, , and whoever the sixpence is it with must be next to hunt it. It is unfair at any time to lay ton the table, but it is quite fair for those who have not it to pretend they are passing eomething, and so bewilder the hunter.— " Little Folks" Magazine. . SAD ACCIDENT ON THB Ter.—Seven men employed at a Dundee shipbuilding yard went down the Tay on Tuesday morning in a small yacht for the purpose of duck shooting. There was a strong squally breeze blowing at the time. Some hours afterwards the yacht was seea floating bottom up, and as some of the men's caps have been found in the river there is little doubt that the whole party were drowned when the boat capsized. The bodies have not been re- covered.

ALLEGED PRADDDLENT 11SE OF THE PREMIER'S NAME.— At the Mansion House Justice-room, on Wednesday, Mr. Henry Skinner was summoned before the Lord Mayor for obtaining a cheque for £lOO by false pretences. The defen- dant carried on a business in Leadenhall-street, under the style of Gladstone an Co., and the false pretence alleged to have been made by him to the complainant, Mr. William Gabbin, was that his partner in the firm was a nephew of the Prime Minister. The money had been paid as what was called earnest money.—The Lord Mayor said it was no use going on with the case, as civil proceedings were pend- ing, and dismissed the summons. A DEFAULTING WITNESS AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, a number of cases, brought by Peter Brown grocer, Kingsley, were struck out in conse- quence of the non-attendance of a witness named William Burrows, of Overton. Mr. Burton,, who appeared for the plaintiff in the cases, said that the witness had been duly served with a subprena and had been paid 2s 6d for his con- duct money, but failed to attend, and be had therefore to to ask his Honour to deal with the witness upon his sub- pcena. The Registrar having called over the witness's name three times and no answer being given, his Honour directed that notice be given to the witness to attend the next Court to show cause why be should not be fined £lO for his non- attendance, according to the statute. - ,

THE EXAMINER
BATIIADAY, FEBURABY 16, 1884.
I

BY a majority of zoo votes the' House of Lords on Tuesday evening censured the Government for their policy in Egypt. The result, we may say, was a foregone conclusion. It is a well - known fact that in the Gilded Chamber the Op- position are in a considerable majority, and it requires but very little effort on Lord SALISBURY'S part to carry an adverse motiofl,. and so strike a blow at the Government. It is not necessary that such a motion should be consistent with the truth, that it should be supported by facts, or that. it should bear scrutiny ; it is sufficient that it breathes a spirit of hostility to Mr. GLADSTONE'S Cabinet, and straightway the mechanical majority 14 ready to support it. Never during the present Parliament have the majority Of the Peers passed a resolution so unjust im- politic, and ungenerous as that which they carried on Tuesday. If there is one question above another on which the policy of the present Government has been sound, it is certainly on the Egyptian ques- tion; and we will add that if there is any English Ministry to be held responsible for the recent painful and distressing events in Egypt, that Ministry must be the one of which Lotd SALISBURY and Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE were members. We have a sus- picion, too, that they know this full well, arid knowing it, they find it necessary to excuse themselves by endeavouring to fix blame upon the shoulders of their successors, who have from the outbreak of the Egyptian com- plications adopted an exceedingly wise course. This was plainly shown, we think, on Tues- day, by the exhaustive speeches of Ea-1 GRAN- VILLE and Mr. GLADSTONE, the latter of whom has placed the whole facts of the case before the country in so clear and succinct a form that there is no escape from the conclu- sion that the disasters in the Soudan are the natural outcome of the Dual Control which the late Ministry set up. Let it be under- stood, too, that they were warned of what would occur, for on the 6th March, 180. M. GLADSTON-2, who, with his wonderful prescience, was able to forecast the future, pcinted out that the policy of the then Government involved not only financial, but political, and probably territorial responsi- bilities. From the evils flowing from that Control the present Government have never yet been able to extricate themselves, and we are afraid that escape now is still a long way of. To us the weakest point in the debates which have taken place in both Houses of i Parliament s that whilst the Conservatives have not been slow to find fault with the policy of the present Government and to condemn it, they have been careful not to promulgate a policy of their own. The Op- position insinuate that the Government ought to have known of the disaster which would befall HicKs and BAKER PACHAS, and to have been ready to avenge them; to have known Sinkat would be besieged, and to have been ready with relief; so with regard to Tokha ; and, indeed, they aver that we should have been able to have prevented every other mis- fortune in the Soudan. Why, the fact is, the very men who condemn the Government for abstaining from mixing up in the affairs of the Soudan would have been the first to have blamed the Government had they been foolish enough to interfere. It is true that the influence of England in Egypt is paramount, that we have put the Khedive upon the Throne and are bound to maintain his authority, and that it is our duty to guide jiirn and his Government by our counsels in all matters appertaining to the internal affairs of Egypt; but we are by no means obliged to follow the Egyptian Government in their wild escapades for the re-conquest of the Soudan, .even though Egypt had been for something like sixty years in possession of it. Yet, if the argument of the Opposition has anY meaning in it at all it must mean this, that seeing the Egyptian Government desired' and certainly the desire was a most unwise one —to hold the Soudan, we ought to have provided or raised an army sufficient for that purpose. The suggestion is altogether too outragous to be seriously supported by 3 majority of the House of Commons, or enter- tained by the country. Lord DUFFERIN, la the guise of an •` intelligent friend, though not of responsible governor," did, we are told, try to persuade the Egyptian Govern- ment to confine their operations in the Soudan within certain limits, but unfortu- nately his advice was not accepted. tended it gave colour to the belief that the force which the gallant officer commande,; would be sufficient to overcome the IVIADDI ; and the mission of BAKER Pacha and his force for the relief of Sinkat and Tokha had at first every prospect of being equally suc- cessful. One thing at least is clear, that those best able to judge were satisfied that the forces at the command of these officers were BUfficient, and that, the officers themselves Were supplied with whatever they wanted in men, arms, equipments, and every other requisite. That being the case, we fail to see that just because England happens to be in temporary occupation of Egypt the English Government is td blame. The re-conquest of the Soudan was entered upon by the KHEDIVE and his Government " before an English soldier set foot on Egyptian soil," its pro- secution was continued against the expressed wish of the English Cabinet, and, as Lord DERBY has sagely observed, the Misfortune to the Egyptian troops Would have happened even if there had been no English occupation of Egypt. What blame, then, can there attach to Mr. GLADsToNE's Government because of these disasters? It was not until the defeat of nicks PACHA that it began to dawn upon the XHEDIVE and his Ministers that they were linable to do that which they had undertaken, and not till then did they offer to act upon the advice of England. The official papers show that since then the English Government have done all they could to accomplish the evacuaticin of the Soudan, and if they have not taken the violent means advocated by the _Opposition for the relief of • Sinkat and koltha—in which garrisons there Were, after all, only about 1,000 men locked up—it was because the lives of 29,000 other persons Were imperilled. „. It would only, as a member of Parliament has stated, have been a case Of "sending troops to kill one set of men in order to save the lives of another set of man," a case in which no feelings of humanity are involved. The objection urged against the Government in :not sending out General GORDON earlier has, we think, beep satisfac- torily disposed •of He was not sent because the KHEDIVE would not at first ?have hint, but it is hoped that, now there has been a reconciliation, his mission may end as there is every reason to believe it will, in complete succeSs. Though many circum- stances have combined tu favour the present attack upon the Government, and though the assault has on the whole been made with c,..,°llsiderable vigour, we feel sure that Mr. `ll-A-DsToNE's historical survey of the events Which have led up to the present crisis Must carry conviction to the mir ds 9i all that there is no blame attaching lo the Government; and whatever may be die upshot of Sir STAFFORD NpRTHCOTE'S r_esolution, we hope with Lord DERBY that the k;abinet will not budge from the position hich they have taken up, feeling sure that "leY will be sustained and supported bY the voice of the country at large.

Urquattart, an inherence agent living in Newtown, failed to make his appearance at the appointed time. The Coroner instructed the sergeant in charge of the case to call the defaulting juror's name three times in the street, and this having been done, the Coroner fined the absentee 20s. THE BIRTH IND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending Saturday, Ferbuary 9th, 1864.—The mean temperature Was 39-7 Fehr., and therefore 2 degrees warmer than preceding week. The maximum temperature 54 Fah- renheit, Was recorded on the 4th instant, and the minimum , temperature 21 Fahrenheit on the 3rd instant. The rainfall measured an inch. The general direction of the wind was southwest. During the week, which was the 6th of the current year, 35 births and 15 deaths were registered. The drieti he thterate from all causes was equal to 177 per 1,000, against average of the previous four weeks, and against 211 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths in- eluded 1 from scarlet fever, 1 from whooping cough, 1 from diarrhtea, 1 from phthisis, 1 from liver disease, 1 from old age, 1 from lung disease and 2 from heart disease. One ease of smallpox and one case of scarlatina were re- ported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.— jc'el.Ft H. Goeteetare, medical officer of health. ZIONEIRY FROM A WIDNES BEER•ROUSH.—At Widnet Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Patrick Ford, a young fellow, _was charged with stealing a shilling from the till of the Lilackburne Arms, Warrington-road, Widnes.—lt appeared from the evidence of Annie Whalley, the landlady of the house, that en Monday morning the prisoner, accompanied by a man named Brannan, entered the inn, and had several glasses of beer in the bar-room. About a quarter to twelve Mrs. Whalley had occasion to leave the bar. On returning she found Brannan Was leaning over the counter with his hand in the money drawer. He was held up and supported by the prisoner, who had hold of his legs. Brannan had his hand full of coppers, but be threw them to the ground, and Mrs. Whalley asked him what he was doing there. He cernmenced to curse her, and then the men went out to.. gether. she gave information to PC. Mootes, who subee- eltlently apprehended the prisoner.—The prisoner, who denied hie complicity in the robbery, was sentenced to a month's d labour.

Dawson and Woolley, two most earnest and sums- ful evangelists, have conducted•revival services in Victoria- road Chapel, and the results of the ministrations have been very encouraging. VALENTINES DAY AT WIDNES—Six thOnSand missives were posted at Widnes on Wednesday night, and Mr. Dan- nett and his assistants had to work several extra hours to meet the pressure. On Thursday several thousand packages more than usual were delivered. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD—For some time past there has been a deficiency of school accommodation in Rancorn, especially in regard to girls, and about two months ago the Board resolved to ask Messrs F and G Holme, of Liverpool, to submit plans for the enlargement of Mill Brow Board school. This has been done, and the suggested additions, if carried out, will provide for 280 scholars. OUR LONDON LETTER.

MR. GLADSTONE'S GREAT SPEECH—ITS MATTER AND HIS MANNER VOLUNTEERING FOR EGYPT MR. BRADLAUGH THE DUKE OF MARLBOROUGH RAISING THE WIND MR. MATTHEW ARNOLD—A SCHOOLBOY'S LETTER —ACTORS AT THE PLAY—"YOU SHOULDN'T" ' ALMA TADEMA AT WORK. LONDON, TILIIIISDAY. yery rarely in the course of politics has a single speech had such a marvellous effect as that which followed upon Mr. Gladstone's oration of Tuesday ,night. The air was thick and cloudy witk misrepresentations trading upon ignorance and generous feeling. People whose notions of the Soudan, geographical and historical, are of the haziest description, talked largely on the subject. The old Jingo spirit shewed that it was not dead, but only sleeping. Once more we heard about England being disgraced, and touching telegrams ap- peared in their old colamns in the Times describing our brethren abroad " humiliated " at the recollection that they were Englishmen. To meet this mischievous muddle of mis-statement and misapplied philanthropy Mr. Gladstone set himself to relate the simple facts of the case. I will not spoil this by attempting to summarise it. I hope every- one has read the speech, as it is everyone's duty to do. What was remarkable about it as compared with other of the Premier's great efforts, was its extreme simplicity. There was, it will be noted, not a single quotation from the classics, a habit which is ever the high-water mark of his speechmaking. There was not even a single passage in prose worked up with elabrirate art. The speech was not rounded off as is his habit by a sonorous peroration. He spoke for two hours, and no one who sat and listened felt that the speech was long, or could place a finger on any sentence that might have been dispeneed Ivitb, He had a story to tell, and he told it with sublime simplicity, con- cealing the art with which it was woven together. It makes a fine piece of reading, but more than is usually the case it profited by delivery. Just before the Premier rose Sir William Harcourt came in, and seating himself by him re- ported that Earl Granville's speech in the other house had ' created some disappointment among the Liberal peers, who I held that he had not put the case strongly enough. "Then yon think I should pitch it high 2" the Premier asked, aftd , he did.

RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.—Among the books ordered to be purchased at the last meeting of the com- mittee, and to be added to the Library, are the following : Men of the Time (new edition), Tennyson's Works (new edition), Saturday Magazine (complete set), Pernor -Magazine-- (complete set), Story of Chinese Gordon, the Art of Soap Making, Ogilvie's Corn- prehensi ve Dictonary, Bearnont's History of Frodsham and Halton, Smiles' Lives of Engineers, Life of George Moore, , Life of Edward the Naturalist, The Huguenots, industrial Biography, Lyell's Antiquity of Man, Emerson's Works (new j edition), and Serjeant Ballantine's Experiences. A JUVENILE THEIF AT WIDNES. —At Widnes Poifce Court yesterday, before Mr. E. K. Muspratt, Mary Mc- Loughlin, 11 years of age, who was a fortnight ago convic- ted for a felony committed in Mr. Littler's draper shop, was charged with stealing half-a-crown from the till of the Queen's Arms public-house, Lugsdale, occupied by Charles Davies. About half-past eight that morning the prisoner went into the bar and called for a gill of beer, with which she was served. The landlord then went into the kitchen. On his return he missed half-a-crown frem the till, the only one he had noticed in it, and he followed the girl, who had gone away. As he was approaching her she saw him, drop- ped the half-crown, and ran, but he succeeded in capturing her, and gave her into the custody of P.C. Moores.—The prisoner was remanded until Monday.

THEFT BY A DOBIESTIC SERVANT AT RIINCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Frances Darley, 18 years of age, was brought up in custody charged with stealing a gold wedding ring and a parse containing 20s, the property of Sarah Phillipa Glover, milliner, High-street, Runcorn. The prisoner was employed by Mrs. Glover as domestic servant. On Sunday morning, the 30th December, Mrs. Glover got up about nine o'clock and found that the prisoner had left the house. She missed her dress, which contained in the pocket a purse, a gold wedding ring, and about 20s. Subsequently she found the dress in the sitting reons, but the pocket had been robbed of its contents. The prisoner, who came from Wifisford, had only been in her employ a few days. On the 3rd January the prisoner pledged the ring at the pawnbroker's shop of George Whit- taker, pawnbroker, Oldfleld-road, Salford, for de. The purse had been given to a boy named John William Cake, of 5, John Wood-street, Salford, in which street the pri- soner lived with another girl. Inspector Hollingworth on Saturday apprehended the prisoner in Manchester. She acknowledged the theft, and the Bench sentenced her to a month's imprisonment. FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE RAILWAY.-011 Tuesday afternoon, the county coroner, Mr. Brighouse, held an in. quest at the Widnes Accident Hospital touching the death of William Mills, 47 years of age, who was killed on the London and North-Western itallseay On Friday night,—Mr, Ferrand, of the solicrtore departmeet, Lidse4.reet gtation, Liverpool, was present on behalf of the company —Evidence was given by John Russsell, a shunter, John Holden, a platelayer, and James Carter, an inspector, all in the em- ploy of the company.—lt seemed that the deceased belonged to Brightside, near Sheffield, but for some time past had been tramping up and down the country, accompanied by his wife, in search of work. On the 4th February he was at Bolton, and next day. he journeyed as far as Ditton, where he was engaged by Mr. Evans, the contrac. or, as a labourer. The deceased obtained lodgings it Wellington- street. On the Bth inst. he and Holden walked together near the Ditton railway station,. where they parted. As the nearest way to the deceased's lodgings was along the line, it was supposed that be used that way, as his mangled body was found near the West Deviation Junction about half. past six. His head, body, and limbs were seriously injured, and he was removed to the Accident Hospital, where he died the same night. A verdict of accidental death was re- turned. Mr. Farrant, the foreman of the jury, appealed to these present on behalf of the widow, who was penniless, and he placed a sum of money on the table. His example was followed by the Coroner, Mr. Perrant, and the rest of the jurynyts, 25s being raised.

At first it seemed that he would not be able to finish since his voice shewed signs of failure. But he got over that with the assistance of his " pomatum pot," and had no more trouble till the end. The effect of this speech was instanta- neous and marvellous. The Liberals, who are curiously prone to believe all is lost, went about exultant, whilst the Con- servatives who, but the day before, had felt victory within their grasp, began to think things were not so good as they had looked. The same effect, though in lest degree, has spread throughout the country. The degree is less because the provincial Liberal is a much robuster personage than the metroplitan, and has the advantage of perspective in taking his view of correct events. But misapprehension existed in tbe country as well as in town, and a plain state- limit of facts has removed it. Napoleon's famous taunt about the English being a nation of shopkeepers seems to grow less and less applicable in its sense that they are not a fighting race. --- --- The person best known to the British public as Lord Blandford is about to celebrate his accession to the duke- dom of3farlborough by selling the family pictures. At this rate there will shortly be nothing left of Blenteim Palace but the bare walls and the pension. The late Duke, antici- pating his hopeful heir's intent, sold off the famous library. Prom information received he was convinced that if lie did not do it his successor would, and he arrived at the conclu- sion that the money would be better at his disposition than at his son's. His object was to obtain as much ready money as he could to bequeath to his favourite son, Lord Randolph Chuichill, This he succeeded in doing, and only just in time, his death following close upon the dispersion of the Sunderland library. The new Duke cannot sell Blen- heim Rouse, but I am not sure that he could not let it for an hotel. If he can he certainly will.

A friend sends me from Chicago a description of Matthew Arnold as he appeared before an American audience. He is described as "a tall spare man with a fine thoughtful face. His hair, which is tinged with grey, is somewhat curly, and he wears it parted in the middle. His aide whiskers are carefully blocked off, while his lip and chin are smooth shaven." This is a very accurate catalogue of Mr. Arnold's personal appearance, though I do not know tbat to those not familiar with it it would bring up a faithful realisation. The most amusing thing made in the Comments on Mr. Matthew Arnold' is the criticism on his accent. It is said that his speech is "marked by a broad English accent." This is striking to the Engliskraan, but it is a frequent ob- servation among the AIIIeriCALIS. I remember in New York hearing a well known man bitterly spoken of as returning from England with an affectation of the English accent. One would suppose that England is the place where it might be sought; but it is not so. America, which sends us beef and corn, might, if it pleased, supply us with the true accent. - The ninth annual metlitg of thla tiQpany was held on Tuesday last under the presideficSo of the chairman, Mr. Joseph Cook, who, in meting the adoption of the report and balance sheet, observed that the directors recommended that a dividend at the rate of 103 per share be paid out of the profits, and £3,000 placed to the depreciation fund, leaving a balance of £B3O to be carried forward to next year's account. Mr. Bancroft seconded the motion. He said the improvement in the position of the company had been very decided during the year. The liabilities had been reduced to an important extent, especia.ly in the department of special loans, and it was the intention of the directors to continue to pay them off from time to time. He hoped the company would enjoy ,in the future such prosperity as it had experienced in the past year. and looking at the en- 'banned price of chemical products consequent on the restriction in the manufacture, he had no doubt that they Might fairly anticipate a good time during the next year. Mr. Robinson pointed out that the profits of the company had been fairly earned in the open market without any adventitious aid.—Mr. R. Cook said 'the directors had refrained from paying as large a dividend as they might have done, in order that they might dis- charge some of the liabilities of the company, and consoli- date the property of the shareholders.—The report was adopted.—The retiring directors, Mr. Joseph Cook and Mr. Thomas Robinson, were unanimously re-elected; and Messrs. Stead, Taylor, and Stead were re-appointed auditors to the company.

Iboarding schools, bow this came to pass. In due course young lout teen-and-a-half returned the following answer:— " The conduct mark is the prefect's mark, and refers to my conduct during play time and meal time. I get a bad Mark in meal time for several reasons. Because I would not eat a pieca of meat one side of which was burned and the other raw; because whenever I manage to get hold of an extra portion of butter I keep it; because I put a bottle of sheepwash on the table and the prefect took it under the impression that it was port wine (he does ,not know I put it there, but he takes that for granted); because when he took some potted meat, from me I smeared it over with butter so that he should ; not get it; because I said a round loaf was a round loaf, , and be said it was a square ens; because I would not 'help eat a piece of a loaf that had been in the basket for two or ' three days; because whenever the prefect wanted to catch a boy doing anything at table I gave the boy warning; because whenever anyone played a joke on the prefect I laughed at him; because I preferred talking in the reflectory, to listening .to A History of Our Own Times by Justin McCarthy, M.P.' As for recreation, there are also several reasons for getting a bad mark. Be- cause I grumbled when the prefect made our school pay 103. for mending a table which we never broke; because I in company with the rest of the school denied having broken a window which was broken while we were in another room; because when he asked me whether I had any matches, in other words, gave me my choice between a dogging and a lie, I would not tell him; because I never believe anything he says. These are all the reasons I can remember at present." They Will probably strike the impar- tial mind as being sufficient, at least in number.

Anything so interesting and so interested as the audience at the Lyceum, on Tuesday morning, I think I have never seen. Mary Anderson followed Wilson Barrett's example, and gave a matinee to the profession. The guests were all invited—no money was taken. Certainly a theatrical audience is an amusing one. I wish I could give you an idea of the dress of these actresses, or of the interest which they took in one another. It was agreed that Mrs. Bernard Beers was the best dressed. She has a way of "assisting " her upper eyelid, which gives her beautiful eyes an additionally languid loveliness. Mary Anderson being American, Minnie Palmer was, of course, one of the guests, and looked in her little pert bat peculiarly piquante. Miss Anderson acted better than I have seen her do. There was more spirit and more subtlety in her "Clarice." How will she do Juliet, and who will be her Borneo? The report is that she wants Drury-lane in the season, and will bring out the play with a magnificence that will scare Irving.

The popular "Don't," that universal guide to good man- ners, hat been followed by "You should not," in which an aristocrat is supposed to lecture us all on the things which we ought not to do. I think for cold impudence and Yankee vulgarity I never read a book like this. The aristocrat gives counsel above everything—negative and minatory counsel. Through all the routine of life, morning calls, afternoon teas, the delacacies of courtship, the conduct of servants, in all these emergencies he is'at our elbow with his "You shouldn't." He stands to his readers even in death, which he charitably , assumes will take place on the scaffold, when his last , warning is that with the noose round their necks they should not turn pale or strive to interrupt the executioner in the discharge of his duty. The humour of the book is very grim, and when you have taken it up it is very hard to lay it down. :Just now London is very full of it. I have been favoured with an opportunity for a visit to the studio of Mr. Alma Tadema, and found him 'still busy with his large picture for the Academy. Enthusiastic as over on all subjecte connected with Roman history, Etna I Which, he reminds us, is also English history, since SO many of our laws, customs, ceremonies, and pastimes, even to our Chfistmas misseltoe, have their origin in Rome, Mr. Tadema has chosen for his present subject the visit of the Emperor Hadrian to Britain. It is related how this wise ruler wished to acquaint himself not only with the extent of the empire beneath his sway, but with the manners and tastes prevailing in different countrles, and the progress made in such branches of science and art as existed in those days. It might naturally be conjectured that while in Britain he would have visited the Potteries to see in what fashion the potter shaped his ware. At any rate, Mr. Tadema would have done so had he been the Emperor Hadrian. Accordingly the scene is placed in a pottery, wherein Sabina and other distinguished Roman guests are being shown the pitchers of many shapes that are placed on shelves around. Many are the trophies lying about in honour of the visit; and Mr. Tadema has given himself some good opportunities for exercising his greatest triumphs in colour and skilful finish. Critics who should look for the renowned marble and blue sky will not find them this time, but may console themselves with the dig- nity and grace of the figures.

PRIMITIVE METHODIbT MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS, RUNCORN. ANNUAL MEETING. The first annual meeting of this society was held in Regent-street Schoolroom, on Tuesday evening. Tea was provided at half-past six, to which about thirty members sat down. The tables were presided over by Mrs. James Stubbs, Mrs. Jabez Stubbs, and Mrs. R. Stebbs. After the tables were cleared fruit was distributed, and Mr. String- fellow was voted to the chair. Amongst those present were the Rev,,J. Pickwell, Messrs. R. Hillidge, Upton, Joseph Ashley, John Shingler, Jabaes Stubbs' Jabez Stubbs, Robert Stubbs, P. Stubbs, W. Hoxworth, and John Nickson. The Chairman called upon the secretary to read the report, which was duly adopted. Mr. T. Stringfellow was elected president for the ensuing year, in the place of the Rev. J. Pickwell, who, it was explained, for obvious reasons and his many duties was unable to fill the functions of that office. Mr. J. T. Nickson and Mr.W.Gittens were re-appointed secretary and assistant secretary respectively. The following were elected to form a committee :—The Chairman, Secretary, Messrs. Ashley, Upton, P. Stubbs, James Stubbs, and R. Stubbs. The following gentlemen were elected vice-oresi- dents of the class :—The Rev. James Pickwell, Mr. James , Stubbs, and Mr. R. Hillidge, and Mr. Joseph Ashley and ' Mr. Upton were re-appointed. After votes of thanks had been passed to the waiters, Mr. W. Gittens for a donation of 48, and the Secretaries, Mr. T, Stringfellow, the newly- elected president,, addressed a few words to those present, and remarked that he took a great interest in the class, and ' mid 09 his best to ensure its success, The Rev. J. Pick- well also addressed the meeting. The remainder of the evening was spent in social diversion, a short programme 1 of music, recitations, &c., being introduced, and taken part in by Messrs. W. Hoxworth, James Stubbs, Jabez Stubbs, R. Hillidge, B. Lewis, W. Millington' F. Eden, and J. T. Nickson. Shortly before ten o'clock the party diapersed. It was unanimously resolved that meetings of a similar kind should be held more frequently, and it is thought that by this means other persons will he induced to join the class. ..........-4111wwwe SAD DEPRAVITY AT RUNCORN. 1 At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. Jas. 'Handley and Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, Mary Kirkham, Elizabeth Cross, and Elizabeth Filkin, married women, were I charged in cureody with having, on the 13th February, [ feloniously stolen nine half-pint glasses and a gallon jug, value 2s. 6d., the property of William Treverton. The pri- soners were further charged with receiving these articles knowing them to have been stolen, and also with having at the same time and place, did aid, counsel, and procure the commission of the said offence. It appeared that Treverton formerly was the landlord of the beerbouse called the Bird in Hand, Ilalton-road, but now lived at 6, Alcock.street. When he left the beerhonse, on the 18th Oct. last, he allowed a dozen half-pint glasses and a 'gallon jug to remain, and having locked the back and front doors be gave the keys to the brewer's agent, who lived at Bedford Leigh. He identi- a.l one of the glasses produced in court as his own, and his wife also recognised it. A witness named Ann Weedall, wife of Thomas Weedall, a boatman living In Irwell-lane, made a statement to the effect that on Wednesday morning she met Filkin going to the pawnshop with s shirt, and having obtained 2s. upon it, they went to the house ef the prisoner Crossl where they remained drinking , until both the money and the liquor was finished. ,It was then suggested, as they must have beer, from somewhere, that they should rob the Bird in Hand. This was agreed to; and with the help of Weedall, Cross, and Kirkham affected an enterance into the house. In a LOW minutes they returned with the glasses and jug, which were given into the custody of Weedall, who promised to sell them. Filkin, who had taken no part in the affair, lent her shawl to the witness to cover the articles. Instead of disposing of the articles however, Weedall went direct to the police station, where ;he gave information of the robbery. Subsequently the ptisoners were apprehended. Weedall was cross- examined by the prisoners to show that she had been a ring-- leader in the robbery, and had even declared that it was only like poaching, and she had done many a trick like it.—Mr. Handley said it was a very disgraceful state of things to exist—that women should spend the day in drinking in this manner. Kirkham and Cross were each fined 20s and costs, or in default a month's imprisonment; but as there seemed to be a doutit in the case of Filkin. the Bench discharged her in tne hope that it would be a warning to her.—Weedall was then called before- the Bench. and Mr. Handley said 1 she was quite as bad as the two who had been convicted. ' (Weedall: Yes, sir.) The Bench hoped she would mend , her ways. She bad had a narrow escape. Weedall (laughing) : I will mind what company I go into next time, air.

He was the oldest member of the Board (apart from the Chairman) and he thought they ought to give preference to seniority and ability as well.— The CHAIRMAN said if he did not stand he could claim to be the returning officer. Rat whether he stood or'not it was important that a returning officer should be appointed, as he could not give a decided answer. The annual tea party, w'as held in the National Schools on Wednesday evening, when there were about 450 persons present. At the public meeting and entertainment which was subsequently held, under the presidency of the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar, the room was crowded to excess. A capital programme of instrumental and vocal music was gone through in unimpeachable style, the following taking part :—Miss Poole, Miss Cook, Miss Fairies, Miss A. Par- ver, Messrs. Wilkinson, White, Powell, Davies, ileyes, San- key, Large, Moulson, and Ireland. Under the leadership of Mr. Crawford the glee class rendered several part-songs in an enjoyable manner. The CHAIRMAN, instead of deliver- ing his usual annual address, referred those present to the Monthly Magazine, which contained an account of all the work of the parish. It would be out of place, however, if he did not express very briefly his indebtedness to the band of lay workers. Last February they had 140 lay workers in the parish engaged in different branches of the church's operations. When people said the Church of England for- got how to use its lay wqrkers he thought they were either before or behind their age. So far as he was concerned he thought the number ought to be multiplied by two, and if they would read the Parish Messenger for that mcmtb they would not be backward in offering their services. He referred to the assistance he had received from the district visitors, Sunday school teachers, the temperance ,workers, glee class, and choir, whose services had been ungrudgingly given. During the eight or nine months he had been without a curate in the parish, be bad been greatly aided by Mr. Imisan and Mr. Neil at the &Horde Mission Room, and to all these various workers he moved a hearty vote of thanks, which was car- ried with acclamation.—Mr. J. B. Imisow, churchwarden, replied, and moved a vote of thanks to those ladies and gen- tlemen who had assisted in preparing tea that evening, and who had given donations.—Mr. Kir.cgoss seconded the motion, observing that 15 new tea urns had been made and presented by three men belonging to the Church of England Temperance Society. (Applause.)—The motion was car- ried.—On the proposition!of Mr. W. TREACY, sen., seconded by M. ATHERTON, the ladies and gentlemen who had pro- vided the evening's entertainment were heartily thanked and a similar compliment having been paid to the Chair man, the proceedings terminated.

UNFOUNDED CITA RGES AGAINST A WIDNES MEDICAL MAN. At the George Hotel, Widnes, on Tuesday afternoon, Mr Brighouse, the county coroner, held an inquest on the body of the infant child of Francis Dillon, a labourer, living in Pitt-street. Inspector Wood was present. It was alleged oy Dillon that the child had died through Mr. ' Richards, the assistant to Dr. McDonnell, injuring it by using instruments. His wife was not yet 21 years of age, I and she had had a mishap before the birth of the deceased. 1 He was much dissatisfied when be discovered that Mr. Richards was note fully qualified medical man. He thought his wifeshould have been longer in labour before the I instruments were used.—The Coroner asked whether the witness, who had no medical experience, and was not in the room with the doctor, was in a position to say the instrument ought not to have been used. Though the lives of the people ought to be protected against unprofessional practi- tioners, at tie same time ttie medical profession ought to be protected from unfounded charges. He could only say that he was the father of a great many children, and he differed entirely from the wituess.—Witness said if he hid known Mr. Richards was not qualified he would not have attended his wife.—Francis Miller. of 5, Sankey-street, Widnes, said she had been a mid-wife for twenty year. under a medical certificate given her by a doctor. , She had lived in Widnes 33 years. She attended Mrs. Dillon on Sunday, and sent for the doctor. Had not Mr. Richards used the forceps the woman might have died. Mr Richards did his utmost to save the child, and he was more subtle in such cases than any medical man that had came under her ob- servation.—Mr. EL A. Richards was then called, and cau- tioned that he did not need to make a statement unless he desired, as it might be used in evidence against him. He said he was quite prepared to make a statement. He was assistant to Dr. McDonnell. He was not a qualified man. He had been assistant to Dr. McDonnell for 18 months, and for several years was assistant to Dr. Davies, of Southport. He left the latter gentleman with a good character, and had splendid testimonials from him and other gentlemen. Be had attended considerably over 1,000 Cases of child-birth, and not a single death had occurred under his practice. He described the course he pursued in this instance.—The Coroner said this was tie whole of the evidence he pro- posed to bring before the jury. They would agree with hire that whatever station a person might occupy it was quite right that his interests should be protected, and that whether he be a labourer or a duke he ought to have the same censideration at their bands. At the same time it was quite proper that professional men should be protected in pursuing their calling. He reviewed the evidence, and the jury were left to consider their verdict. After the lapse of several minutes the Coroner was recalled, and the jury in- timated that they had come to the conclusion that the child died from exhaustion, and that neither the midwife or Mr. Richards were to blame.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Messrs. Wm. Bankes and Henry Reynolds.—Thomas Hodekinson, , landlord of the Feathers Inn, Church-street, was -charged with haying, on the 31st January, permitted women of bad character to remain on his licensed premises longer than was necessary for reasonable refreshment —Mr. W. H. Linaker defended—P.S. McMichael said on Thursday night, the 31st January, about ten minutes past ten o'clock, he was on duty in Church-street. He remained in front of the defendant's house from that time until 10-35, in order to notice if any person went in and came out. P.C. Kelly was with him, and they only saw one man go in, and the same man shortly afterwards came out. At five and twenty minutes to eleven he (witness went into the house with the Constable. In the bar parlour he found three fallen women sitting down with a number of men. Their names were Annie Radford, Sarah Blower, and Mary Wilson. In the tap-room he found three other fallen women, and there were a number of men in the room. The women were named Elizabeth Ann Barr, Mary Walsh, and Louisa Spencer. He called the defendant's attention to the women, and he replied that they had only just come in. He (witness) then went outside, and remained where he could watch the house until a quarter to eleven, when the women came out The men in the house appeared to be seafarers. The house was the habitual resort of fallen women, and he had on several occasions cautioned the defendant—P.C. Kelly corroborated this testimony.— Mr. Linaker asked the Bench to dismiss the case. Twenty- aye minutes was not an unreasonable time to stay in a house

for refreshment, and surely these girls, alth-3ugh they were unfortunate, had as much right if they behaved themselves to the privileges of English people. The .police had not alleged that there was anything indecent taking place. There was no drunkenness—in fact nothing was going on that , might not properly go on; and Mr. Linaker asked the Beach to extend the same rights and privileges as to anyone else. He pointed out that the Act of Parliament was to prevent these girls following their vocation on licensed premises. —The defendant was called, and stated that the girls were not in the house more than a quarter of an hour, and were only served with one glass ot beer —Thomas Tiodgkinson, junr., stated that he was at the theatre on the night in ques- tion, and arrived home at twenty minutes past ten. There were then no women in the house, and ten minutes elapsed before any entered. John Shaw, labourer at Messrs; Ockirston's and Geo. Dunning, Weston Point, gave corroborative evidence. The latter said be hid always found the Feathers a respectable house. Alexander Beech, a flatman. and Thomas Goodier, a flatman, having been ex- amined, Mx. Bankes said the case has been clearly proved, and we fine the defendant £5 and costs. It is the second conviction for tbe same offence within 12 months. We shall endorse the license.—The costs amounted to 165 dd.— Mr. Linaker asked the Bsncb to rrconsidor thslr decision with regard to endorsing the license.—Mr. B4nkes : The house has been thoroughly badly conducted and the Bench must put a stop to it —Mr. Linaker said he appeared for I Mr. Jones, who WAS the owner of the property, and it was a at o very. seriousce. Th matter. Benchatte r . declined in.oed to reconsideruidClearoilttbe nreqnt tenant the matter, and Mr. Linaker gave notice of' appeal.

div.p: should adjoin. Dr.O'KEErmt, moved and Mr. Canny seconded the adoption of the minutes. Mr. WatGrtv congratulated the committee upon having, stamped oat smallpox, and also for bringing forward the question of a public cemetery for Widnes. It was a question with which they would have to deal with in the immediate future, and they could choose whether they would deal With it now or wait until they were made to take it up. He suggested that the subject should be referred to the General Purposes Cemmittee.—Mr. WEBSTER thought they should approach the subject without haste, and consider it carefully.. —Mr. WRIGHT observed that it would take two years to bring the matter to a climax.—Dr. O'KEEFFE said the com- mittee had been successful in stamping the smallpox out. The last case in the tent was removed 18 days ago, and there had been no other outbreak in the township since. They were, however, keeping the tents up as long as Major Cross would allow them the land. The committee thought it advisable to carry out the resolution that was passed by the Board several months age, viz., to provide a suitable . site for an Infections Diseases Hospital, in order that they could adopt the recommendation of Dr. Thorne. That gentleman on his recent visit to Widnes said that if they got a site now they need not build the ho4pital in a hurry, but do it gradually and carefully, and in such a way that would prevent the public from having any objection to be removed there no matter what condition of society they be- longed to. Dr. Thorne was an important and most intelli- gent official of the Local Government Board, and a highly capable medical man, and he (Dr. O'Keeffe) thought they could not do better than take the measures he recommended with regard to the hospital. There were two cemeteries in the township that must necessarily be closed soon unless they were extended, and he thought the Board ought to make provision. As Mr. Wright had lastly remarked, it would take them about two years to make the arrangements • complete. They would have to secure a field about 20 acres in extent, and centrally situated, en that it would not be objectionable to any class of the community. Mr. Cope- land informed him that at Middlesborough they had the Infectious Diseases Hospital in one nice cosy corner of the cemetery, and he did not think there would be any objection to such an arrangement in Widnes. (Laughter.) The coMmittee only desired to have the opinion of the Beard on the snhject. There were one or two of the cemeteries in the town that were unsightly, and, speaking frput a medical point of view and as a member of the Health Committee, he wished that one of them was closed now and no more interments allowed to take place there.—The Chairman suggested that the Health Committee should gather more intortnation on the subject. There was no doubt a hospital and cemetery would shortly became necess.ties of the place—Mr. WEBSTER IVAS of opinion that it would be objectionable to have the sites for the hospital and cemetery adjoining each other, and Mr. HANDLEY and the Crtervemera concurred.—The matter was referred back to the committee, and the minutes were passed.

TUESDAY. PARTNERSHIP DISPUTH AT RUNCoRN.—Peter Sinnott. of Top Locks, ship chandler, sued Messrs. Amer and Co., of Fleetwood, ship brokers, for the stun of £2 Is., which he alleged was due to him for freight as the owner of 2-64th shares in the "Polly Whittaker."—Mr. Linaker appeared for the plaintiff, and called Robert Dixon, master mariner, of Fleetwood, who said he was captain of the "Folly Whittaker" during some portion of last year. Towards tho latter portion of last year he made a voyage from Birken- head to Havre, and from St. valery to Birkenhead back again. The total freight for those journeys was £230 183.3 d.. from which must be deducted the expenses of the two voyages—£99 ffs. 7d., leaving a balance of £l3l Ss. M., out of which he received his share as captain amounting to £65 14s. 4cl. and there was also to be deducted accounts contracted during the voyage amounting to about £2, as well as some wages, the balance to be divided amongst the shareholders. He was a shareholder, and received a dividend on his shares.—Robert Foulkes, Runcorn, was called, and stated that towards the latter end of October or beginning of November, last year, he received from Messrs. Amer and Co. a cheque for £2 is., as dividend due to him on the two voyages which bad been referred to.—ln cross- examination by Mr. Edmondson, of Fleetwood, who ap- peared for defendant, he admitted he did not receive any statement of accounts with the cheque.—Mr. Edmondson, in defence, said he should prove that after paying all the expenses in connection with these two voy- ages the plaintiff had had all the dividend he was entitled to, and, in fact, was in debt to the defendant to the extent of Is. He ad- • mitted a cheqae was sent to Mr. Foulkes, but this was in mistike. He called the defendant, John Amer, who said he paid the captain, Robert Dixon the sum of £8 10s for wages and disbursements, bat had not the recipt with him. The practice was for the captain to receive the freight in the first instance, and then take his books to the managing owner when the accounts were settled pro and con, and if there was a balance it was paid to whoever was entitled to it. The vessel was sold for £2,210, the commission on sale was £22 10s, expenses of sale £5, and various disburse- ments, leaving the amount available for dividend on the freight £2B 9s id. The dividend due to plaintiff on this sum would be 17s 9d, and his share of the purchase money from the eels of the ship would be £69 Is 3d. making a total of £69 195., but in reality he had received £7o.—Wm. Cooper, sail maker, Top Looks, said he was a shareholdar in the "Folly Whittaker," and had not received any dividend on the freight for the two voyages before mentioned. The ship Was sold to his entire satisfaction and the mosey in- vested in another ship.—His Honour said that he thought from the evidence the plaintiff had had all he was entitled to, and he must therefore give judgment for the defen- dant.
