div.head: tittrs to flit editor:
div.p: tittrs to flit editor:

, . THE RECTOR AND HIS Cl/RATES. Sir —1 was much impressed with your report of the pre- sentation of such substantial tokens of respect and esteem to Mr. Cory and Mr. Mitchell. I have, no doubt that the extreme diffidence and modesty so characteristic of our charitable Rector caused the town to lose the effect that would have been produced had he made the presentations instead of Mr. Pierpoint. It is no light matter for the Rector to lore the services of "two of the best curates War. rington has seen ;" and seeing that the congregation wor- shipping at the Parish Church have received such spiritual benefits from the labours of these two gentlemen, his anguish must have been too severe for public exhibition at a farewell meeting. Still, one would think, that the Rector's good lady might have summoned a little fortitude, and by her presence have cheered the parting friends. The kindly feeling dieplayA in the public streets when this lady and the curates met was but another convincing proof of the power of love. The song has it, "We never speak as we pass by." In thel matter I refer to feeling would be too strong to allow of speaking. Mr. Cory, in acknowledging the presentation, spoke rather enigmatically at one point—" When pastor and people were about to be separated, wholly against their will, in accordance with the wishes of the powers that be." What could this mean? Was not "the peace that passeth all understanding" complete between the Rector and his curates ; or could it be that the curates' loving ministrations amongst the people had so endeared them to each other that the Rector was reminded of the worn out broom? Mr. Mitchell referred to "his tongue having been silent so long that it had had time to grow longer." Surely jealousy had nothing to do with this. Instead of physical help being required to help the Roctor into his pulpit, the strong and nimble curates ought to have oMciated, and the bond of love already strong in this happy family would have been made stronger. But I have no doubt that should Mr. Mitchell find time to run down to Warrington, the rectory doors will always be found wide open to welcome as a guest one so loved by the people.—! am, &c., Warrington, February 5,1884.
CLIFFORD DIX.

Sir,—ln your last issue there was an account of a meet- ing held at the Rectory by invitation of the Rector of War- rington. Now, sir, it seems to me to be a most cowardly action on the part of the Rector to have called a meeting after the curates had left the town. I think that the parishioners have seen grossly insulted by the Rector in not having called all the parishioners together, which I submit was the proper thing to do. But the Rector was meat careful as to whom he sent invitations to. Our curates, whom all (but the chosen few) respect, have been compelled to depart from amongst us, and find labours elsewhere. And I hope they may receive kind and just treatment such as honourable gentleuien . ought to receive. Well may our Church feed dissent and disunion when our clergy are torn away from the people they love, and the parishioners get no explanation of it.—l am, sir, yours truly, A PARISHIONER. Warrington, February, 1884.
SUCCESS OF THE WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF AR C. .

Sir,—As the subscribers to the new building will be in- terested to know how far their efforts have been successful in promoting the welfare of the school, I shall be glad if you will permit me through your issue to make the fact public that since the opening of the new rooms 70 new students have joined.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, WM. OWEN, Hon. Secretary. School of Art, Museum-street, Warrington, February 14th, 1884.

"POT-HOUSE ARRANGEMENTS." Sir,—l rather envy "A Ratepayer's" sublime state of mind. Perched on the Olympus heights of conceit, he drags up the abusive phrase at the head of my letter with the fell intention of hurling it at the poor devoted heads of all who fail to see eye to eye with himself. If I may pre- sume to give a little advice to "A Ratepayer," it would be this—" If you wish to teach the people, plant yourself on firm ground; give yourself a personality when you are per- sonal to others." I have very rarely met with teetotalfers who understood temperance. It seems to be a fatality that these men should be a narrow-minded lot of abusive despots, who think to reform the world by pushing the teapot down everyone's throat. Your correspondent, referring to publi- cans, calls them "a class of individuals '." further on he re- fers to "one gentleman, a publican, who had signed the petition,was actually objecting to his own brother's increase of salary." Now, here we see that publicans can be "a class of individuals," " gentlemen," and honestly sign a petition having for its object the general welfare. In the special case referred to the official concerned had never, according to the report, asked for an increase of salary. But what is the spirit that rune through "A Ratepayer's" abusive letter? A guarded nish to do his brother officials a good turn, and then mount his teetotal hobby-horse and have a tilt at everything that does not emanate from the pop bottle. lam not in favour of the business of the town being settled in public-houses, and lam not aware that our Liberal councillors do this thing. The Conservatives I leave to defend themselves. I am also mach opposed to a respectable bar parlour being called a " pot-house." I am sure that men of temperate habits, who know how to control the appetite as well as the tongue, are much superior to men who have to pledge themselves to a rule of conduct in consequence of their own weakness; and that they have as much right to meet during their short intervals of rest at a public-house.- odor a pipe or a glass, as our pastors and masters have to meet at a gentleman's club, smoke sixpenny cigars, and drink expensive liquors. As noble actions and good solid work can come from the " midst of smoke and beer" as ever came from a teetotallers' lodgeroom. "A Ratepayer" cannot go into a bar-parlour in the town without meeting with men whose aid he would be proud to accept in any ameliorating • work that might be going on. Nay, I will say more, it is the influence of moderators that will have to regenerate society. The leaven preceeding from a temperate towns- man must in the end have a beneficial effect; while the ranting and raving of fanatical men like your correspondent has the opposite. I state clearly that I go occasionally to the public-house; he never saw me the worse for it. I am not a shareholder in a political club at which "nth drinking and, lam sorry to say, gambling are allowed. Can he say the same? The fact is, a certain section of the Liberal party want to force their watery nostrum to the front. It won't do. The party will split on such despotic notions. I myself would never vote for a man pledged to float the tee- tetal plank to the front. I must say more than this. There are publicans who are a disgrace to their manhood, who would take the last halfpenny from a man yen when they kaew his child was starving. This class are happily dying out. They are not the fittest, therefore they do not survive, but why are they not the fittest? and how is it proved? The answer is given constantly in bar-rooms. A publican who encourages drunkenness does it to his cost. I have more than once, aye, more than a dozen times, lectured publicans of the desirability of keeping their houses free of bad lan- guage, and clear of licence. Where is the teetolar in this town who does this? Not one. With respect to the peti- tion, I have reason to think that nearly all our tradesmen would have signed it had they bad the chance. It was but a vary few hours before the public. You can scarcely speak to a shopkeeper without hearing complaints of heavy rents • and heavy taxes. Anxious thought is required for the safe conduct of their business, and at the end what is their gain? The right to be enrolled on the bankruptcy list. The same with working men. Trade bad, wages tending th,-; wrong way, inability to pay their way, the fewest pos. sil.le of UN 'S luxuries; and with all this we are asked to raise the salaries ef men who are already receiving better wages than they could earn in other spheres. Ido not wish to -an them down, they may be very capable men, but then Oil is no special qualification now-a-days. In conclusion, attention to the 15th of allow me to tarn "-.A.Ratepayees,, St. Matthew, 11th verse, "Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man." It he will study this verse a little a guide his tongue in the future.— _ 11. WHITHA'aI. ii 1 I help him to • Warrington, February, 11,18.4

JOSEPH ARCH AT RUNCORN. Sirt—lt may be interesting to those of vier readers who were present at the great Liberal meeting at Itnnisorn last week to know something of the early struggles of the man to whom they, in commurtwittrtiaertnet of that magnificent audience, de- lighted to do honour—Joseph Arch. The Rev. Mr. Atten- borough, in his biographical sketch of Mr. Arch, alludes to he hst days of his father, who, after more than fifty years of Wearisome toil, and when he could no loner drag his tired limbs to the fields, was compelled Wake to his bed and turn his face to the wall. The savings of a lifetime of pain- ful industry and thrift amounted to four shillings and six- pence! "The worn crumbling Arch, just tumbling &mist was to be propped up with good support,' and there was four shillings and sixpence towards providing it. 'Give him sons beef tea, get him a drop of good wine if you can, '

and take this prescription to the chemist's.' The poor patient's friends sat wondering and weighing his four- and sixpence against the doctor's counsel ; it was nowhere. The old man wept, knowing he was, after all his work, to become a burden to those he loved, and who, as he knew, had barely enough for themselves. 'I be afeard, Joe, the parish will give thee nethin' for me, be'n as yer a Dissenter. Joe was not anxious they should; but Joe's wife had been in the habit of earning a couple of shillings a week at charing, and now That the old man wanted nursing she had to give this up and stop at home. To the guardians Arch made a reasonable offer: Gentlemen, I don't want you to support my aged father; but if you will give my wife one shilling and sixpence towards nursing him, now that she is cut off her charing, I shall be much obliged to you; it isn't much; We less than the loss of my wife's earnings, and nothing to- wards the expense.' 'Certainly not, Arch, your father can go to the * the house," and you must pay one and sixpence towards his support.' 'Goal morning, gentlemen I'd sooner rot under a hedge than he should go there.' The old man lingered for ten months, and during the last few weeks of his life the parish, against Arch's will, but with the consent of his wife, allowed him one shilling and sixpence and a loaf. Then he died, and his son bought him a coffin and hid him down in the earth, on whose broad, bountiful breast there seemed to be no room for him. Fifty years a worker, thirty years a ratepayer, a life's saving of four shillings and sixpence, a choice between the workhouse and his son's poor cottage, eighteen pence and a loaf for two months—thie was the life.story of Arch senior ! " With such sad experiences as these it is no wonder that now and then we hear an ominous growl from those whose position is between the hammer and the anvil such as— Beware— Lest when our latest hope is fled, Ye taste of our despair, And learn by proof in some wild hour How much the wretched dare." After the many struggles incident to the early career of a ploughman we find Mr. Arch at the age of twenty arriving at the acme of an agricultural labourer's position, earning the highest wages to be obtained, viz., eleven shillings a week. He became a local preacher at this time. lie married, and in course of time two children were born, when unfortunately wages fell to nine shillings a week. This was too bad; and Mrs. Arch went to charing and Joseph trudged away in search of more remunerative employment. He was unsuccessful and returned to Bar- ford, after having seen poverty, beside which their stan- dard was one of plenty. He tells how in Herefordshire he found able-bodied men with wives and families toiling from morning till night for seven shillings a week. With one of these he once lodged. How the wife and children sub- sisted he could never ascertain, but the husband fared thus —breakfast, a dry crust; dinner, ditto ; supper, the great meal of the day, sometimes scalded chops, a dainty dish, consisting of broken bread moistened by pouring hot water upon it, and sometimes a pint of cider warmed over the fire and a crust dipped into it. This from Monday till Satur- day, and on Sunday, occasionally; a bit of bacon !" He beheld the tears of the oppressed, and they had no com- forter, and he vowed in the bitterness of his heart that if ever an opportunity presented itself he would try to be that comforter. The opportunity came sooner than he expected. The National Agricultural Labourers' Union was formed in 1872 with Mr. Arch as president, and his career since is familiar to all students of modern politics. The tide of popular sentiment is rapidly running in the direction of democracy in this country, as the agricultural labourers have as their champion and spokesman a man like Mr. Arch, who knows at once their wants and how to express them, who is not an agitator for the sake of agitation, but for the purpose of redressing acknowledged grievances. He will soon sit in the House of Commons with others like-minded—that is if the working men stand aloof from the contamination of the caucus, Whig or Tory, and stand shoulder to shoulder, when enfranchisad, in the war against the feudalism of the land- owner, and "the smug philosophy of the breeches pocket" of the capitalist. The stirring words of the member for Newcastle with which he closed his eloquent address last Christmas deserve repeating here ;—" Democracy is people's rule—the rule of all, rich and poor, lord and labourer, priest and layman. It draws its strength and its dignity from its universality and its freedom. It cannot disown the past, and it does not disparage it. Each order has done its alloted task, and has been useful in its day. All were links in the unerring pro- cess of the political and social evolution. The aristocracy broke the power of the court, and gave us national courage, culture, and refinement. The middle classes broke the power of the aristocracy, and gave us liberty of thought, education, and commerce. The workmen are in embryo. We cannot foretell their future. They are untrammelled with old habits and systems, and they have a progressive spirit and broad sympathies. They should lift politics out of the idealess level of hucksterers and drill sergeants. They should move at times not in the beaten tracks, but upon new ground. They should be something more than a link in the chain of machine politicians. They should be the propagandists of noble principles—should seek the vic- tory of reason over force, enlightenment over superstition, justice over caime, morality over vice. Philosophers tell us that life consists in the effort to assert itself, but . it cannot assert itself if it is to be a bold copy of some one else's life, whose judgments are to be unquestioned, and whose behests are to be obeyed. Let every man use his own faculties, inquire for himself, and when he has arrived at a conclu- sion, let him speak it—act it—act it regardless of any mys- tifying despotism that may have temporarily got astride the popular breath. Do not let him duck under it, nor go about to circumvent it or pinch it to suit an audience, or water it with honeydrops to suit the prejudices of his friends. Out with it bravely and take the consequences, whether it be anathema or ostracism. A man may get notoriety—the juggler's reward—by pretence; but nothing more, not even so much as belief. Struggle as he may, he cannot shuffle himself out of his responsibility. In the end he must rely upon himself. Better live in a tub with Dio- genes and be free than be a whimpering puppet or bedizened lackey in the palace of any Alexander. But with your in- dependence mingle toleration, and with your courage sym- pathy, for on the eve of the natal day of Him who, eighteen hundred years ago, preached the glad doctrines of humanity and brotherhood—this sin-stained world is in sad want of both. The stifled echo of His trials and teachings reverberate through the ages, and calls us all again to faith and labour, to duty and to service." If the newly enfran- chised see the duty of the vote in this light, and take up the responsibility which their new position in the State will bring with it, in a spirit of true devotion to the com- mon weal, then indeed, as Mr. &awe quoted at the meeting the other night, blessings Shall (imp like happy sunlight, • Dow)) int ) the hearts of suffering men, And teach them t) rejoice again. Yours, &c., JUNIOR LIBERAL.

-FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL AND THE LATE HEAD MASTER. you more thanks than I can express for so kindly inserting the letter I addressed to you' and hope you will think it no unreasonable request if I ask the favour of your courtesy to enable me to place before the general public of the chapelry of Farnworth the main facts relating to my administration of their school; to the circumstances that led to the erection of the convenient and spacious build- ing in which it was carried on; the motives which influenced me in giving in my conditional resignation in September 1876, and the causes that induced me to return two months subsequently. If all the facts relating to these sayeral matters be clearly and faithfully placed before there, they will have the materials whereby to form a cor- rect judgment as to the justice that has been mated mot to me by the governors in confiscating, at a blow, all the money I bad spent during 16 years to promote the efficiency cif one of the oldest schools in the county, and which might be made one of the most useful and important; and which confiscation has reduced me, already weakened men- tally and physically by more than five and a half years' ' sickness, to not merely relative but absolute poverty. Herodotus, one of the most ancient, as be is perhaps the most amusing and unreliable of the historians of olden times, tells us, in a well known passage, that behind the north wind is situated a very beautiful and salubrious country, but that there was . great difficulty in reaching it ; and we English people, owing chiefly to our insular position, are perhaps among the most prejudiced in the world; but the man, who is fortunate enough to get to the back of that prejudice, will find behind a kindness of heart and generosity of sentiment such as perhaps exist in no other people in the world; and, sir, with your kindly and powerful aid, it is my desire to reach that fair land and to get at the bock of those preju- dices which, if they did exist to the detriment of the school, took their origin, I am sure, more from imperfect and false information than mere vulgar The attempt to re- suscitate Farnworth School was the one effort of my working life. I began it a young man of 24, and left it a man of 40; and in the following lines I shall try to make clear the principles which dictated the plan I adopted. I don't pre- sume to suppose that I was always right in what I did; on the contrary, it is to be feared that in the heat of active work many mistakes may have been made, things said that would have been better unsaid, things done that it might have been wiser to leave undone; human nature is im,nwfiahtantol eldl infallible hen; edr bevtsuheutraldltt wcwotihi total that askeat:he per. ot errorslhi at y general c y ,m of may policy oeolntriakoci ytl maymbt ehaaypt bhr we ju dged a prejudiced eidbpi geeneeerd.d. notcasuos med a by m. wh es sm appointed to the mastership f the school • D and entered upon- my duties in I camber, 1801, 1882. The position at that time was much as follows' :--Y, The endowment in the gross yielded about £so per annum, but as much of it was derived or tfromThis s wasthe madenvalueeto did not average more than z to me, indeed, under the then existing law, the freeholds of Grammar Schools were generally supposed to be vested in the master for the time being. There were ten foundation boys who obtained a free education, one being appointed by

div.head: EXAMIN
div.p: THE EXAMIN
, . each of the .trustees from the particular township he bad
been elected to represent; other pupils were subject to such fee as the headmaster might impose. There were at this time about 12 or 14 pupils, 8 of whom were fousdationers ;

their ages varied from 11 to 15. The ntandard of scholar.- ship (if I may employ such a term) was not high; the first exercise I gave, I well remember, was to .copy about 10 er 12 lines from the beginning of Lord Macaulay's essay on Warren Hastings, and the most advanced pupil did not make less than An average of four mistakes in each line. The education given had apparently been confined to read- ing, writing, and arithmetic ; the writing in most cases was very fair, but the knowledge of arithmetic was limited, not one having an idea of fractions. The subjects which are usually supposed to enter largely into the course of a Grammar School education were altogether wanting. The building which the trustees provided to carry on the Gram- mar School was a kind of shed. There was a single room about 35 feet long by 12 feet wide, and 8 feet high. Against the wall on one side, and upon which two windows opened, was usually placed a neauure heap of from 10 to 15 tons. The other side adjoined a not very clean: public footpath. There were no offices of any kind, no desks for boys or masters, no . maps nor teaching apparatus of any kind, nothing, indeed, but the, four tare walls, such as they were, of .a single room. I 3may say when appointed I had drawn attention to this state of things, and plainly said that it would not be possible for any man to develope the school under such conditions, and while it'would be untrue for me to say that a new building was explicitly promised, yet most unquestionably was led to believe that, in the event of the numbers increas- ing and the school gaining in respectability, the trustees would not be found wanting in doing their duty. Had it not been so I should have taken the advice of my friends and never gone to Farnworth. The first thiag I did was to spend about £5O in providing school fittings and making the interior as decent as I could. The trustees did send round the hat, and raised between them something under £6 to assist; but this was the only pecuniary help I received while at Farnworth ; not so much as a sixpence for a school prize was ever given. The next matter that demanded at- tention was the drawing up of a scheme ef education adap- ted to the needs of the neighbourhood. A purely classical , education was out of the question; still it seemed to me • that the study of language should be the foundation of any , educational edifice, as a clear idea of the meaning and force . of words is the key to all knowledge. With it a student . can do almost anything by himself, without it he can do , nothing. English, Latin, and French were therefore made the ground-work of my plan. Greek was omitted, not be- cause it was under-valued, but by reason of the mental training given by it being similar to that given by Latin; in short, I regarded Latin as an educational necessity, Greek as an intellectual luxury. The second great element in my scheme was to make provi- sion for a sound course of mathematic,. viz., an elementary stage taking in arithmetic, elementarf algebra. euclid, plan trigonometry, to the solution of triangles, and so much of mechanics as could be profitably read without the aid of the calculus; and a more advanced stage taking in the higher parts of the above-named sub- ject, together with conics and the more elementary portion's of the calculus—a rather ambitious standard perhaps you will think, sir, for a coaetry school, but we reached it, al- though there were never more than one or two boys in the school at the same time who were reading the more ad- vanced stage. To explain this somewhat advanced course, , I may say that I have always bedn of opinion that what are , called the higher mathematics might be reached by a much , shorter course than is usually pursued by but ; and that . the elements of the cedilla which give to mathematicians , such enormous power, might be acquired by any boy of t average ability by the time he reached the age of 18. I , also wished to add to my educational course some elementary ' branch of popular science such as botany; but at the time I did not see my way clear with the limited means at my I disposal; chemistry, however, I introduced later, but more in obedience to popular demand than in accordance with my . own judgment as an educationalist. Them can, I think, be no doubt that it is better to select a few subjects out of the , many that constitute the mass of human knowledge, where-, , with to train and develope youthful intelligence than to , weight the brain with a mass of information relating to various subjects which it has not the pewer nor the time tri assimilate. If I may be pardoned an illustration I would say that it is notthe shallow lagoon which perhapslays waste many thousands of what would be otherwise fertile acres; but the stream confined within narrow limits, and of great depth because so confined, that bears on its bosom the com- merce of the world. I fear, too, that those educational' theorists who advocate a great multiplicity of subjects In school often forget that the actual teaching hours can hardly be more than twenty a week; that out of these five at least must be given up to English, and, if real progress is to be made, as many to Latin; mathematics will take at least five more, and thus only five hours are left for French, essay- writing, drawing, dm., which few will, I think, consider too many. In short, I may say that the object of my scheme was to develope, as far as I could, the three great intellec- tual faculties of observation, memory, and reason, and to adopt such methods of teaching the various subjects I might select, as the instruments for effecting this, as would tend to keep the brain of the student clear, not to cenfnse it. I fear• , many modern theorists will consider my scheme rather a narrow one; but to those who have had any practical ex- perience of educational work it will, I think, be considered sufficiently broad and not ill calculated to enable the youth ' who had thoroughly mastered it to encounter the real diffi- culties of life, and to form a foundation on which he might ; build more and more as opportunity came in his way. Such, sir, was the position of the school with respect to " scholarship and habitation, and such were the principles I endeavoured to apply to advance the former. What coarse I took to improve the latter forms the next part of the story. The school increased steadily though slowly until the numbers reached about 25, and I then offered the trustees to give up the endowment for five years if they would erect buildings more worthy of a Grammar School. They ra, fused. The numbers, drawbacks notwithstanding, continued to increase, and boys commenced coming from St. Helens by train. I then induced my landlord, Mr. W. Longton, who always aced most fairly and honourably, to add some rooms to my house. The school then numbered about forty, and rapidly rose to sixty. We were again too crowded, and I was driven to engage a kind of barn from Mr. Knight. We could manage in this way for the summer, but it was uninhabitable during winter, and I was obliged to return to my own residence. I then appealed once more to the trus- tees to build, and a memorial of the inhabitants was largely signed and presented to them, but nothing came of it. My life in a small house with eupwards of sixty pupils was almost unendurable, and, after much consideration, I de- cided upon erecting, suitable buildings myself. The trustees had, by a clause in my_ agreement, stipulated that a board- ing school should be established in connection with the Grammar School, because, as the chairman remarked," it brought money into the village." At the time there were about twenty boarders and forty day • pupils, and in calcu- lating the size of the building to be erected, I did not think it judicious to make provision for less than seventy day pupil., forty boarders, and a staff of three assistant masters. How, in addition to the labours of the school and with Mrs. Raven almost constantly ill, I got through the extra work .thus placed upon my shoulders I cannot tell ; suffice it to say, that it was dens at the cost of many sleepless nights and a good deal more money than had been anticipated. I experienced much kindness, more than I shall ever forget, from the gentlemen who supplied RIP with the materials and no workmanship could be better than that done by the various contractors. They one and all acted most honour- ably with me, and it gives me much satisfaction to have an opportunity of openly acknowledging it. The school was removed to the new premise S in July, 1873, and continued gradually to increase until in 1876 there were about 90 pupils. The standard of scholarship, had also been quietly advancing. With the exception of the first year or two after my appointment, candidates had always been sent to the Oxford or Cambridge local exatninations, and with fair suceess ; for eight years in succession pupils from Farn- worth had been placed in the honour classes, as distinct from the pass class, gaining thc highest possible positions. The school was beginning to send students to the old Uni- versities. themselves; one took mathematical honours at Cambridge, another would have done so had his health per- mitted; a third, who indeed left us young, but not before he had laid a solid foundation in the subject in which be after- wards distinguished himself, took a first class in the honour school of mathematics at Oxford; and only last year, Mr. Shaw, a son of an old engineer of the Local Board, took a esg;eaeecamet ;inenhe adirt frit wegnFLii ateoyltrmh.t anxietyheo sshnt ioef uhyoref constant sficefoht building,hoe school lo was, aemodernaf fh ha ifs tmo rey, one e theo f which any body of governors might be proud. About a month afterwards I suddenly lost all sensation in my left side and consulted Dr. Greeneys. Lee made liglA of the matter, and, as there was little or no pain, I thought nothing more of it; but the part never re- covered its normal sensitiveness, and from that time my nervous system began gradually to break down, until, try, to. control myself as I would, I was scarcely. fit to be With boys. It was under these circumstances, in May, 1876,that I asked the trustees to take over the building and allow Me to retire. They refused. Feeling myself getting worse I repeated the request. They still refused. I then asked 'them to allow me six months' rest; that they would not do. There remained only ode course for me to take, viz, to find a successor to take over the school. A clergyman applied, recommended by Lord Winmarleigh and others. He agreed to purchase the household and school furniture for a given sum, about 3-51 he of the cost. I carefully ab- stained from asking anything for goodwill ; to that I did not consider myself entitled, although the school was car- ried.on in buildings of my own. To protect, in some mea- sure, the £5,000 I bad expehded. I intended to ask the trustees to appoint Mr. Hutchinson to the Grammar School on my resignation. But there was another difficulty. When the time came for payment Mr. Hutchinson could only pay one-third in cash and wished to give bills for six, nine,olr,etfweglvfao monthsarra nz e terms b eforbalance. y rTehsiegtnrauteitoene,s na Idl e in a n in then pointed out that I must be, in some measure, secured not only for my great outlay, but also against the eentin- 4ency, which fr hoped might not happen, of Mr. Hutchinson not being able to meet his engagements, and to meet that contingency I suggested to them to give me six months leave of absence.

his slight favour the trustees refused me, why,! could not tell, and, being annoyed at the refusal, I bluntly declined to give in my resignation; the discussion continued, and had lasted upwards of two hours, when Mr. Tipping suggested that I should retire for a few minutes and the trustees would discuss the question among themselves. I left them and walked to and fro in front of the old Grammar School. In about ten minutes Mr. Holloway, the vicar, came out to me, and said that he himself had made a proposition to the trustees, which they had accepted, viz, that I should resign and they would appoint Mr. Hutchinson as acting head master for the time being, and in the event of his failing to most his engagements with me, pledged their word of honour to reappoint me as head master of the school. Sir, I had every ,confidence in the personal honour of the trustees, and in a weak moment I accepted this arraagement, and in good faith signed the instrument which left Me at•their mercy, and has caused my ruin. lam now a broken-down and broken-hearted man; for more than five years a helpless invalid, with no hope of relief and with every prospect of being called at no distant date to meet that great crisis we all have to encounter, and, sir,with the full solemnity of my position confronting me, I venture to challenge the Rev. George Holloway, as a clergyman, . and therefore presumably as a gentleman, on his oath in a court of justice, to deny the substantial accuracy of this statement. Sir,! am exhausted, and so probably is your patience, and I must again trespass on your good nature to give me space for a short and final letter in a future issue. I have been obliged to write at greater length than I purposed, because these letters are intended to meet another end for which considerable detail is necessary.—l am, sir, y,,ur faithful and obedient servant, JAMES RAVEN.

Egypt was at present a source of anxiety to the Government, and then there was a source of anxiety in the sister isle, which, however, was lessening. The other night, in an admirable speech, Mr. Trevelyan had informed the House that there were fewer agrarian outrages committed in the whole of the year 1883 than had been committed in a single month of 1880. (Applause.) There had been twice as many agrarian outrages during the last six months of the last year in which the Conservatives held office as there had been in the last six months of the year just ended. Notonly that but while in the Conservative reign the rates went on increasing, during the present Liberal government the exact contrary had been effected. The great difficulties that the Government now had in Ireland were mainly due to the self-styled loyal Orangemen and the Nationalists. The fact that the Government were being abused by both parties showed that a pretty fair coarse was being steered between them. As regarded Egypt, Ike noun- , try was at present a source of anxiety to the Government, and almost every eye ha England,. figuratively speaking. was centred upon that noble figure which had been. flitting unarmed and without an escort, beyond two or three guides and friends, hastening through the desert to the Soudan to arrange, if possible, a peaceable evacuation of Khartoum. If mischief should befall him' which Heaven forbid, they would hav,e an attack on the Government by the Tories, who would lay the responsibity upon them*. But had the Conservatives protested in any way against his going? They had suggested no other course; so had they any rea- son to say that they would have done other- wise than the Government had done? There was one more subject to which he would allude, affewing the agri- cultural interests. There was now considerable agitation respecting the foot-and-mouth disease, and not a little pressure had been brought to bear upon the Government to prohibit the importation of live cattle, even for slaughter, from those countries where foot-and-mouth disease was known to existoThe contentiOo WM that the dieeetle wee in- troduced into the country in that manner; secondly, if that suggestion were carried out it would exclude from oar markets only a very small percentage of our meat supply; thirdly, that the dead meat trade woulo develops and take its place; and fourthly, so far from thepricas of meat being raised to the population of this country, by the increased number of our own herds and the development of the dead meat trade, the price of meat would be actually decreased. But there were always two sides to a question, and these statements were combatted. It was difficult to and any actual evidence that the disease was introduced into this country by the' im- portation of beasts from foreign countries; it might be imported by persons in their clothing. He feared they would always be subject to a certain amount of the disease, and that if they were to cut off, even temporarily, a small portion of the meat supply, it would have a serious effect upon the price. He thought the Government were taking a right course. The subject ought not . to be made a party question because everybody was in- terested in stamping out the scourge, but it could be plainly seen that the Tories were trying to make political capital out of it. The difference between the two parties was that the Liberal party did what was just for all cl asses, and the Conservatives, on the other hand, appealed to selfish class interests where they could catch votes. He thought his hearers were pretty well convinced that the interests of the country' were bound up with the continuance of a good Government in power, and he had great pleasure in moving the resolution. (Applause.) Mr. J. T. BanattPu aeeoilded the resolution, 'and said that the Reform Bill which was soon to be introduced into the House of Commons was founded upon one of two prin- ciples—the principle of the representation of numbers, or the principle of the representation cf interests. They wished for government for the sake of the people by the people. (Applause.) Their opponents, on the other hand, wished to continue the bad old system of the representation of interests, or, in other words, a government of trades unions. The first was the trades union of the great landowners of the country, the most powerful ant the most selfish of all the trades unions in the couhtry. (Applause.) The second was the trades union of the establishment of the Church of England, and he could enumerate others. These were, unfortunotely, banded together not as it Was desirable , for the Houses of Parliament to be banded together, for the 1 good of the whole, but for the sordid interests of the few. They wished to bring an end to this state of things, and to have a Government not for the sake of interest, but, to use the words of their opponents, for the sake of mete numbers. (Applause.) Mr. F. MILNE supported the resolution in an earnest and eloquent speech. The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. G. W. LATHAM moved the following resolution : " That this meeting trusts that the present Parliament will not be dissolved till residential household suffrage Allan have been established throughout the United Kingdom, to be followed as promptly as possible by a large measure for the redistribution of seats." (Applause.) All depended upon the august House of Lards whether they had this bill for enfranchisement before a dissolution of Parliament. If there were a dissolution, and if the Con- servatives . came into power, he defied any Conservative Government to exist two sessions without giving that boon to the people. (Applause.) Some people might say that it was necessary to reform the House of Lords, but although he was a pretty strong Liberal he was not for doing that. He could conceive of no possible way of reforming the House of Lords which would not make it more Conservative and more troublesome than it was at present. save being bound to pass a bill after it had been carried twice for two years in succession in the House of Commons. But it would then take two years to pass certain bills because the House of Lords were determined to show their power. It had been suggested that life peers should be introduced largely. Unfortunately they had seen the effect of intro- ducing new blood into the House of Lords; from Lord Brabourne upwards or downwards they all became Conser- vatives, however good Liberals they were before. Let them keep the House of Lords as it was. They might depend upon ielhat when the people got the lowered franchise the House of Lords would condescend to do what the monarchy had done. They would be given to understand that they were net to stand in the way of the people, and that the will of the people was to be supreme over all. (Ap- plause.) Sir Stafford Northcote, in a speech at Reading, said "You are not going to have this franchise until you tell us what you are going to do with it." (Laughter ) That was a very hard matter to put. He did not know what politics these new voters would have, but he had his suspicions. There was a considerable portion of the new Voters of whom the Conservative squires and pastors of the Church of England had had the solo training. The agri- celtural labourer had lived and been educated under their care, and he for one did not know, though he had his sus- picions, which way they would vote; but he would say decidedly that these men most be admitted to the franchise whatever their vote might be. (Applause.) They had all heard of the "bitter cry of outcast London," a cry which unfortunately might be repeated in every large town, how the poor were miserably housed, he/ poverty, misery, vice, are-built all those slums, madend diseasethe were mcl clean nm p a and .d If them, till they altered the land laws, it Would be money thrown away, for the'reason that the labouring men, and the best of them, were driven from the country to the great towns, because they had no hope where they lived in the country. It was forbidden to the workingman to be a landowner, and however hard he might strive he could never hope to raise himself from the life of a slave and the death of a pauper. (Hear, hear.) He would not establish peasant proprietorship by law, but would merely alter the _law so that there should be fairplay for small occupiers. At this time, above all others, he thought they should have a change in their land laws. More than the shadow of Socialism had been thrown upon the public mind, and men were listened to who proposed wild and chimerical schemes simply because people despaired of attaining their object in any other way. He believed that the common sense of England would reject any scheme which involved anything like confiscation if they could see any legal way in which their objects could be gained. The best and easiest way to refute men like Mr. Henry George would be to alter the land laws. There were other matters to be considered by the Government. There was the question of the government of counties, the establishment of the Church, and the traffic in liquor. These were the people's questions, and he was not there that evening to say how they would be answered, hut be knew that when the time came for the people to give an answer they would be answered rightly. div.head: _BRITISH WORKINGMAN.
div.p: THE _BRITISH WORKINGMAN.

Sir,—We sometimes hear from Conservative platforms rather glowing accounts as to the great advantages and comforts enjoyed by the British workingman. He is always told by such advisers to rest himself and be contented with his lot in which it has pleased Providence to place him, hs he enjoys all the blessings attendant upon living in a free country, and consequently, according to their view of his position, the workingman has nothing more to desire for improving his social standing. But we know that this view of his case is to a great extent false and misleading, and I am inclined to think it is designedly so. Should be base far enlightened as to see his position as it really is, and view the great social disparity that exists between his class and the capitalist or the aristocracy, he is looked on by that fraternity after as a dangerous individual But, I will ask, is

there not room left in his case to be dissatisfied with his present lot? Let us view his case for a brief moment. He commences to work early in youth as his father did before him, and continues to toil on in the same way year after year until he is rendered incapable through infirmity or old age of doing so any longer. And here, let me ask, what has he been earning all this time? Simply enough, and perhaps not that, to satisfy the commonest demands of life from week to week, and ,con- sequently being in such a position in most cases he has nothing left for a rainy day. But his wealthy ad- visers would tell him that this is owing to his extravagance and want of thrift. To such I would put this question, where is the room left for the exercise of thrift to any extent, out of the paltry earnings of 15s or 20a per weak? I, sir, am inclined to think that they who are so ready in advising thrift in the labouring man would, if placed in his position, find it rather difficult to practice what they preach. But now as to the other side of the question. He sees that during the years he has been toil- ing for a bare living his master has been able to amass a fortune of hundreds of thousands, and in some cases more, and yet if there be any depression in trade the working man is informed that he must have his wages lowered in consequence. This is how his case stands, and in such posi- tion ft will remain until our Government takes a more lively interest in it. To my mind this is not very likely to be the case so long as the capitalists' interest is so strongly represented in Parliament. The working man's is represen- ted by one or two members. Until we have more thorough labour representatives in the House of Commons, then, and not until then, will the British working man enjoy true in- dependence and freedom. At least, this, sir, is my opinion. —I am, iltc , VOX POPULI. February. 12th, 1884.

THE CORONER AND THE REGISTRAR. Sir,—Mr. J. C. Satton, the Superintendent Registrar, has requested me to forward the following communication, which you will be good enough to publish in your next issue.—Yours, W. H. HARRISON, Registrar. "Adverting to the proceedings 'at the inquest upon the body of John McGinn, held at Warrington, last week, and fully admitting the absurdity of inquests being held in many of, these cases, it is clearly impossible for a registrar of deaths to make the necessary entry in his register'without information of the cause of death. The registrar in this case had no such information given to him. He did not, however, require it from the Coroner—that would he unreasonable. If fur- nished to him from any other source, accompanied by a letter from the Coroner, he would act upon it. The Coroner appears to have been under misapprehension of the circum- stances.—Yours, dm. (signed), J. C. SUTTON, Superintendent Registrar." Warrington, 14th February, 1884.

THE PULPIT FROM THE PEW.. Sir,—l have read with much interest a letter signed 0 A Very Lay Layman," hailing from Runcorn, in your issue of February 2nd. He evidently sees, as well as many others, a sad state Of things existing amongst Nonconformist Churches, and suggests a careful looking into for fear these churches should become weakened. He probably knows they are strong numerically and flaancially, and con- sequently is afraid, as be puts it, "their fine gold becomes dim." "A Very Lay Layman " sees a weakness and offers a remedy, viz., an interchange of pulpits, which would undoubtedly be a means of cementing the various religious bodies together. The fact we so seldom see or hear of such changes go to prove that there is something wrong, lathentably so. Bigotry, prejudice, and jealousy exist to a very large extent (and I have been an eye witness of it) amongst Nonconformist Churches between ministers and their flock. Therefore, peace and love and unity are wanting in the hearts of a great many who profess to be followers of their Master. lam of opinion that members of the various churches nurse and love their creeds or doctrinal views more than their Master. They miss the one great object of laying hold upon the people and bringing them within the pale of the church by jealously protecting and pushing forward its owtedenomina- tional views. It would appe ir every sect are aiming at sectarian progress, aggrandisement, and selfishness; if 80. how cm an interchange of various ministers be frequent? First of all remove the barrier of sectarian bigotry, let every member and minister have one common object in , view, the salvation of mankind, and then there will be no complaining when the next religious census is taken. Your correspondent longs for a better state of things at Runcorn, and I should like his gentle hint to be of service to others. The Salvation Army lends an example to "sects of religion" to press forward the one great object of salvation to man- kind and sink all differences of opinion of a religious or doctrinal character. Hence the frequent inquiry at their meetings is " Are you saved ?" This question absorbs all their thoughts and creed, and gives them no time, or desire, to cavil with those vexed questions which have done so much to cause discord where unity, peace, and love ought to dwell.—Yours truly, A LOOKER ON. Warrington, February, 1884.

FRODSHAM. DAMAGE TO A LAMP PILLAR. The traction engine Enterprise, from Barnston, near Birkenhead, while passing through Frodsham on Wednesday accidentally knocked a gas-lamp. pillar 'down. Further mishap was averted by the gas main being promptly stopped up. WESLEYAN HOME Mismosts.—Special sermons were preached in the Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, on Sunday, by the Rev. G. Lupton Allen, and on Tuesday evening the annual meeting was held in the same place, when Mr. Thos. Norman, of Runcorn, presided, and addresses were delivered by the Rev. Simpson Johnson, of Hull, and the Revs. G. L. Allen, F. F. Edmonds, Mr. Samuel Walker, and Mr. Proud. A collection was made at the close of each service on behalf of Home Missions. RUNCORN STARR-BOWEETT SOCIETY APPROPRIATION.— A meeting in connection with the above society was held in the Girls' School, Frodsham, on Thursday evening, when Mr. Peter Riley presided. The secretary, Mr. William Handley, read the minutes of the last meeting, and after a few remarks from Mr. Foulkes, of Runcorn, the appropria- tion was proceeded with, Messrs. J. Jones and J. Hough being the scrutineers, and Miss Kate Booth drew the lucky numbers. It was stated by the secretary that 447 certificates had been issued, leaving only 53 available certificates to make the society complete. On the ballot being taken number 17 was drawn, and for the second time rejected on account of the subscriptions being ia arrear. The next draw resulted in number 52 being declared the winning number, and entitling Mr. Joseph K. Digges, of Runcorn, to £2OO, free of interest for 12-i years. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the meeting. LUCA. Ftnz--About half-past eight on Saturday night •a fire broke out in .9 stable belonging te Mr. Thomas Moston, Whitbarrow' and two horses narrowly escaped being burnt to death. Immediately on the fire being discovered Mrs. Moston r knowing that the two horses were in the stable, bravely rushed into the building, and fighting her way amidst the smoke succeeded in rescuing the frightened aM- mals from their perilous position.. In the meantime an alarm had been raised, and the fire brigade, under the super- intendence of Sergeant Harrington, were soon on the spot, but the are was extinguished without the engine having been brought into requisition. One of the horses, a mare which Mr. Moston bad newly bought, was severely blistered in several places, and the building was slightly damaged, but the loss, which is estimated at £lO, is covered by in- surlnce in the General Life and Fire Insurance Office. PROSECUTIONS FOR BREACAS OF THE CATTLE DISEASES REGULATIONS.-11enry Balshaw, auctioneer, of Altrincham, was summoned to the Lymrn Petty Sessions, yesterday, for committing a breach of the cattle disease regulations on the 17th lost, by offering for sale a heifer which had not been on the premises for 14 days prior to the day of stle.— Sergeant Harrington stated that on the 17th inst. there was a sale at the Burford-lane farm, the premises of the late Mr. Edmondson. A week prior to the sale he visited the pre- mises, and there saw a cow and a heifer. On the day of the sale the cow and two heifers were sold. He told the defen- dant he should report him for having illegally sold one pf the heifers.—P.O. Autrobus corroborated.—Mrs. El inbeth
Lea, of Burford-lane, said that her husband sold the heifer

in question to a man named Gatley. On the morning of the day of the sale it was removed across the road to the place of sale.—The defendant said it was customary in farm sales far adjoining farmers to sand stock for sale, and on this occasion Mr. Galley went to him and asked him if he would offer the heifer for him. He immediately said he would, but had he given the matter a thought he would have refused. If Sergeant Harrington had had anything like good feeling ,he would have called his attention to the matter before the sale. Half a hint from hitn.would havesaved all that trouble. He did not charge anything to Mr. Gatley for selling the heifer, and the animal was only removed across the lane.— The Bench said that the la,w had been broken, and the de..

fend aht must pay Is and costs.--Wm. Gatley, cattle dealer, Timparley, was summoned for exposing for sale the animal referred to in the previous case, and he was fined is and costs --Thomas Harrison, Brook Farm, Patricroft, and George Thorpe, Ecclesi were summoned that they being, the occupiers of the Burford-lane Farm, did allow the heifer to be sold by auction there when it had not been on the premises 14 days.--Henry Atkinson, landlord of the Green Dragon Inn, stated that the defendant's were the executors of the late Mr. Edmondson.—The defendant Har- rison said that although he was nominated as ose of his executors he had refused to act as such, and therefore he was not an executor. He had given instructions in the carrying out of the business of the farm, but had not acted officially, being simply a friend, of Mrs. Eirmondson's.— Each defendant was ordered to pay expenses 14s Gd. PADGATE. CHRIST Cuoncs ,Scitoor, TuEaT.—The children of I Christ Church schools, Padgate, held their annual tea party I on Saturday afternoon, when there were about 120 people present, besides many of their parents and friends. The schoolroom was neatly, decorated by Miss Yates and Miss Wrightson. Some remarks having been offered by the Vicar (Rev. W. H. Williams), pieces were recited and songs given by the scholars la a most creditable manner. Prizes were given for good conduct and attendance; and the teachers were also presented with a book as a mark of esteem, and for the interest they had manifested in their classes. Each child was presented With an orange—then followed a scramble for nuts. The entertainment was brought to a conclusion by singing the National Anthem, three cheers being given for the Vicar. It is stated that during the four years of Mr. Williams's incumbency, a sum of £1,300 has been expended on the church and school, and that a debt still remains. Building the wall and the introduction of the gas have added about £lOO to the bill of items.

• PARTINGTON. The annual tea meeting in connection with the Cotigre- grational Chapel of this place was held last week. . There was a goodly gathering at the tea, which was well served— evidently giving satisfaction. A public meeting was held at the close. The pastor of the church, the Rev. Mr. Wood- bourn, occupied the chair. Addresses were delivered by Mr. Wood, merchant, of Manchester, by the treasurer of the Rural Home Mission Fund, and by the Rev. R. Dillon, (Wesleyan.) The Primitive Methodist Minister was pre- vented from being present by domestic affliction. The choir rendered very excellent service during the evening.. The selections were above the average, and were sung with pre- cision and taste, evidencing careful training. The organist ably presided at the organ. The pastor, in his report, spoke thankfully of success in the past, dwelling upon the present condition of the church in the village, and looking forward hopefully to. the future. THELWALL. UNLAWFULLY FIRING A Gina —William Miller, a young man residing in Thelwall, was summoned to the Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterday, for unlawfully firing a gun within 50 feet of a carriage road.—P.C. chatterton stated that on the 19th instant he was near the defendant's residence at Thelwall and saw him fire a gun within 50 feet of the public road. A number of children were in the road, and they appeared to be very much frightened by the report of the gun. The defendant told him that he had been firing the gun at a mark on a tree.—The defendant stated to the Bench that he went into the garden to shoot sparrows, which had become quite a pest, and that he was not shooting at a mark.—The Bench dismissed the case. ALLEMID CRUELTY TO A Doa.—Yesterday; at Lymm Petty Sessions, Albert Miller, a boy, brother to the defen- dant in the previous case, was SuMmoned for cruelly ill- treating a dog belonging to John Eden, 'of Thelwall.— Inspector Wills, of the 5.P.C.A.,. stated that having re- ceived information that the defendant had ill-treated a dog on the 10th instant, he visited the defendant on the 18th and charged him .with the offence. The defendant replied that he was very sorry for what he had done. The society was very reluctant to prosecute the lad owing to his tender age, but the case was such a flagrant One that they consi- dered it their duty t0.de.,.50..-e-John Eden stated that the dog was about 17 years of age. On the day in question as he was seated in hie own house, he heard the animal yelp., and immediately afterwards it came into the house, appear- ing to be in great pain. He examined it, and came to the conclusion that its ribs were broken. The animal died two days afterwards.—A lad was called, who said he saw the de- fendant throw.a piece of coal at the dog.—The defendant admitted that he hit the brute with a piece of coal, and
said that he did se Isecaase it Wail fighting a dog which t..)1 Wormed to his father.—The defendant was dismissed with a caution.

ILLEGALLY EXPOSING PIGS FOR Snit—Yesterday, at Lymm Petty Sessions, John Egan, of Warburton, was sum- moned for Illegally exposing two pigs at a public sale, the animals not having been on the premises 14 days prior to the day of sale. It appeared that on the 17th inst. a public .; sale took place at Burford-lane Farm, Lvmm, at which the , defendant sold the two pigs in question, the same having - been taken to the premises on the day of sale only.--SuPte'3 Leighton stated that swine fever was very much on the in' 'll crease, and it was necessary that the regulations respecting the sale of these animals should be enforced.—The defen- dant, who pfeaded ignorance of the regulations, was ordered - Ito pay 2s. 61 and lOs 63 costs. TRINITY COLLEGE Lonoon.—Tbe Christmas examine,- , tion held at the Academy, Winsford, resulted in the succeee- of Master John Bate, who nearly gained full marks in the - pass examination, and Miss Needham, who gained both the pass and honours. Richard Trotter, of Frodsha.m, to very good congregations. There was a juvenile service in the afternoon, when addresses were giver; by Messrs. S. Bennett, T. Dodd, and John Buckley, and several recitations by scholars, &c., were admirably ren- dered, while the choir, with their usual ability, rendered anthems and hymns. On Monday night the public meet' hag was presided over by Alderman Slater, who set forth the benefits of missions. He was well supported by the Revs. Trotter, Symons, Maxwell (In ependent), Wright, and Messrs. W. Dodd and J. Buckley (sec.), the latter of whom presented the financial statements. The contriba- lions from Winsford, last year, reached the nice sum of £29 10s. 7d., of which the voting people contributed by cards, dm., no less than £l5 17s. Id. The amount realised this year so far is £214 with some items to come in at the week- end. Votes of thanks given and responded to brought the meeting to a close. WINSPORD LIBERAL CLUB: LECTURE ON "IRELAND." The members of the Winsford Liberal Club had a treat GE Thursday night last, when Captain Tomkinson, J.P., gave them in their club-room, which was well filled, as complete a history of the Irish question as could be crammed into nearly two hours. Having carried his A tulitory back to the idays of the conquest, be showed the unjust manner la I which that unhappy isle had been treated from the coin- ' mencement. The benefits of the ccnquest were pointed out, but few very unfortunately had fallen to Ireland—the role of grasping all, confiscating the good, and leaving the barl too often having prevailed. Could it, be a subject of wonder that the Irish were turbulent, rebellious, and unsettled 1 Ile spoke of tbe'different developements of trade and reionieee which had been attempted from time to time, and as often negatived; ,how one Government, -after another up to the present time had tried its legislative hand and met with difficulties to which they succumbed, ending in force and repression too often. "The grand old man," Mr. Gladstone, had tried to reach the root of the evil, and was likely te effect a cure if the people themselves would let him. Even the agitators acknowledged that his measures were taking the sting out of their movement. The country was risiagi

_ agrarianism ceasing, and safety, peace, and prosperity were looking Ireland in the face. Mr. Slater (ex-Mayor) prs. Bided in his usual happy way. Mr. Johnson proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer, who, in replying, spoke of the Soudan affairs, and proposed a vote of thanks to the chair. man, which was seconded and carried. CHESHIRE FARMERS FARMERS AND THE AGRI- CULTURAL HOLDINGS ACT. A special meeting of the Chester Farmers' Club WAS held at Chester, on Faturday, to discuss the working of the Agri- cultural Holdings Act. Mr. John Roberts presided, and there was a large attendance. Mr. Beecroft, the secretary of the club, introduced the subject, and described the recent attempt that had been made on the Ashton estate to induce the tenants to sign away the benefits offered by the Act, lie himself was a tenant on the Ashton estate, and he thought that the agreemet that was put before them for signature was not fair to the tenant. When he took his farm four - He had since

Years ago the rent was raised by £4O a year. ,rie tau - laid out about £5OO upon the farm, and he thought it was most unfair that if he were to leave .he should leave hie money in the land. An aniouted die- tussion then took ' place upon the case of Mr. e'aga, who refused to sign the agreement on the -, Ashton estate, and ,who received notice to quit. Mr. 'Jenson, who was present, unneeded to the request of the Club to explain the circumstances of his case. lie said that he BDoke to Mr. Wright, the agent of the estate, about the graining and told him it was an improvement for which he Could claim under the Act, and that he could Call in valuers to value it. Some of his laud required to be redrained, and he was doing the work limself. Mr. Wright brought round the agreement and be refused to sign it. Whereupon he received notice. He did not want to leave his farm, imt he did not want to lose his money. The agent first asked him to give notice to leave his farm, and as he would not do that the agent gave him notice.— Mr. Davies, who said he was one of the old,st tenants ,nth Ashton estate, remarked that he bad always found the tens- tees and agent most fair and honourable in their dealings , with the tenantry. They had spent a considerable sum of money in improving ,the estate, and he knew that before Mr. Denson entered upon his farm £l,OOO was laid out upon it. In 1871 they spent £4,000 on his little farm. Ile defended the trustees from the insinuations that had been cast upon them, and suggested that there must have been some fault on Mr. Denson's part. Mr. Denson, however, denied that he had done anything to provoke the hostility of the agent or trustees. All that he wanted was hie 0Wn.....-A king discussion followed, Mr. Denson's case • beingtaken up with a 'great deal,of 'warmth by some of the members. Mr. Taylor urged that as all the facts had not come before them, they should not be too hasty in passing judgment.—Mr. Davies said that he would as soon be under the six months' notice to quit as the twelve months.—Mr. . Baxter said that a great deal haj,d been said and written about farmers preferring six months' notice, to quit their ' holdings instead of twelve.—The opinion of the Club 'Wes taken on this point, and there was a unanimous feeling in favour of twelve months' notice. Mr. Baxter afterwards moved a resolution expressing the sympathy of the Clab with Mr. Denson for the action he had taken in defending his right to compensation for improvements, and condemn- ing any action that may be taken by landlords or agents to avoid their responsibility under the compensation clause of the Act. Mr. Taylor sumsted that all reference to this particular case should be left out, but Mr.. Baxter declined to amend his motion, and it was carried by twenty to eight. SILO AT TATTO—NWRIC. , -There was a considerable gathering of farmers, cow- keepers, and milk dealers in Tatton Park on Tuesday, to 'opening •of the-..5i10 which hiaLordahip tad ;filled milling, ago as. July. last year... The silo in this case was alnifetready. to hand, being, in -fact, an ice house situa- ted on the-breast of a little hill, near to the classic temple ;in the &tads,. and -in close.proximity to the hall. The grass used was no choice herbage, but, on the contrary, ro ugh.; Yell lonle grias. cut itt the open Alailr.'• 41511 At noon the cutting of the :silo was commenced, and the ensilage, which was Maio-what debayed on the top, was found to be perfectly good beneath. It Vas slightly moist, brownish green in cblour, and of a somewhat pungent hut not unpleasant odour.' The horses to whom it was offered sniffed at it a little suspiciously some of them, but most of them eat it freely. Lot'd Bean:rote welcomed all present, ana said he thought that they would all have by this tinae'cOncluded that the silo, as a means for preserving grass, ' was a success. '(Ap- plause.) The only question now was' whether it could be carried out economically. The expenses which had heed I incurred in the construction of this silo were not at all '0 be'taken'as a standard, because expenses had not beeirrilt.; garded in order that accuracy of details might be secured. I (Applause.) It remained to be seen whether it was neces- sary to chop the grass or even to mix ,salt with it at all. i He thought that n all probability it wOuld be found that grass ' might 'be preserved in this way, with ordinary care, 'without ;either of these two; sources of expense—salt and chopping. If terj,i tie had no doubt of its being an economicalj, luacess. (Applauto ) The first foot or nine inches of this- ,sild seemed to be mouldy; but the rest was of averagel "quality. It had evidently undergone a great chemidal change. Mr. Saletharn,- the analyst, would tell than' whether the nutritive' qualities of the grase were unchange',. and they Were all anxiously looking -forward balis report on that point. The question as to whether tows would thrive upon it aid give better milk to the winter than upon the ordinary feed of hay and turnips- was also full of interest; also wlether it could be Made as cheap as hay.. He hoped to -make further experiments upon these points, And also in making ensilage without salt or chopping. Had ' it not been that foot-and-mouth disease had broken out at Knutsford on Ile previous day he would have bad some cattle there to try them with the ensilage. But he would carry his exieriments further, and 'they would, in ' due,tirne hear of the results. (Afiplause.) Mr. J. T. Smlth, his lordship's agent, had drawn up a written statement, from which we gather that the walls of the icehouse hod been plastered with cement. The entrance at the side was bl.cked up, and a new entrance made from the top of the dome. The height of the house is II feet 6 inches, area 101 square feet. The part of the park-chosen to obtain the grass from had never given any fair return for mowing. There was amongst it a certain proportion' of fine grass, but the greater part watt rough and course, On July 3 the chaffcutters, portable engine, and other- necemary ap- paratus was on the ground. On the first day they Put in 8 tons 16cwt. and lqr., adding salt at the rate of 11b. to the cat—the cut being equivalent to 'cwt. 2qrs. nibs. For covering, Ik-inch boards were used, and on these 30 boxes of bricks, each weighing. *wt. were placed, the total weight with the boards , being four tons. On the following day it was found that the ensilage had sunk a foot. On this day the work of filling proceeded, but the proportion of salt was altered to lib. to every 2cwt. lqr. Illbs, of hay. When the work of filling was nom; pleted, over 13 tons had been put in, and flinches of bran were placed on top. The sinkage Was tilled pp et varioni times, and this brought the total weight of Mass to 16 tons llqrs. 2cwt. and 22Ibs. The total acreage mown was 5i acres, and the cost of filling, including cartage? mewing, cutting, Jac., was £l3 105. nd. In conclusion, a vote of thanks was conveyed to his lord- ship, on the vote of Messrs. Charlton and Deakin, two of his Lancashire tenants.

THE POSTMASTER-GENERAL AND THE WINSFORD LOCAL BOARD. Mr. W. Wynne Foulkes, county court judge, again sat at the Grosvenor Hotel, Chester, on Saturday, as arbitrator in the action brought by the Postmaster-General against the Winsford Local Board to show cause why the Post-office should not be allowed to erect an overhead line of telegraph through the district of the Winsford Local Board.—Mr.Cas- serley appeared for the Postmaster-General, an Mr. J. Eldon Banks for the Local Board.—The inquiry was opened at Northwich, when Mr. Doherty, superintendent engineer of the north-western district of the pest-office telegraphs, and Mr. Groves, chief engineer of the postal telegraphs, were called to show that the postal authorities were erecting poles to carry additional wires from *London to Liverpool, in order .to meet the increased pressure consequent upon the introduction offixpenny telegrams, and that all the authori- ties through whose jurisdiction the wires would pass had given their consent with the exception of the Winsford Local Board. The evidence on both sides was concluded at the previous sitting. Mr. J. E. Banks ranged his objections to an overhead line under four heads. First, that the nature of the locality was unsuitable for posts and. stays; secondly, that there was considerable danger from accidents by the posts and wires ; thirdly, there was an objection on the score of noise; and fotirthly, on the score of impeding the traffic. The main objection was the first, for Swanlow-lane in which it was proposed to erect the posts and stays was a thoroughfare in which there was only bare room for two vehicles to pass, and the—itays would be even a greater nuisance than the posts. He also contended that the Post- office authorities were not oven now in a position to ask for his Honour's consent, for the proposed position of each post should have been specified. He further pointed out that the property owners-strongly objected to the proposed route, and that there was another route available and E qual ly suitable at the back of Delamere-street, without extra expense to the Post-office. There was no reason why the Post-office short' d prefer the one route to the other. The Local Board made no unreasonable demand but were acting under the powers given them in the Tidegraph Act of 1863, and they asked nothing which was inconsistent with the public interests.—Mr. Casserley, in reply, submitted that the Winsford Board was under a ' delusion as to the powers conferred on them by the Act quoted by Mr. Banks. According to his friend's contention the Legislature in the Act of 1863 had regarded telegraphs as nuisances, and had passed the Act to protect the publie from nuisance. On the contrary, he pointed out to his Honour that this Act was an Act for enabling such work to be carried out without creating a nuisance. If his friend's contention was correct it would come to this, that no over- head wires could be erected in any district where houses existed and the property owners objected. The Act of 1863 simply provided that they might put up telegraph wire and posts provided they first got the consent of the road authority, whatever that authority was, and such con- sent had been obtained in rural districts, in districts mode- rately built upon, and in the crowded thoroughfares of the metropolis.—His Honeur reserved his decision.
