• RbNCORN BURIAL WJARD. - The monthly meeting of the Board was held at the Board-room, Cemetery, on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. Geo. Moss presided, and there were present Messrs. J. Handley, JP., T. Norman, W. Whittaker, Littler, and balkeld (secre- tary).—rne minutes of the Finance Committee stated that 1 1.53 15e. had been received for fees during January, and LS Ifs. had been paid for wages and sundries, leaving a balance of £45 2s. 10d. which had been paid into the bank. The minutes were adopted.—The SECRETARY reported that there had been 262 interments during the 10 months ending deanery 25th, against 328 in Lie coTresponding period of lest year. The amount of fees received for the same period was £290 16s. Bd., against £3Ol ss. sd. The Secretary read a letter from Mr. Beckett, Hartford, in which that gentle.. man sated that he did not admit any responsibility for the destruction of the palisading at the Cemetery through a building which be had erected. The cause was so entirely beyond man's control that he thought it was unreasonable for the Board to ask him to make the damage good. The Secretary was directed to write to Mr. Beckett, informing him that unless he commenced the work within seven days the Board would undertake•the work themselves and charge bimwith the cost.—There was no other business of public interest.

, - MYSTERIOUS DEATH IN A CHEMICAL WORKS AT WIDNES. Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner, on Saturday, held an inquest at Walker's vomits, Materloo-road, on the body of John Murray, 22 years of age, Who was found dead in Messrs. W. Pilkington and Sons chemical works on the pre- vious Thursday.—Mr. Richmond, Her Majesty's inspector of factories, was present and Mr. W. T. Husband, solicitor, watched the proceedings on behiflt of the firm.— From the evidence, it seemed that the dece.:sed lodged with James Smith, of 7, Water-street, Widnes, and went to his work at the ordinary time on Thursday morning. About 11 o'clock he was seen standing in the centre of the "still shed" by a fellow-workman, Michael O'Connor, who lives at 15, Victoria-street, and four hours afterwards the same workman found him lying dead in a hole in the main sewer lending from the works. He was laid on his face in the sewer, and water covered his bead and part of his hick. It was stated that the men were in the habit of using this hole, which was about five feet long and three feet wide, inste_ul of going to the closets, and the men had been warned not to do so on several occasions. The deceased's waiatccat and trousers were unbuttoned ; and Robert Camp- bell, of 5, William-street, Appletoo, stated that he WM of opinion the deceased had fallen when descending to a plank which was over the hole. His head had come in contact with some projection, and, being stunned, he had lain in the water until he was dead. The witnesses agreed that the acc.den: could not have happened if there had been a grid over the hole as the gases given off from the liquor flowing through the sewer was not strong enough to smother a man. —The Coroner, in summing up, sold the jury would have to say whether the occurrence was accidental, whether the dscxised contributed to his own tath, and whether they thought any blame attributable to 'anyone. It was quite clear that the accident could not have happened had their been a grid over the hole, but it did not follow that it was necessary for the employers to place a grid over it. In a pubic street it would be necessary that a grid should he over such a hole—the law would require it, and the safety of the people demand it—but in this case the hole was used for a specific purpose, and the workmen had no right there except when ordered to clear the sewer out.—The jury re- turned a verdict to the effect that death was accidental, and attributable to the deceased's want of caution. There was no blame attributable to the Company, but the jury thought the whole ought to be protected with a grid.—The Coroner said Mr. Richmond had instructed the foreman of the works to place a grid over it, and this would be done.

NO RTEI-WESTERN ASSOCIATION OF MEDICAL OFFICERS- VISIT TO WARRINGTON. With the view of inquiring generally into the sanitary condition of Warrington delegates from the above Associa- tion visited the town on Thursday last, and made a tour of inspection of various places. The party, who were under the direction of Dr. J. H. °mall, of Warrington, comprised the following :—Drs. J. Makinson Fox (Mid-Cheshire) pre- sident, F. Vacher (Birkenhead) hon. secretary, T. W. A.8.,M.8. (Bradford), G. W. Pettinger (Altrincham), Bar- nish (Wigan), E. Rayner. 8.A.,M.D. (Stockport), G. A Kenyon, M.B. (Chester), J. 'Rhodes (Glossop), and J. Corbett (Manchester). The associates assembled about one o'clock in the Mayor's parlour of the Town Hall, where luncheon was partaken of, and then for the information of the visitors Mr. T. Longdin (the borough surveyor) explained the map, showing the entire drainage district of Latchford, and pointed out that by means of ejectors the idea was to get as few outfalls as possible into the river Mersey, but to bring them all into one common outfall. The associates afterwards proceeded to inspect the pail system as applied to various classes of property in the borough, after which the Corpora- tion Works at Longford were visited alai the process fcr dealing with the pail contents was demonstrated. Sober. quently a visit was paid to the new hospital for cases of in- fections disease. Shonl's principle of draining applied to a , low-lying district (Latchford) was exhibited by Mr.

Long-din. About four o'clock the associates returned from their ex- cursion and adjourned to the Council Chamber, when the President (Dr. Fox) presided, and in addition to the above- named gentlemen there were also present—Dr. Hewes (Ashton-under Lyne), Dr. Hope (assistant medical officer, Liverpool), and Dr. McNicoll (St. Helens.) The assembly first took the form of a business meeting.—The Host. SECRETARY (Dr. Vacheri read a letter from the Local Go- vernment Beard acknowledging the receipt, on the 16th instant, of a memorial, dated the 14th January, of the asso- ciation in regard to the Public Health (Dairies, Sm.) Bill, and stating that the subject of the memorial would receive the consideration of the Board. Another letter was read from the Local Government Board, to the effect that they had received with satisfaction the expression of opinion in the letter of the 14th January on the part of the association with regard to the clauses on retail bakehouses in the Factory and Workshops Act, 1883.—The SECRETARY observed that it would be remembered the association ex- pressed their satisfaction to the Board in the efforts they mide in the introduction of the measure to which the last letter referred, and of it having passed, and they had I aysured them of their willingness to give effect to the pro- visions which it contained. (Hear, hear.)—The SECRETARY D,st read a letter from Dr. J. Mitchell Wilson, on behalf of the Yorkshire Association of Medical Officers of Health, easing whether they could arrange a combined meeting of the two associations again soon. The Yorkshire Associa- tion would be having a meeting in the third week of March most probably at Leeds, and he was wondering if the time and place would be suitable to the members of the North-Western Association to meet them.—After come conversation on the matter, the ' secretary was directed to make arrangements for holding the combined meetiag in April instead of March. This concluding the formal part of the business, the PRESIDENT said it was their pleasing duty to thank the Mayor of the borough for kindly allowing them the use of that room and the hospitality he had shown them during their visit to Warrington. Next their thanks were very much due to Dr. Gornall for giving them an opportunity of seeing the very interesting works they had inspected that day. Dr. Gornall was a most es- teemed member of their Association, and they were always very glad to see him, as hecontributed in a very interest- ing manner to their discussions, and they were exceedingly pleased to see the effect of his work in Warrington. (Ap- plause.) There were two papers to be read at that meeting, and his own paper was on the subject of water. He was like the well which was always dry (laughter) so as Vacher was a stranger to Warrington, and as the time at their disposal was getting short, he would ask Dr. Vacher .to read his paper first. THE PERIODS OF INFECTIGCS DISEASES. A very able paper was then read by Dr. FRANCIS VeicnErt On the duration of the latent period, the fever, and the infectiveness of the exanthemata and some allied diseases." br He divided his suject into three groups, which were illus- r-ated by a skilfully worked out diagram. The first group included small-pox. modified small-pox, chicken-pox, measles, and German measles. The peculiarity or feature If this group was that from the time the disease was taken until the commencement of the rash wee nearly always about fourteen days. The symptoms which preceded the rash of all these diseases only lasted two or three days. The period of the fever varied considerably from two weeks in small-pox to five days in chicken-pox. The period of infectiveness varied from about eight weeks in small-pox and about two weeks in German measles. The next group of the disease included scarlatina, diptheria, and erysipelas, the peculiarity of the noun being that the latent period was only about five days, the stage of invasion being also very brief. The reariods4 infectiveness varied from about seven weeks in st,htzpdhiosiedas, disease scarlatina to about four weeks in diptheria. The third group Tahpeeatirmanecebeotfwethene tinhcelcudatecichinYgtthol ndmuthmeptis;st rash or glandular swelling was about three weeks • the symp- toms previous to this were exceedingly severe and protrac- ted toabout a week. The period of infectivenesswassimir to the former—about a month. Dr. Vacher explained that the reason he had spoken of the these particular kinds of disease and no other, was the fact that it was of these which he was perfectly competent to speak as coming from hie own personal knowledge, and which were the only diseases that were admitted to the Fever Hospital. At the conclusion of the reading of the paper Dr.l McNicoes, made a few remarks upon it, and. said that Dr. Vacher had thoroughlY mastered the subject rii all its par- ticulars and details. He spoke of the varied period. of the diseases, whereas in vaccination they could tell the very day when the symptoms would make their appearance...-. The discussion on the paper was adjourned to the next taking of the association in Manchester, as was I,i so the reading of Dr. Fox's paper on "Water analysis.—The party were entertained at tea by the Mayor in his Worship parlour. The associates subsequently visited the Bewsey and Dal - lam Forges.

The troupe wis under the leadership of Mr. J. Leyland, and tke enter- tainment was much appreciated. The proceedings concluded with a representation of the laughable farce entitled "The Llayclock Barber."

WARRINGTON INFIRMARY AND - DISPENSARY. . ANNUAL MEETING. The annual general meeting of the life governors and honorary officers of the above excellent institution was held yesterday afternoon at the infirmary for the transaction of the yearly business. Mr. William Beamont presided, there being also present the Mayor (Alderman J. Harrison), Alderman Pickraere, Rev. S. Wilkinson, Captain Litton, Messrs Ziba Armitage o John White, W. Sharp, R. Dobson, John Tinsley, John Fairclough, Thomas Jolley, Thomas Birchall, J. R. Buckton (hon. treasuter), Joseph Davies (hen. secretary), and Dr. C. E. Richmond (house surgeon). The following members of the Ladies Committee attended: -Mrs. Armitage Mrs. Litton, Mrs. Pickmere, Mrs. Stubs, and Mrs. John Armitage, . 1 HOUSE SURGEON'S REPORT. The following report was read by Dr. RICHMOND :- Resident• Surgeon's Report for 1833.-Infirmary: During the past year the patients admitted into Hospital numbered, 147. viz ,99 males and 43 females. Amongst these were 10 deaths, the causes ot which were-burns 4, meningitis 1, com- pound fractured skull I, compound smash of legs 1, inkaries to thoracic viscera I,linjuries to abdominal viscera 1, strangulated hernia 1. In all, except one, of those cases inquests were held. The following fractures have been treated in the Hospital :- Skull 2, ribs 2, forearm 2, femur 6, leg' 25, nose 1, astragalus 1., ascalais 1, humeras I. Nine of these have been compound fractures. Only one dislocation (of the foot) has been treated amongst the in-patients. The following is tbe list of operations during the year :-Amputation of leg 2, amputation, of arm 2, amputation of forearm 1, amputation of hand (partial) 2, re- moval ot tumours 1, remova of diseased bone 1. strangulated hernia 4. old dislocation of thumb 1, parocentesis thoraces 1. parocentesis abdotninis 3, legation of arteries 3, aspiration of knee 1; total 22. It will be noticed that while the number of In-patients is less than last year, the severity of the nature of the cases has been somewhat great.w, as can be seen from the increased number of operations. The number of violent dea:Jas from accidents of a nature that defied all treatment is also seen to be increased. The surgical practice of the Hospital continues to exhibit cases of rarity and Interest; and lam again glad to report an entire freedom from cases of septic Infection incurred during stay In Hospital.- Dispensary: Those out-patients who have in the course of treatment become home patients, are not enumerated in the to lowing list of cases treated: Home patients, 443 ; out- patients, 1,617 ; a,cidents and emergencies, 630. Amongst these 116 deaths have occurred: January 8, February 15, I March 9. April 9, May 15, June 8, July 9, August 11, Septem- ber 7, Octeber 3, November 9, December 13 ; and the ages at which these occurred-under 1 year 39, 1 to 5 years 20, 5 to 10 years 4, 10 to 20 years 6, 23 to 30 years 6, 30 to 40 years 4, 40 to 50 years 11, 50 to 60 years it, 60 years and upwards IS. These statistics show no special feature of variation from preceding years, except, perhaps, that the number of out-patients and accidents has increased, the latter showing an advance on evea the large total of last year,. the succeeding numbers for the last three years being 460, 663, and 630. The following fractures and dislocations have also been treated among our out-patients :-Fractures: CLavicle, 11; humerus, 3; fore-arm, 33; femur, 1; nose, 5; scropula, 3; total, 56. Dislocations: Radius, 1; clavicle, 5; ulna, 2 ; humerus, 4; thumb, t; knee, 1; total; 14. During the past year the point• ing.and repairs which,in my last report report were indicated as necessary have been done, the committee having at consider- able outlay, and with multi personal supervision, carried out a great many of those very much needed improvements. New furniture and fittings have been pr cured to remedy the desolate condition of affairs necessitated by the previous want of funds. Structural defects have from time to time beep remedied, but these will of course recur with each =needing year. One matter which, however, I think calls for speedy 1 attention is the exceedingly defective condition of the chimnies throughout the building. not one of which Is free from the fault of smoking; in seine the down draught is so p,:eat as to render ' the rooms uninhabitab'e. The ward shim-les are as bad as the others-a very serious defect, causing grave annoyance to patients, whose state of health renders them unable to support it. . The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report and that it be circulated in the usual way, remarked that it was stated ih the report that some of the cases which had been treated had been very interesting. He could imagine them to have baen interesting to a doctor, but at the earns tiralt they must bane been a great trial to the skill of those who. had had to attend them. There had been 10 deaths during the year, mostly 61 persons who had been admitted when they were in the last stage of life. He thought the report a most satisfactory one. (hear, hear.) Mr. JoLLEv seconded, and the report was adopted. THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT. The TREASURE read the balance sheet, from which it appeared that the permanent income amounted to £5)13 6s 7d, annual subscriptions £341 5s 6d, donations £7B us sd, con- gregational collections £lB2 lOs 6d, the employes of various works £399 12s 3d, proceeds of working men's donned £6l 13s 6d, proceeds of annual ball £54 17s sd, and other items including £177 2s 7d balance brought forward, made the total receipts £1,828 4s Bd. On the expenditure side there were salaries £492 Os 7d, food for patients and servants £346 3s id. furniture, &c., £316 14s sd, transfer to capital account £2OO, leaving a balance in hand of £B5 17s. The Treasurer explained that the expenditure for 1883 was £1,543 as compared with £1,309 in 1882, the increase being due to the purchase of new furniture and matters connected with the house. The CHAIRMAN thought the financial repoit was a very satisfactory one. Notwithstanding the expenses of new fur- niture, &c., which they had had ordered on a previous occa- sion, they managed to keep their heads above water, and had saved something for the future. He moved the adoption of the accounts. Agreed to. -

Alderman PICKMERE then moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Buckton for his services as hon treasurer, and that he be elected to continue in office another year. As auditor he (Alderman Pickmere) had gone through the whole of the accounts, and did not find a single mistake.—Mr. BIRCHALL seconded.—Carried.—Mr. BCCICTON expressed the pleasure it gave him in satisfying the governors, and hoped he would continue to do as well.—The CHAIRMAN expressed a hope that Mr. Buckton would at least he enabled to lay before them as good a balance next year. (Laughter.)—The following resolution was next unanimously carried "That the thanks of this meeting be given to Mr. J. R. Pickmere for auditing the accounts, and that he be elected to continue in office another year."—A hearty vote of thanks was, on the motion of Captain LITTON, seconded by the Rev. S. WILKINSON, accorded the hon. secretary (Alderman Davies) for his services during the past year, and he was again elected to the office.—The SECRETARY, in reply, expressed his gratification at the fact of workingmen taking an increased interest in these works of charity. He remarked with pleasure upon the fact tkat close upon £4O had been contributed by the employes of various works, besides £6O as the proceeds of the workingmen's coucert. He thought that was a matter to congratulate Warrington upon, that these workingmen were putting their shoulder to the wheel of charity, and recognised how very valuable this one was. (Hear, hear.) He was rather dis- appointed that the general subscriptions did not amount to so much as they did before. Their annual subscriptions during the past year amounted to £341 5s 6d, and in 1882 they were £342 2s 64. That was a very slight -decrease they might say, but in those matters they were apt to think they notp o eerhwu t ahmi s oenygesst ttoh otshee whofact hadtha t bt eheenr ei nw at hs ought to grow high rather than grow less, but he could esohmabeitamofoguinvtirogf to the institution. Altogether he thought the statement of accounts was very sitisfactory, and with the transfer of £2OO to the capital account they would ask that meeting to instruct the Board of Management to invest £323 111 104 in 41 per cent. Warrington Water Works Preference Stock—a home stock in which they had great confidence. They might congratulate them- selves upon the progress they had made during the year, notwithstanding the increased amount of expenditure.—The following resoletions were also unanimously agreed to : ." That the thanks of this meeting be given to the honorary medical officers for their gratuitous services, and that they be elected to continue in office another year." "That the thank 3 of the meeting be given to the Board of Management, House Visitors and Finance Corn- mitteo, and Ladies' Committee, for their services.. A special vote of thanks was given to the Workingmen's Committee and those they represent for the handsome sums which they have subscribed to this institution during the past year, and that they be enceuraged to continue their praise- worthy labours. Reference was made to the interest dis- played in this committee by Mr Ziba Armitage.—The fol- lowing elections were made :—" That Colonel J I Black- burne, M.P., be the president; and that the Mayor of Warrington uekett A Q M • (Alderman J Harrison), Right Hon Lord Win- W marleigh. T H Lyon, Esq, the Rev William Beamont, Esq, Samuel Right,' Esq, William Charles Jones, Esq, and James Nicholson, Esq, be the vice-presidents for the current year." A vote of thanks to the Chairman, with the hope that 'Mr Baamont might be spared to preside over their meetings many years, concluded the business.

DARING ROBBERY AND ASSAULT IN AN EARLESTOWN STREET.—One of the most daring and ruffianly attacks which has been known in Earlestown for many years past was made on Friday evening last, when John Lindsay, 69 years of age, residing at 54. Houghton-street, was brutally robbed of about £3 53. "Old Lindsay" is well known to the people of Earlestown. fie is a dealer in tripe, trotters, ie., and rents one of the huts on the market ground, where he carries on his trade. On the night in question be was on his way home with his day's takings in a bag in his over- coat pocket. On crossing over the bridge in Bridge-street, three men commenced to attack him, and after knocking him down they robbed him of his money and made off with it. Though information was given to the police the men have not yet been apprehended, but it is to be hoped that the cowardly assailants will be brought to justice. EXTRAORDINARY CONDUCT OF AN EARLESTOWN MAN: TWICE Jcstriso INTO THE CANAL—What is supposed to have been a most determined attempt to commit suicide was made by William Wynne, a wagon maker, residing in Earle-street, Earlestown, on Saturday night It is stated that in company with other men. Wynne was drinking in the Ship Inn. Newton Common, when a dog, which he was teasing, bit him over the eye. Whether or not this fact preyed upon the man's mind is not known, Inn. Some shortly s oi n e after. m e n wards tie rushed out of the house without any warning and jumped into the canal close by the Ship find that thbatedh, e but tiheeftthe inmatesho awe were u s onlye - q immediately ran to his assistance, and the fellow was pulled out of the water and Conveyed to the house where he lodged, alarmed il e was to pfiunt in his shirt. A search was at once instituted for him, and it was discovered that he had again made his way to the canal and plunged into it. He, however, afterwards strug- gled to the side without assistance, And appeared to suffer but little from the effects of his double "ducking." It is stated that the man has since to work.

OPENING OF HOLY TRINITY SCHOOLS, WARqINGTO.N. The formal opening of the new schools in connection with Holy Trinity Church, Warrington, took place on Thursday evening, when L idy Greenall was announced to perform the opening ceremony. The evening's proceedings took the shape of a soiree, and there was a large and fashionable company present. Amongst those who attended were Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall and the Misses Greenall, the Mayor of the Borough (Alderman J. Harrison), the Rector and Mrs. Qaekett, the Rev. T. P. and Mrs. Williamson, the Rev. W. H. Williams (vicar of Padgate), Cancel Dodd (Stratton), Rev. E. C. E. and Mrs. Carleton, Rev. S. and Mrs. Wilkinson, Rev. A. Harrison (curate), Rev. J. Ward, Rev. S. Slater, Rev. Morley Stevenson, the Hon. Miss Elizabeth Patten, Alder- man Webster, Councillor W. J. and Mrs. Burgess, Major Hamilton, Mr. and Mrs. John White, Mr. Wm. Sharp, Mr. Thomas Morris, Mee and Mrs. John Hatton, Mr. Win. Owen, Mr. James Faircluugh, Mr. Edward Rose, Mr. John Hard- ing, Mr. Rowson' Mr. Richard Feirclough, Mrs. Willcocks, Mr. John Houle ale-. John Dun, rzc. The schoolroom was decorated with banners and a number of plants, and pre- sented a very pleasing appearance. Rev. E. C. E. Cmaturott opened the proceedings in a few remarks, in which he tirst expressed his regret at the un- avoidable absence of Mr. and Mrs. Peter Stubs, and Mr. Charles White, who were always reader to help them in any work they had ishand in that district. With reference to. the schools, he observed that possibly some of those pre- sent might remember that five or six years ago their Sunday school was held in a small room in Bank - sireet, and then they took it to the church, but there were many difficulties and inconveniences manifest in holding Sunday school in the church. Afterwards they secured the old Girtarelian Office in the Market-place, and they had gone on until they came to possess the present building. In the erection of that building they had an evidence of something that he had noticed very much since he came to Warrington, viz., that the townspeople had no cause to complain that their richer Mends outside neglected them altogether. (Hear, hear.) In Warrington he thought the working classes generally were not forgotten by their richer neighbours who lived round about, as it only required someone to go and speak to them in their behalf, which he supposed it was the clergyman's duty to do sometimes, and if the assistance sought for was considered fair and right be generally succeeded in obtainining it. (A ,planes.) They would agree with him that the schools looked very handsome, but the better guide was to take the opinion of the Building Committee, and when he said that that committee regarded them as perfectly teatisfacteryeand convenient in every respect, he thought the general public ought to be satisfied also. They would have to answer more than one purpose. They would have to answer the purposes of a Sunday school, likewise a day school, and they hoped also the pur- poses of the ordinary parish meetings, congregational tea parties, and such like. Speaking of voluntary schools gener- ally, he was glad to say that the efforts made to support voluntary schools throughout the country were in no way being relaxed. He Was reading statistics published in a newspaper the other day, which showed that although School Boards were increasing each year the volentary schools were increasing by re'far higher ratio throughout the country. He believed those who supported the volun- tary system ought not at all to be disheartened or to relax their efforts, because he eonsidered the time would come when the people would get pretty well tired of the School Board system. He supposed every man had his crotchet, end he had spoken a good deal upon this question of late, as he felt very strongly concerning it, and he should be sorry, indeed if the people were to become disheartened regarding the future of the VOlOntary system, Mr. Carleton spoke of the heavy rates wbieh the introduction of School Boards involved, and concluded his address by asking Lady Greenall to declare the schools open. (Applause.) Lady Greenall's appearance on the platform was greeted with much applause. In a few graceful words her ladyship declared the schools open, with the hope that they would be a blessing to the children in that part of the parish for many years to come. Mr. BEAMONT, in one of his happy speeches, proposed a vote of thanks to Lady Greenall for attending there that evening, and took occasion to refer to the liberal manner in which her ladyship had assisted in the erection of the schools. He did not think there was 'a more beautiful school in Warrington, end they. were greatly indebted to the lady who had contributed so largely to the consummation of that which they had so long wished and which they, had seen that night. He proposed that their heartiest thanks be given to Lady Greenall for her attendance there that night, and for the services she had rendered in the erection of those schools. (Applause.) Councillor W. J. Bunnuss, in seconding the vote of thanks, said that from first to last both Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall had evinced a warm interest in the schools. It was no secret that Mr. Carleton was encouraged to com- mence the work through the spontaneous liberality of Sir Gilbert Greenall, whose munificent gift was followed by a very handsome donation from Lady Greenall. The parish was now under an additional indebtedness to her ladyship for the very graceful manner in which she had opened those schools that night. There was no duty more im- perative on the Church of England at the present moment than that of educating the children of the poor, and it was well that the Church seemed fully alive to her duty in this respect. Mr. Burgess gave statistics showing the large sum of money spent annually in support of Church schools, and pointed out that the ratepayers generally were gainers in not having Board schools in their midst. He believed that se long as the Church continued to perform her work with the zeal and activity which characterised her to-day so long would she maintain her influence in the minds and hearts of those people who were loyal to their church and country. (Hear, hear.) Tha resolution was carried wsth acclamation. Sit GILBERT GREENALL (who Was garally greeted) re- marked that he could say with the most perfect truth that he stood their somewhat reluctantly, but he hoped. not un- feelingly. He cordially and heartily congratulated Mr Carleton on the fact that he had now almost accomplished his desires. He hoped the rev, gentleman would go on and prosper, and that God's blessing might rest upon him and his school, and that his ministrations in the district might extend God's glory and promote the welfare of those of his congregation. (Applause.) The REcroß next addressed a few observations to those present ceecerning education, and showed the practical in- terest the Queen herself took in the culture of the young. The MAYOR said the broad, and far reaching system by which in this country they could confer the blessing of edu- cation upon the whole population could hardly be over estimated; but it was well to bear in mind the fact that education was after all not so much the positive unmixed good in itself as it was the power of doing good and produc- ing good. That was often overlooked by those who made most strenuous and laudable efforts to raise the coming generation both intellectually and socially. They saw so clearly the need of mental development, and the result which it was capable of producing, that they very naturally concluded that when they had secured that for the young people who would in a few years manage the world that they had done all that was necessary to fit them fog their very important and responsi- ble duties. Education undoubtedly gave strength, energy, capacity, and influence, but there was one thing which it did not give, and that was direction. It enabled the future men and women to achieve great results, but it did not ale ways follow that they would be as good as they were great: The combination of vice and crime, the low standard of honour in commerce, and particularly in politics, proved it. The repeated triumphs of selfishness over sympathy proved it. The multiplication of new and complicated forms of deception proved it. It must convince every thoughtful person that the education so freely given and bestowed upon the young was too often used in t: o interestsof selfishness, cunning, and deceit, and might be n i indirect agent for evil instead of a powerful agent for good. However, they must not throw discredit on mental education, nor relax one single effort on its behalf. Power was always good ix its way, and when it was put to bad purposes it only showed most plainly that something else was wanted, and that something else was direction. Now, his belief was that the most probable place to find that direction which was so necessary to run along with education was in schools of r Se ea r mena , hear.) erectinge ar is. a) r that kind, where religion was not altogether ignored. (Hear, .LbsouHrti de Was proud rei g ,4t r. . Warringtonßearn 0 couldnt, si r boast Gilberto suchGreenall, n f Stubs, like theanlidot others contribute to purpose o of educating their future men and women, and where they would not only obtain a good secular education, but a re- ligious instruction in combination therewith. (Ap- plause.) The programme of the entertainment was as follows: Song, "Carrier John," Rev Morley Stevenson ; humourone song, Mr William Johnson; duet, "Howebeautiful is night," Rev T P and Mrs Williamson; song, Miss Riley; reading, " Pollie " (G R Sims), Mr Dun: song," The owl," Rev T P Williamson: song, "Golden love," Mrs Lyon; pianoforte sole," Mrs Bell ; song, " When the heart is young," Mr John White; reading, "The lifeboat" (G R Sims), Mr Dun; song, "My love has come," Mrs Williamson; humourous song, Mr William Johnson • pianoforte solo, Mrs Bell; trio from lolanthe," Mrs Williamson, Rev T P Williamson, and Mr John White. Each item was well pre- sented, and Mr Dun's readings were most entertaining, especially "The lifeboat," one of G R Sims's soul-stirring narratives, and which was delivered by Mr Dun with much power and pathos. The humourous songs by Mr William lohnson also deserve special mention. The evening altogether was a most enjoyable one. E. Warburton. A capital programme of songs, recitations, Ac.. was effectively gone through, those taking part in the entertainment being Mr. T. Nuttall, Mr. G. Warburton, Mr. Walker, Mr. J. OCCUPATION OF UNCERTIFIED HOUSES At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, before Colonel George McCorquodale, It. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkineton, and A. C. McCorquodale, &ors , Sarah Porter, of Poulton- with-Fearnhead, was summoned for allowing cottages to be occupied before they were certified fit for occupation.—Mr. Rawlings, sanitary inspector, of Warrington, stated that the defendant commenced building three cottages in June last, I and allowed them te be occupied before a certificate was eiven that they were fit for such.—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s. and costs.

ST. BITTTERIIA.RKET STREET • WARRINGTON • OPENING OF THE NEW PULPIT. Tnere were crowded congregations at St. Mary's Catholic Church, Buttermarket-street, Warrington, on Sunday last, on the occasion of the opening of the handsome new pulpit, of which the following is a description:-The pulpit is constructed entirely of marble and alabaster, to designs furnished by the eminent architects, Pugin Brothers, of Victoria-street, West- minster. It is needless to say that the design is in excellent I taste. A very striking effect has been produced by the elegantly perforated alabaster panels, surmounted by a bold moulding and terminated by a capping ef Anglesea marble. The balustrade is also of open Gothic work in alabasLer, and the handrail is a really beautiful specimen of Anglesea. Enclosed between two mouldings,of alabaster is a band of Victoria red marble in which in carved, in gold letters, the appropriate inscription, "Blessed are they that hear the ' Word of God and keep it." The work has been executed with great care and diligence by Messrs. Williams and Clay, of this town, who had previously made the marble altar rails, and reflects great credit upon them. It is a. work worthy% of the beautiful church for which it is made. The services on Sunday were of a very edifying character. In the morning Mozart's No. 1 Mass was rendered by the choir with full orchestral accompaniment, under the con- ductorship of Mr. B. Eccles. In the " Kyrie" the voices showed a weakness, but the " Credo " and " Agnus Del," the latter being one of the best pieces in the Mass, were given in a manner winch left little room for criticism, whilst the band Were well up to their work. The pulpit was occupied for tile first time by the Very Rev. IV. R. Woods, Canon of Newport and Minervia, who delivered an eloquent discourse from the words "Blessed are they that hear the Word of God and keep it." Those words, he remarked, were inscribed in-letters of geld around that beautiful pul- pit, and if they had been inscribed in still more brilliant characters it would have been well, because the words were those of God. Canon Woods showed the power- ful force of mere human words in exciting nations to rebel- lion, and of their tenderness and pathos in bringing tears to the eyes of the listener, and spoke of the power, above all, of the Words of God, from which the most abandoned and outcast of creatures could not fail to find consolation and joy. In conclusion, he asked his hearers, as they loved the Word of God, t contriblite liberally towards the structure from which His teachings were poured forth.—ln time even- ing Canon Wood again preached, and officiated at Benedic- tion. The music was exceedingly impressive.

div.p: STOCK AND SHARE MARKET.

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Feb. 11 14th) : During the greater part of the week the market 4 have been unsettled owing to fears of complications at the settlement, and consequently prices experienced further downward move- ment. As, however, toe account which ttfezretically is com- pleted to-day biz passed ff satisfaet 3rlly, confidence is, to some extent. restored and helped by some better returns of Railway earnings, a better tone has been imparted and values have rallied a little in some English Rails. Foreign Stocks are very irregular, and with only a moderate number of alterations In which dpanish, mar Ling about 1 lo wer, is the foremost. Egyptians fairly steady, the Unified I and preferred lower, but paira Sanieh is better. The other changes are not of any impogtance Mexican Rails keep having to announce decreased traffics (this week's being £10,2u0 down) and are, heavily de- predated again. They have been as low as 444, and after some rapid and severe fluctuations now stand at 48 to 481, or a fall of over 9 on the week Suez Canal shares are lower also. Miscellaneous investments have produced a mi,erably poor re- cord of transactions, and quotations herein are not altered to an zxtent showing positive leaning of these markets in either direction.

THE THEFT OF A PUDDING AT EanratsTowsr.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, John Hillocks, a glass-maker, residing in Gas-street, was charged, on remand, with stealing a dish and a quantity of tapioca pudding, the property of Joseph Shone.—Superintendent Jackson briefly stated the facts of the case, to the effect that on the pre- vious Sunday afternoon, after drinking in the prosecutor's house, the Old Crow lon, the prisoner picked tip the dish containing the pudding and wallrevi home with it. Informa- tion was given to the police and on the prisoner being ap- prehended and charged with the offence he replied, "I did take it, and I eat it too, and it was good, but a little burnt. I did it in a lark."—Mr. R. Houghton, J.P. : J he a relation of the family? Supt. Jackson: No, sir, but he frequents the place very regularly, I believe.—On the dish and the remainder of the pudding being produced in court, Colonel McCorquodale said: He has not finishEd it, I see.—P.S. Cornelius: No, sir. He wanted to after be was apprehended. (A laugh.)—The prisoner said be only took the pudding in a bit of nonsense. He pleaded guilty to taking it, but he had not the least intention of committing a theft or anything of that kind.—Superintendent Jackson observed that there was nothing against him.—The Chair- man said the Bench would take a lenient view of the matter. They had decided to fine the prisoner Is. and costs.

REINFORCEMENTS FOR THE SOUDAN. The Admiralty have engaged the following ships to con- vey stores from Woolwich to the Soudan :—The Justitia, 1,000 tons; the Dunluce, 1,290 toes; the Myrtle Branch, 1,800 tons; and the Lochard, 1,400 tons, all of them fast steamers ocommodious build. The Justitia is now at Woolwich loading with ordnance stores, conspicuous amongst which are the first portions of a heavy:siege train. The first shipload of ordnance will start about Tuesday next for Alexandria for orders. The Army clothing will be put on board the Lochard at Woolwich, together with shot and shell and a battery of artillery. The Lochard will proceed direct to Suakim. The Dunluce will arrive at Woolwich on Monday, and will be loaded chiefly with pre- served meats and other provisions, which she will convey to Alexandra. The Myrtle Branch will take the remainder of stores to Alexandra, there to await further instructions. A field hospital and a bearer company is now being prepared at Woolwich, and probably will be placed in charge of Surgeon-Major Evans' who; with Surgeon-Major Godwin, has been ordered to Egypt. The Central News understands that in the event of General Graham not being able to reach Suez in time to take command of the expedition for the relief of Tokar, the command will devolve upon Major General tke hon. T. C. Dormer, C. 8., who served as Brigadier General on the staff during the Egyptian Campaign, sod afterwards suc- ceeded Sir John Adye, as chief of the staff. Major Gen'eral Earle will take command of the troops which remain at Alexandria. ,The 2nd Battalion of the Duke of Cornwall's Ist In!arstry will be removed from Alexandria to Cairo, the 26th company Royal Engineers will accompany our expedition to Tokar. Her Majesty's ships Albacare and Express ware commis- sioned yesterday for service on the Mediterranean station. Her Majesty's ship Teddington has been ordered to proceed from Suez to Suakim with camels for service id the Tokar expedition. Intelligence received at the Admiralty yesterday states that Her Majesty's ship Euphrates passed Gibraltar yesterday en route to Egppt. Her Majesty's ship. Myrmjdon having completed her repairs and undergone satisfactory machinery trials, will start for Suakim to-day.

SIB LEOPOLD WeLINTOCK.—bir Leopold M'Lintock, the celebrated Arctic explorer, has been elected an alder brother of Trinity House to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Admiral Coil bison. DECAPITATED ON THE RAlLWAY.—Yesterday morning Mr. Flint' coroner for East Staffordshire, held an inquest at Stallington Crossing, on the North Staffordshire Railway, on the body of Prudence Wild, aged about fourteen, who bad her head cut from her body on Wednesday. Whilst in the act of crossing he line the girl was knocked dow'n by the engine of a passenger train and decapitated, one of her feet being also taken off. A verdict of accidental death was returned.

RAILWAY RATES FOE IRON GOODS.—.At the annual meeting of the Wolverhampton Chamber of Commerce, yesterday, the chairman announced that a communication had been received from the Great Western and London and North Western Railway Companies to the effect that they had withdrawn the reCently issued 90 per cent. increaes in the rates of carriage of heavy castings from South Staffo,d- shire tc theseaports, and they were also making reduc- tions in their rates for the cahiage of hardwares to the Con- tinent.
A BAILIFF BLOWN OUT OF POSSESSION.—AO extraor- dinary gas explosion took place yesterday morning at a gentleman's house in Ladvpool-road, Birmingham. From

home cause not yet ascartained a large volume of gas had got into the dining-room and become ignited. A violent explosion followed, wrecking the room and one adjoining, in which was a man in possession. He was ejected into the street, and received serious injuries which necessitated his detention in hospital, Much damage was done. BOILER EXPLOSION AT A NEWSPAPER OFFICE.—A disastrous explosion occurred, yesterday, at tb,e printing office of the Yarmouth Independent, by which the office was wrecked and two men injured. From some cause the boiler suddenly burst, blowing up the floor above. and scat- tering the machines, type,and other printing material in all directions. The windows were bloWn, but with two exc2p- tions the employes escaped injury. The foreman was much cut and scalded, the other person injured being a lad: IMPORTANT NEW IRISH LAND COMPANY.—An iMportaht company has been formed to put into operafion the provi- sions of the Irish Tramways Act by purchasing estates in Ireland with the object of relieving the congestion existing in some districts, and the establishment of an °occupying propriatory. The capital of the company is fixed at £250,000. The list of directors include Mr. Jacob Bright, Mr. Dwyer Gray, Mr. Parnell, Mr. Charles Russell, Q.C., Colonel Nolan, and Captain O'Shea. The services of Pro- fessor Baldwin will be secured as managing director of the company. The title of the company is "The Irish Land Purchase and Settlement Company (Limited)." Estates are said to be available at a remunerative price, and the present deadlock in the Irish land market will, no doubt, be taken advantage of.

div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

The Intestates Estates, Bankruptcy Appeals, and Matri- monial Causes Bills were read a second time.—Earl GRAN- VILER, replying to Lerd Ellenborough, said a large addition had been made to the police force in consequence of the number placed in charge of public buildings—ln reply to Lord Cranbrook, Earl GRANVILLE said the telegram from General Gordon would be in their Lordships' hands to-day (Saturday).—The House adjourned at 4-40.

HOUSE OF COMMONS. ERypr.—Sir H. TYLER gave notice to move an amend- ment to Sir W. Lawson's amendment, to the effect that Her Majesty's Clover ,ment at once assume the responsibility of directing the affairs of Egypt. _ . _

_ THE lama LAND ADL-Mr. TREVELYAN, replying to Mr. P. Martin, said the total number of appeals from the decisions of the sub-commissioners under the Land Law (Ireland) Act, exceeded 12,000. The appeals were being dealt with all speed, and the Government did not propose taking any steps on the-subject. THE SOUDAN.-••Mr. BANNERMAN, replying to Sir John Hay, ,said Sir W. Hewitt was invested with fall powers, civil and military, on' the 9th of the present month—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Sir D. Wolff, said the expenses of the Egyptian expedition as regarded the movement of British troops would be borne by this country. Tan VOTE OF CENSURE.—The adjourned debate on the vote of censure was resumed by Mr. JOHN MORLEY, who took great objection to the statements made by Sir R. Cross, with respect to recommending annexation in one part of his speech and repudiating it in another. Dealing with the speech of Mr. Forster, he contended that the right hon. gentleman was himself to some extent re- sponsible for the expedition to the Soudan. He thought it a great mistake to have sent Clifford Lloyd I to Egypt; and dealing with the reform of the Egyptian administration, he said we could do nothing whatever in that direction without touching finance, on which he tliciught Franca would have something to say. He insisted there had been two occasions when we might have with - drawn the greater part of the British force from that country, and not having done so we bad brought about a state of affairs that would be severely felt by the British tax payers for the sake of pursuing a policy which would do no real good to Egypt. He was strongly in favour of our getting out of Egypt as soon as possible, and altogether pposed the schemes of annexation in any shape or form. He, however, gave tbe Government his support, deol;ning to vote for tke motion of Sir S. Northcote.—Mr. A. flam-orn supported the motion, and accused the Government of inaction, in proof of which he said they had waited until there had been two bloody defeats before they summoned up their courage to direct with a strong hand, affairs in Egypt. As regarded the intentions of the Government as to withdrawal from Egypt, he said the matter appeared quite uncertain, because they told the country one ,thing and, to conciliate their Radical friend,they promised another. The whole policy of the Government had been in his opinion weak to a degree, and, retire when they would from Egypt, the Government would leave behind them anarchy, conducted on philanthropic principles.—Lord E. FITZ. maunicE entered into a detailed defence of the policy of the Government, and quoted largely from published docu- ments to show that the Government had taken steps with regard to the relief of Sinkat at the earliest moment, and insisted that the papers presented to Parliament proved they were not open to the charge either of vacillation or incon- sistency.—Sir P. Mrmenn supported the motion of Sir S. Northcote. Ho was of opinion that even supposing the purchase of the Suez Canal shares and the dual control were mistakes, that did not justify the blundering policy that had been adopted by Her Majesty's present advisers.— Pr. LYONS contended that the English Government were not responsible for the destruction of Hicks's army. [LEFT SITTING]

DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES AT HAYDOCIE. - The annual distribution of prizes to the scholars attending, the Haydock Colliery and Blackbrook Sunday Schools took place in the Blackbrook School on Monday evening. Mr. J. Jagger, of Haydock, occupied the chair. A number of recitations, meted ies, Sic., were effectively given by the scholars, and upwards of 90 prizes were presented for good attendance during the past year. At the close of the proceedings a col- lection was made in aid of the prize fund. TEESPASSINOt IN PITESITIT OF GAME AT HAYDOCK.—At Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last, Thomas Travers, of Haydock, was charged with trespassing in pursuit of game on land at Haviock, in the occupation of Thomas Alker.—The defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Moore, of Warrington* appeared to prosecute, and stated that on the 29th ult. one of Mr. Leigh's keepers, named Watkins, was on Woodhouse House, occupied by Mr. Al ker, when be saw two men, one of whom had a gun in his hands. On seeing him (the keeper), the men ran away passed Alker's house. Mr. Alker happened to see them, and identified the defen- dant as one who had the gun in his possession.—After evi- dence to this effect had been given, the defendant called witnesses to show that he was elsewhere at the time, but the defence was a very weak one, and the magistrates imposed a penalty of 108 and costs.
